Before you crank up the thermostat, try these tips to keep you and your home warmer for longer

BBC News Fri, 23 Oct 2026 23:50:45 GMT

As the UK braces for a chilly weekend, with powerful winds and heavy rain hitting parts of the country, people are looking for ways to bring some warmth to their homes without cranking up the heating just yet. It is autumn after all.

But with rising energy prices making heating homes more expensive, taking action now could pay off in the long run.

Experts warn, though, that if you're elderly or vulnerable you shouldn't compromise your health.

To help you prepare for the chillier months, BBC News asked families and experts to share their tips for keeping your home warm and cost-effective.

When it gets cold, many people turn to hot water bottles and blankets - but there are other ways to warm your body.

The British Heart Foundation recommends wearing lots of thin layers, rather than one thick layer, to trap the heat in.

Natalie, 29, says she's replaced some of the clothes she wears round the house with supermarket thermal leggings and tops and says "it's made such a difference".

Amber Waring, 27, from Devon, says she eats warm meals like stews and pasta bakes, and dances round the kitchen with her toddler while they cook to help keep warm.

With the clocks going back this weekend, the nights will be drawing in.

So if you have a thicker duvet, now is the time to bring it out. Some supermarkets sell winter duvets for under £20 - look for 10.5 tog or higher.

But there's something to be said for a craftily placed blanket, too. When it gets cold, Rebecca, 44, from Hertfordshire, sleeps with a blanket underneath her mattress, which she says stops draughts. "This was passed to me by my nan, she swore by it," she says. Others swear by placing a blanket above the mattress but under the bedsheet.

You can heat your bed before getting in with a hot water bottle, but make sure you check the expiry date. A guide by NHS Scotland says to let the water from the kettle cool for a few minutes before filling, only fill it two-thirds full, squeeze air out of the top before putting the stopper on, and don't hold it directly against your skin.

Using an electric blanket - to heat your bed before you get in or to wrap around yourself on the sofa - is "one of the cheapest ways" to stay warm, says Emily Seymour, energy editor at consumer organisation Which?. Testing by Which? shows it typically costs between 2p and 8p an hour to run an electric blanket at its highest setting. The London Fire Brigade says to unplug your blanket before you get into bed unless it has a thermostat control, not to use a hot water bottle at the same time, and replace it every 10 years.

Keep doors closed to trap heat in the room you're in. You can place curtains or blankets over your doors for extra insulation.

Embrace the daylight. "If it's sunny outside, open the curtains so the sun heats the room, then shut them when the sun sets to keep the heat in," says Rebecca.

"If you're using a hot appliance, let the heat into the room," says Lianne Macfarlane, 40, from Cheshire. She recommends leaving your oven door open after using it to help warm your kitchen, though this isn't advised if you have small children who could injure themselves.

As well as curtains, other soft furnishings like rugs can help keep a room warm, says Seymour.

If you have a fireplace, lighting a fire to warm the room you're in can be cheaper than turning on the central heating for your whole house. Elin Davis, 30, from South Wales, says her log burner is more economical than turning her heating on - though she added that "logs can cost quite a bit these days".

Gaps around doors can cause heat to escape, so place draught excluders around your door frames. You don't need to buy them - you can use towels or stuff socks into a pair of tights.

When it's a windy day, Seymour recommends looking for other draughts in your house and either finding ways to seal these spots yourself or calling in a professional to help. These include using foam strips, sealant and specialist chimney draught excluders if you don't use your fireplace. Things such as extractor fans and purpose-built ventilation shouldn't be blocked, she adds.

If your windows are single-glazed, then Sophie Burr of charity National Energy Action suggests looking at secondary glazing or investing in thermal curtains to help keep the heat in. Or for a cheaper option, some people suggest placing bubble wrap on your windows.

Even though it may be tempting, don't keep your windows closed all the time. Seymour notes that it's important to allow some ventilation in your house to prevent damp.

"I wouldn't recommend not having your heating on at all," says Seymour, pointing to both the health issues this can cause as well as how pipes can freeze over.

But there are ways you can use heating wisely. These include checking whether your energy supplier offers cheaper prices at off-peak times, bleeding your radiators so that they're more efficient, and turning your heating up in small increments until you reach the right temperature. If you have furniture in front of your radiator, then try moving it to avoid blocking the heat.

You can also buy dedicated radiator foil or make your own with kitchen foil to reflect the heat back into the room rather than losing it through the walls, says Burr. She points out that about 35% of heat that comes from radiators is lost through walls.

Cora Harrison, 34, from Wakefield, says that she only turns the radiators on in the rooms her family is using and keeps the heating on at a low level when they're on holiday to avoid mould or pipes bursting. Some radiators have a snowflake symbol on the valve that activates the frost protection setting, meaning that if the room gets very cold, the radiator warms slightly to stop the pipes from bursting.

Another way to potentially reduce energy bills is to lower the flow temperature of your combi boiler. If you book a boiler service, an engineer can do this for you.

You can also find free warm spaces such as libraries and community centres in your area by looking online or contacting the council. Some spaces also provide free hot drinks.

Household energy prices are set to soar in January, with a typical bill expected to jump by £276 a year, according to a forecast last month from consultancy Cornwall Insight. The 16% predicted increase would mark the biggest rise for four years.

Rising bills are "particularly concerning for people with kids, people with health conditions and the elderly," says Emily Jeremy, project manager at Manchester South Central Foodbank.

An estimated 9.4% of households in England lived in fuel poverty in 2025, according to the latest government figures.

Rodney Winchester, 65, from Thetford, who spoke to BBC News through the charity Christians Against Poverty, says he's "extremely worried" about rising energy prices. Because of health conditions, he says he has to keep the heating on throughout winter but is concerned he won't be able to afford it.

"It's so scary," Rodney says, adding that he's been cutting back on food spending and keeps getting ill in the cold weather.

If you are struggling with prices, the debt charity StepChange recommends checking whether you qualify for any additional support, like the Warm Home Discount and Winter Fuel Payment. It also advises contacting your energy supplier, which may be able to agree an affordable repayment plan or discuss support schemes.

Strictly's new presenters - after frosty reviews have they warmed up?

BBC News Fri, 23 Oct 2026 23:15:47 GMT

Strictly Come Dancing's new hosting trio received a very mixed reception when the latest series began a month ago. Ratings have dipped and the jury's still out, but critics say they are slowly getting into the groove.

Changing the hosting team on the BBC's flagship Saturday night entertainment show was never likely to be a waltz in the park.

And going from two presenters to three, and giving them slightly different roles, upset the show's rhythm even more.

Tess Daly and Claudia Winkleman were always going to be a hard act to follow.

Into their sparkly shoes have stepped the safe and smooth Emma Willis; the flamboyant former professional dancer Johannes Radebe; and cheeky comedian Josh Widdicombe, a wildcard who was not hitherto associated with either the dance world or prime-time TV.

Willis and Widdicombe have been paired on the live shows, where he is tasked with injecting humour into the moments before and after each dance - with mixed results, say critics.

Radebe, meanwhile, has taken over from Winkleman upstairs on the mezzanine, bringing his warmth and dance expertise to the celebrity interviews following each routine.

After they made their debuts in September, the Times' Carol Midgley billed them as "TV's most awkward ménage à trois".

The Daily Telegraph's Chris Bennion declared that Strictly's "new 'throuple' is an utter disaster", adding: "It's a mess, a muddle, a confusing pudding."

Metro's Adam Miller said their debut was "a triumph", however, and the i Paper's Sarah Carson wrote that Strictly had "played a blinder", even though the hosts "looked a little awkward as a three at times".

Widdicombe has come in for particular flack. He "felt like an awkward spare part" and looked like "the work experience boy", wrote Sasha Morris of the Daily Express.

And the Independent's Isobel Lewis said Widdicombe "is a problem the show needs to solve".

She believes things have now improved, although the show hasn't completely solved the problem.

"He's basically acting too much like a comedian to be a presenter," the freelance culture journalist tells BBC News.

"I think he's getting more comfortable with it. When it's him and Emma doing the bits when they intro each act, and they're obviously reading off an autocue, they feel way more confident there, and it feels more like it works."

The problem grows when Widdicombe does what comes naturally as a good comedian, Lewis says, and tries to be spontaneous.

"They've got, like, 20 seconds with each judge. It's such a tight amount of time, and that's what lends it to feeling sloppy and like he's constantly jumping in.

"Unfortunately it reads a bit like trying to steal attention and have the last laugh. I actually don't think that is what he's trying to do as a selfish act. I just think that is his comedic impulse."

She says it's unfair to put the criticism on Widdicombe, and says as time has gone on he feels less awkward, with comments online suggesting some fans are "warming to him".

"But at the beginning there's always that knee-jerk reaction of, 'I don't like this'," Lewis says.

Radio Times TV and podcast editor Caroline Frost agrees that the trio have gradually settled in.

"I think it's fair to say there were some bumps in the road in the first couple of episodes," she says, "but they do appear to be very slowly relaxing into their new roles."

When it comes to Willis and Widdicombe's double act, Frost would like to see more spontaneity, not less.

"They've been relying quite visibly on scripts and gags, and I would like to see them relax into themselves," she adds.

"It's completely understandable that they would be very scripted, very alert to the clock and to all of the other many demands of running a live show of that scale - but the really talented people can do that on the fly.

"Josh is very likeable, and we know he's a very funny man," she notes. "He doesn't need the shackles of the script that he's currently handcuffed to, and I would love to see him take off those cuffs and become more spontaneous."

Frost suggests sending Widdicombe upstairs to conduct the post-dance interviews instead of Radebe, who at times struggles to control his exuberant former fellow dancers. "It's a bit like when you get an internal promotion at work," she reflects.

The producers should make the most of Radebe's strengths and make him "a sort of talent pundit", she suggests.

"Have him in the rehearsal rooms, telling us what's going on. He would be a lovely middleman between what we're seeing on the dance floor and what is going on technically."

Ahead of the series, there had been reports that Radebe would be used as a "roving reporter".

Widdicombe previously suggested the trio's roles would be fluid, telling The Rest Is Entertainment it was "going to be like total football... We're going to be moving everywhere".

But while some segments are flexible - especially in the Sunday result show - their main roles appear fixed.

Some fans have been won over by Radebe since he took over Winkleman's old domain.

"JoJo has been really brilliant up in... I guess the Claudatorium, but I'm not sure what we call it now," says Flo Sayers, co-host of the Strictly on the Sofa podcast.

"He is the link to previous Strictly, and I think he has taken to that role really well. I like that he's a bit different from Claudia. He's less the comedian and more the supportive friend for the contestants when they've got off the dance floor and they're probably feeling a little bit vulnerable.

"And his fashion has been amazing, so I'm excited to see what he wears every week."

Sayers isn't sure whether the new line-up has contributed to lower ratings - about six million people are tuning in every week this year, down by about a million.

But overall, she believes that the trio are getting used to the demands of the series.

Dr Karen Wood, associate professor at the Centre for Dance Research at Coventry University, agrees and says the trio "are now really starting to feel a bit more settled".

"I think JoJo has transitioned beautifully from professional dancer to host, and obviously he comes with all his fabulousness," she says.

"He's able to talk about the technical details as well as be very supportive to the professional dancers and the celebrities. And his outfits are just marvellous. So I think he suits that role very well.

"Likewise, Emma is holding her own when she's with Josh and when she's not. She's an experienced presenter. You can you can tell.

"And Josh is bringing the humour. I know it's come with some criticism. But last week was the first week that I felt, oh, these two are actually funny."

She concludes: "It's really feeling like they're finding their stride and their rhythm with it. And I think that's going to develop more and more - very much as the celebrities do."

Just as the show's celebrity contestants improve week by week, the same may be true of the hosts - except viewers can't vote them off if they don't like them.

The next episode of Strictly Come Dancing airs on BBC One at 18:30 BST on Saturday.

Are California voters about to impose 'world's first' tax on billionaires?

BBC News Fri, 23 Oct 2026 23:11:31 GMT

Few places on the planet have as many ultra-wealthy residents as California, a US state known for glamour, coastal mega-mansions, and being home to the rich and famous.

Now voters are about to decide whether the mega-rich among them - including media mogul Oprah Winfrey, Meta head Mark Zuckerberg, Skims cofounder and reality television star Kim Kardashian, and filmmaker George Lucas - should hand over billions of dollars to pay for improvements to healthcare.

Proposition 40 is aimed at levying a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of all of California's billionaires.

There are a little more than 200 such individuals in the state - but that hasn't stopped the measure from dividing leaders and causing some of its ultra-wealthy residents to flee. One billionaire businessman says he's brought jobs to California, but the proposition made him feel "a little bit like I wasn't wanted".

But the vote is also offering regular residents a voice on an issue that has roiled politics for decades.

"I believe this is the first billionaire tax - meaning a wealth tax that is targeting a very extreme percentile of the wealth distribution," says Francesco Trebbi, a public policy professor at the University of California, Berkeley. He noted the measure's historic nature and how it could help even out California's wealth gap.

The state has the largest economy in the country and boasts the fourth largest global economy, bigger than India and the UK. And it is home to one of the highest concentrations of billionaires in the world. But it also has the largest share of homeless people in the nation and one of the highest wealth gaps.

Those who back the measure have argued it helps ensure that the ultra-wealthy are contributing their fair share and will help backfill gaps in the state's budget. The move aims to raise $100bn (£75bn) to make up for federal funding cuts to the state's health-care system.

Suzanne Jimenez, chief of staff for Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, which helped lead the charge for the initiative, says the measure is a "short-term solution" for massive federal funding cuts coming to California as a result of US President Donald Trump's sweeping tax and spending bill.

"If we do nothing, we're going to see a collapse of our healthcare system, while we figure out a longer-term solution to fund our healthcare," she tells the BBC.

While the ballot measure has many supporters - including some billionaires like Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang - it has faced fierce opposition from a variety of figures, from billionaires to the state's liberal governor.

Google co-founder Sergey Brin has given more than $100m to a political organisation funding ballot measures that could block the wealth tax, the Los Angeles Times reports.

California Governor Gavin Newsom, whose tenure is coming to an end, is perhaps the most notable political leader opposing it. He has voiced concerns that the measure could cause the wealthy to leave the state and drive out their crucial income tax revenue.

A September poll from the Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies and the Los Angeles Times found the proposition has not clearly won over a majority of voters, with 45% of likely voters in favour of the tax, 42% opposed and 13% undecided.

The statewide ballot measure would need to be approved by a majority of residents.

California is not the first place to toy with the idea of taxing the rich. Also on the West Coast, voters in US state of Washington are considering whether to accept or reject a "millionaires tax" - a 9.9% tax on income over $1m a year.

While wealth taxes were once a fairly common form of taxation in Europe, they have rapidly fallen out of favour and now only exist in three European countries – Spain, Norway and Switzerland, says Dr Kristian Niemietz, head of political economy at the Institute of Economic Affairs.

Niemietz believes wealth taxes are "more trouble than they are worth" because they cause administrative issues, suppress investment, lead to capital flight and, in the end, do not raise much revenue.

In the case of Norway, a local news organisation found that an increase in the wealth tax led to more super wealthy people leaving the country in 2022 than in the preceding 13 years combined. A study on Switzerland found that a 0.1 percentage point increase in a wealth tax reduced taxable wealth by 3.5%.

The California measure, if approved, would apply retroactively to those with a net worth of at least $1bn who resided in California as of 1 January 2026. At least six of the state's 200 plus billionaires have reportedly left California ahead of that deadline to avoid the tax.

They include Google co-founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin, venture capitalist Peter Thiel, former Uber CEO Travis Kalanick and Hankey Group founder Don Hankey.

Hankey, a Los Angeles billionaire who has lived in California all his life, told Forbes he left for the state of Nevada as a result of the proposed wealth tax.

"I think we've created a lot of jobs in California. We have a few thousand people working for us and we have a profit sharing plan. And I have to leave the state," he said, adding that the measure made him feel like he wasn't "wanted" in the state.

Meta chief executive Mark Zuckerberg told the company's board last month that he was thinking of moving his primary residence out of California over the proposed tax.

To prevent him from leaving the state - where the company is headquartered - Meta agreed to a new stock deal that gives Zuckerberg, whose wealth is estimated to exceed $200bn, even more shares in the company to make up for the billions he would lose if the measure passes in November. Estimates say he could owe as much as $12.5bn.

DoorDash cofounder Andy Fang, who has an estimated net worth of $1.6bn, has called the measure "stupid" and wrote on X that "proposals like this make it irresponsible for me not to plan leaving the state".

Meanwhile, businessman Tom Steyer, who ran an unsuccessful bid for California governor earlier this year, is one of the few billionaires who has said he would vote in favour of the tax. Steyer said that although he believed the way the measure was written was "problematic", it was necessary to protect vulnerable Californians.

Huang, too, has expressed support of paying the levy.

"I don't mind paying taxes. The more you make, the more taxes you pay. I'm okay with that," the Nvidia chief said in an interview with the BBC's US partner CBS. "I am the ultimate American Dream."

Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont, a vocal champion against income inequality, has campaigned in support of Prop 40.

While at a Los Angeles rally, Sanders said billionaires "believe, like the monarchs of the 19th Century, that they have a God-given right to rule".

"They have all the wealth, they got all the power, and who the hell do you think you are challenging them? Well, I think on November 3 they're going to learn a very powerful lesson."

Income inequality in the US is at some of its highest levels in over three decades, with the top 1% of households owning nearly 32% of all US wealth in the third quarter of 2025. It is also near historic highs in California.

Economic inequality is a concern among most Californians, with 72% believing that the gap between the rich and poor is widening and a similar share holding that state government should do more to reduce the gap, according to a statewide survey from the Public Policy Institute of California.

Trebbi says it is an "anti-elite, anti-system sentiment" driving the policy.

"This is really not about Prop 40," he says, but rather about trying to "re-balance the scale a little bit".

Correction 24 October: An earlier version of this article contained a graphic which incorrectly said median income in California was $288,000. This has been corrected to median household net worth.

The artist dropping her debut album after a billion streams

BBC News Fri, 23 Oct 2026 23:08:55 GMT

Releasing your first album is a big step for any artist, but for Jazzy it's one that's followed some huge strides.

The Irish singer and DJ has been streamed more than a billion times and worked with industry heavyweights including Calvin Harris.

If that's not enough, on Saturday she has her biggest gig yet when she'll be playing tracks like No Bad Vibes and Someday in front of a home crowd in Dublin.

For Jazzy, writing an album has always been in the back of her mind and now, finally, it's time to hit send.

She's previously released dozens of singles, building up a monthly listenership over 10 million strong, but Peace and Patience is her first full-length work.

"It's been quite a few years of creating some smaller projects," she tells BBC Newsbeat.

"That's given me enough experience now to feel like it was the right moment."

The 30-year-old, real name Yasmine Byrne, has been putting out music for more than five years and collabed with the likes of Sonny Fodera, Rossi. and KILIMANJARO on some of her biggest tracks.

Dance music has boomed in recent years, with Spotify previously telling Newsbeat that since 2020 the amount under-25s listen to the genre has grown by more than 73% globally.

It also dominated festival line-ups over the summer - including Radio 1's Big Weekend which dedicated all its stages to dance music on the opening night.

But artists in the genre have often moved away from albums, opting instead to release EPs and singles.

Jazzy has noticed the change, saying it feels "a lot different now, with people kind of siding with virality rather than quality of music".

"When I was making the album, I wasn't thinking about going viral or anything like that. I just wanted to make something that was true to me and sounded like a Jazzy album.

"I like to let things happen quite organically and I try to just let the music speak to me."

Jazzy is rooted in the Dublin club scene, starting her career as part of a group called Powerful Creative Minds in the city.

But as more and more clubs close, the DJ says there are fewer opportunities for artists to cut their teeth offline.

"When I first started going out, there was a lot more going on," she says.

"There was a lot more nightclubs to go to and it's very different when we look at it now, which is sad.

"There's definitely a home for dance music on the internet of course but club culture is very important and I think that's something that we need to keep going for sure."

Latest figures from the Night Time Industries Association suggest about 12 venues are closing across the UK every month, with almost 30% of the night time economy lost since the coronavirus pandemic.

"I hope to God that it doesn't disappear, the club scene altogether," says Jazzy, who describes a similar issue in Ireland.

"We all need to try and put a hand in to keep it going."

Jazzy's taking her new album on tour across the UK from next month, but first she has her biggest gig yet: Dublin's 3Arena in front of a home crowd.

Even after a Coachella set and supporting Calvin Harris, she describes this as the "biggest milestone of my career to date".

While she says fans can mostly expect her brand of uplifting records on the album, she says it's also more personal than her usual work.

She highlights one track in particular, Invisible, as a change from her more upbeat releases. It deals with a bad experience she had in the music industry, describing it as "like my first ever diss track".

"I hope [fans] learn a little bit more about me, because that was one of my goals with the album - to open up a little bit about experiences in life as well.

"So there's a little message from me in each song."

Tiny ‘solar flares’ recreated in the lab may explain corona mystery

New Scientist October 22, 2026

With powerful lasers and a tiny piece of plastic, researchers have for the first time emulated a violent process that may take place on the sun. The experiment could help shed light on why the outermost layer of the sun’s atmosphere is so mysteriously hot.

For decades, scientists have struggled to explain why the sun’s outer atmospheric layers – a region called the corona – are thousands of times hotter than the sun’s surface, reaching several millions of degrees. “It is as if the air grew hotter as you walked away from a campfire,” says Wei Sun at the China Institute of Atomic Energy.

Now, Sun and his colleagues have emulated some of the conditions on the sun in the lab and, for the first time, observed how tiny bursts of electromagnetic radiation, or solar nanoflares, could power the corona’s puzzling heat.

Advertisement

Sunquakes may be caused by weird beams of electrons from solar flares

Nanoflares are known to occur when magnetic fields within the corona abruptly rearrange themselves and emit energy in the process. But for this rearrangement to happen, the exact conditions, such as the shape of the magnetic fields, must be just right, says Sun. He and his colleagues investigated how these conditions could arise and ultimately lead to nanoflares. They fired four very powerful lasers onto a tiny plastic target, which produced a patch of plasma – a hot mixture of charged particles – about 2 millimetres across. This plasma was not an exact recreation of plasma in the sun’s corona but behaved analogously.

The team created plasmas in two different scenarios, once using a flat target and once using one with a wavy surface. In the second case, the plasma became unstable and the magnetic fields it contained rearranged themselves and ultimately produced a nanoflare.

This nanoflare made a big difference to the temperature of the plasma. It reached temperatures of 799,726°C, which was nearly double the temperature achieved in the flat target version of the experiment where no nanoflares occurred.

A similar process – instability leading to nanoflares leading to plasma heating – could feasibly happen on the sun, says Sun. In fact, the parameters that determined their tiny plasma’s behaviour matched those observed in regions of the sun where blobs of colder plasma “rain” down through the corona. He and his colleagues also completed a computer simulation that corroborated this.

Coronal holes allow more charged particles to escape the sun as solar winds, and on 29 January, NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory spacecraft spotted a vast new one

Rony Keppens at KU Leuven in Belgium says that these simulations support the team’s interpretation of the experiment and make for an interesting entry on to the list of effects that may be contributing to coronal heating. Coronal rain blobs really could lead to the kinds of instabilities that the researchers now spotted in the lab, he says. Yet, in Keppens’s view, the new experiment does not definitively resolve the coronal heating puzzle, as other plasma behaviours, such as certain types of waves in it, could also contribute to it.

Going forward, Sun and his colleagues want to upgrade their experiment to create more three-dimensional plasmas and use more precise techniques for diagnosing its behaviour. And they want to make their laboratory measurements more directly comparable to reality – for example, by using data about the sun collected through telescopes, says Sun. “It is important to check that the laboratory is reproducing what the sun does,” he says.

Physical Review Letters DOI: 10.1103/tmll-158c

Earth entered its ‘bad decades’ after dinosaur-ending asteroid strike

New Scientist October 22, 2026

Decades of chaos and destruction, filled with devastating earthquakes and tsunamis, followed the asteroid strike 66 million years ago that wiped out all dinosaurs apart from birds.

The long-term global chaos inflicted by the Chicxulub asteroid, which was up to 15 kilometres in diameter and struck what is now the Gulf of Mexico, has been revealed through analysis of sediments preserved on the New Jersey coast, thousands of kilometres away from the impact crater.

It has become increasingly apparent in recent years that the asteroid’s effects weren’t confined to a single, disastrously bad day, but instead lasted a lot longer. For instance, the deformation of the crust to a depth of 35 kilometres left the impact site hot for millions of years.

Advertisement

We could protect Earth from dangerous asteroids using a huge magnet

It is also now thought that in the shorter term, a catastrophic maelstrom of fire engulfed much of the planet as debris that was hurled into space rained back down on Earth, burning up as it re-entered the atmosphere.

“Earth’s ‘bad day’ is when the Chicxulub impact occurred,” says Kenneth Miller at Rutgers University in New Jersey. “However, that was just the beginning of the story.”

The asteroid strike unleashed an earthquake felt around the world that was between magnitude 10 and 11, creating tsunamis that may have been a kilometre high close to the impact zone.

“Chicxulub rung the bell of the planet, and then it continued to ring for decades,” says Miller.

Free newsletter

“These deposits in New Jersey change our view about how long organisms were exposed to extremely detrimental environmental degradation,” he says. “That’s a fancy professor way of saying shit was really bad for 20 years.”

The researchers took rock cores from multiple sites on the New Jersey coastal plain, more than 2500 kilometres from the impact crater, to study the geology in the area in the years following the disaster.

These cores show that sediment layers deposited after the fallout from the asteroid were mixed and remobilised multiple times.

Such reworking of deposits is only possible through large, ongoing earthquakes and tsunamis, says Miller. Possibly more than a dozen aftershocks, which may have been in the order of magnitude 7 and 8, were felt on the New Jersey coast alone.

Earliest alligator flourished in the wake of the dinosaur extinction

Miller and his colleagues say the cores recovered from New Jersey record the transition from the catastrophic moments following the Chicxulub impact right through to a longer-term disruption, a period they have now named Earth’s “bad decades”.

Another intriguing finding from the New Jersey cores is the presence of large quantities of kaolinite, which normally forms over centuries from weathering in tropical regions, but may have formed in just years at the team’s study sites.

This could have been due to the presence of vast amounts of fungi, which can accelerate the formation of kaolinite, says Miller. The team speculates this is possible evidence that, during the nuclear winter-like conditions thought to have followed the impact, much of the planet’s vegetation died, providing a veritable feast for microorganisms.

Top predators still prowled the seas after the biggest mass extinction

The team has developed a new timeline for the first 20 years post-asteroid, beginning with the extraordinary and dramatic events of the first day.

This was followed by dust settling back to Earth from the atmosphere, leading to near-complete darkness for up to three years, followed by nuclear winter-like conditions for up to 20 years and fungal proliferation. All the while, the planet was beset by aftershocks and tsunamis.

“New Jersey preserves one of the highest-resolution records yet recovered of the first decades after Chicxulub, allowing researchers to resolve environmental and geological processes year-by-year to decade-by-decade, rather than viewing the aftermath as a single catastrophic instant,” says Miller.

Craig O’Neill at Queensland University of Technology, Australia, says the team has presented a record that “lets us really unpick what was going on immediately after the impact”.

“This builds on a long compendium of work globally suggesting that the environmental and biological impacts of ‘mega-events’ like Chicxulub go far beyond the impact blast itself,” he says.

The Chicxulub impact 66 million years ago filled the sky with fine silicate dust, which blocked out sunlight and lingered for 15 years

Chris Kirkland at Curtin University, Australia, says the site records processes that operated over years to decades after the impact, rather than simply its immediate aftermath.

Annemarie Pickersgill at the University of Glasgow, UK, says the New Jersey findings provide further evidence for long-term seismicity also recorded in other regions of Earth.

“These [New Jersey] sites preserve a detailed record of the geological and environmental conditions in the decades following the Chicxulub impact, providing new insights into the aftereffects of a very large impact event,” she says.

Imagine a world without tropical coral reefs, a world nearly devoid of iconic species like elkhorn and pillar corals and sea creatures like the clownfish from Finding Nemo. That world could come to pass within 50 years due to humanity’s continuing fossil fuel emissions.

The IUCN assessment was presented at the biannual UN biodiversity summit now taking place in Armenia. It shows countries where they need to protect reefs by reducing fishing quotas and pollution, according to Valderrábano.

Scientists have previously cautioned that warm-water coral reefs are probably crossing a tipping point beyond which they couldn’t recover, but the IUCN warning demonstrates how quickly and massively reef die-offs could unfold.

The shallow reefs in tropical and subtropical waters undergird ecosystems that can include thousands of species of corals, molluscs, fish and larger vertebrates like sea turtles and sharks. They cover only 1 per cent of the ocean, but support 25 per cent of marine species. Up to 1 billion people rely on coral reefs for fishing, as well as for tourism income and for protection from erosion and storms.

Free newsletter

While small pockets of coral could live on after the collapse of larger ecosystems like the Great Barrier Reef, they could become too dispersed for the eggs and sperm they release into the water to cross-fertilise.

“If the population size gets so small that you don’t have another coral to mate with nearby, then reproductive failure will happen,” says James Guest at Newcastle University, UK. “That species is in what’s called an extinction vortex.”

Coral reefs also exist in deeper, colder waters, including around the UK coast, but they are much less biodiverse and corals there don’t form symbiotic relationships with algae.

Coral reefs on a remote archipelago shrugged off a massive heatwave

So far, only one shallow-water coral reef ecosystem has collapsed. The reefs of the western Galapagos Islands lost 95 per cent of their coral – the IUCN’s threshold for ecosystem collapse – after the 1982/83 super El Niño climate phase unleashed a marine heatwave, turning golden brush corals into white skeletons overgrown by string algae.

But since then, four mass bleaching events have devastated many other corals. These animals form a symbiotic relationship with algae, which live inside the coral’s tissue and provide it with sugar from photosynthesis. However, algae stressed by warming or polluted waters can give off damaging reactive compounds like free radicals. It is thought that corals temporarily eject the colourful algae in self-defence, leaving the coral a ghostly white. If the warming lasts long enough, the corals essentially starve to death.

All these mass bleaching events came after strong El Niños, and experts fear the current record El Niño will usher in another one. Regardless, individual reefs are now bleaching nearly every year due to global warming, according to the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.

Yet another mass-bleaching event could speed up coral collapse, since reef ecosystems don’t have time to recover if they are hit by more than three bleaching events within five years, says Valderrábano. “It would definitely reinforce that perverse loop,” he says.

The IUCN projection is based on a “middle-of-the-road” scenario with moderate emissions reductions. His research in the Pacific archipelago of Palau suggests corals there have been developing 0.1°C of additional heat tolerance per decade.

“But if we get a really severe heatwave, it’s quite likely that the increase in heat tolerance isn’t going to be enough to protect those reefs,” he says.

Some scientists have called for interventions like spreading sunshades over reefs or geoengineering clouds over the ocean to protect species like coral from the record current El Niño. But the best defence for corals is reducing emissions, says Valderrábano.

“The more we can do to reduce pressure on them, the better chance they have of using their natural capacity to adapt and recover,” says Guest.

Adults are often thought to be less creative than children, as we swap painting for presentations and sandpits for spreadsheets. But in a new study, children actually performed worse on creativity tests than adults – yet made up for it in confidence.

“We found that adults are actually more creative thinkers,” says Mathias Benedek at the University of Graz in Austria. “But children enjoy creativity more and are much less worried about what others think about their ideas.”

How to extend and improve your life by getting more creative

There is a popular belief that children are more creative than adults, he says, which may come from children having more time and opportunities to engage in creative activities. Yet prior research suggests that creativity actually increases with age.

Advertisement

These studies were often based on a single task, like imagining alternative uses for everyday objects, says Benedek. Taking a broader approach, he and his colleagues recruited 92 children (aged between 4 and 7) and 70 adults (aged 25, on average) to carry out three creative tasks.

First, they had to come up with as many alternative uses for a tin can as possible within 3 minutes. Then, they drew freely for 8 minutes, and in the final task, they had 8 minutes to draw an animal that doesn’t exist.

Five people who weren’t involved in the research were then trained to objectively judge creativity based on originality and whether the final result fulfilled the brief of the task.

In the first task, the adults scored 3.9 points, on average, out of 5, while the children scored 2.9 points. One of the adults imagined a tin can could be used as a “Halloween candy box when on (a) diet”, whereas some children imagined it as a rattle.

Free newsletter

In the second and third tasks, the adults scored 0.6 and 1.9 points higher, respectively, than the children.

The findings underscore how creativity draws on combining ideas from prior experience, says Wendy Ross at King’s College London. For instance, adults are probably aware of more animals than children, so have a greater variety of creatures to draw from when producing a fantasy animal.

After completing the tasks, the participants were asked questions like “How well do you think you performed the task?”, “How much were you worried/anxious to not perform well on the task?” and “How much fun was the task?”.

The researchers found that the children were substantially more confident in what they produced, scoring their performances 4.8 and 4.6 points for the free drawing and animal tasks, respectively, compared with the adults’ 2.8 and 3.3 scoring.

An experiment showed AI users had the most creative ideas when they used it in moderation – not too much and not too little. Columnist David Robson puts the finding to the test, and explores what we lose when we over-rely on AI

The children also reported lower anxiety compared with the adults. “If the purpose of creativity is to have enjoyment in it, to play and to be unfettered humans, then children are doing better at that,” says Ross.

But the two groups got a similar level of pleasure from the animal-drawing task. Adults may have liked that task’s specific instruction, which may have meant they worried less about being judged for their idea, says Benedek.

Regardless of the quality of the end result, people should try to be more creative for their wellbeing, says Ross. Engaging with the arts has been linked to reduced mental health problems and greater social skills. “Creativity, especially when done with other people, is really beneficial to your mental wellbeing – and you don’t have to score 5 out of 5 on a ranking scale,” she says.

Cybersecurity experts around the globe are racing to update systems and prevent the most disruptive AI-enabled hack yet discovered. A flaw uncovered in widely used code has made 70 per cent of websites worldwide vulnerable to data theft and defacement.

Government websites in France, Denmark, Finland and the Netherlands were taken offline as a precaution when the news emerged.

Will physics be the next field to be turned upside down by AI?

PHP is a computer language commonly used to power interactive websites, such as the content management system WordPress, which runs news sites and blogs; social networks like Facebook; and key reference tools like Wikipedia. The hack therefore affects websites, rather than individuals’ personal computers.

Advertisement

The issue actually involves two flaws, both found by cloud security company Wiz. They relate to how PHP handles errors involving memory: in certain circumstances, data can be left behind after an error, which can then be accessed by a malicious actor. That data can include private information, but it can also allow an attacker to run malicious code.

Every PHP version released in the past decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities, but the PHP Foundation, which oversees development, has already issued an update to overcome this.

The foundation didn’t respond to a request for interview, but said in a blog post that signs of the vulnerability emerged in 2024. Yet nothing was done. This is because there was no immediately obvious practical way for hackers to exploit it at the time, and because there was debate about which of several fixes was most appropriate.

Free newsletter

“We won’t pretend otherwise: the delay was a structural failure, caused by both the security team’s decision process and its lack of resources,” the PHP Foundation said.

In 2024, the flaw was thought to be impractical to take advantage of, but Alan Woodward at the University of Surrey, UK, says AI has moved the goalposts of what is possible since then.

“It’s actually very, very difficult to exploit it. It requires millisecond timing,” says Woodward. “The reason it was thought to be too complicated was it would have taken a team of people yonks to actually work out the right timings. But what AI does, it doesn’t go for tea breaks, it doesn’t go home at 6 o’clock: you can just set loads of them running and eventually they’ll come up with the right answer of how to exploit it.”

Wiz said in a blog post announcing the discovery that there are probably further bugs along similar lines in the PHP code base, which developers will also need to identify and rectify. Wiz didn’t respond to a request for comment.

Every time a new technology hits the internet, there is a battle between the rights of users and major companies. To see how this will play out with AI, columnist Jacob Aron looks to examples from the past

Independent cybersecurity expert Junade Ali told the Science Media Centre that two thirds of websites use PHP and may be vulnerable to this latest technique.

“The key long-term risk with these new vulnerabilities is that organisations fail to implement protections and update software, particularly in legacy systems,” said Ali. “The security posture of websites using PHP has dramatically improved over the past decade, but this highlights that this is an ever-present problem – particularly when AI agents are capable of remorselessly pursuing the goal of finding new vulnerabilities.”

Woodward thinks that while most large websites will have already patched their systems, smaller sites with less expertise and resources could still be vulnerable months or years from now. “There will be this long tail and you’ll find some surprising sites have not been patched,” he says.

AI has grown extremely capable in the field of cybersecurity over recent months, which includes working out how to hack computers and how to defend them from hackers, creating a destabilising effect that is yet to reach an equilibrium.

There is a growing backlash against the way AI companies have gone about tackling mathematical problems – and now some mathematicians are opting to avoid AI altogether

In April, news broke of an unreleased AI model created by Anthropic called Mythos, which the company had kept under wraps because it had been found to be extremely good at hacking. The news sparked panic among cybersecurity experts. NHS England pulled its open-source projects, for instance, over fears Mythos may scour code for flaws and exploit its systems.

Three months later, OpenAI admitted one of its prototype models had escaped a testing environment and hacked another company, Hugging Face. Not to be outdone, Anthropic announced within days that its Claude model had gone rogue and broken into machines at other companies on three occasions.

We even learned from the National Cyber Security Centre, the UK government department tasked with securing the nation’s IT infrastructure, that the country’s four main cyber adversaries – Russia, China, North Korea and Iran – are using AI to boost their ability to perform “relentless” attacks on the UK.

A personalised mRNA vaccine for melanoma, the deadliest form of skin cancer, is expected to be approved for use in the US, Europe and the UK next year. The vaccine is designed to stimulate immune responses against genetic mutations that are unique to an individual’s cancer. When used alongside standard treatment in a late-stage trial, it substantially cut the risk of cancer recurrence or death within the next two years.

“I think approval could be quick, and next year sounds reasonable,” says Alan Melcher at the Institute of Cancer Research in London, who wasn’t involved in the trial.

“It is a huge deal,” says Rebecca Lee at the University of Manchester, UK, who also wasn’t involved. Thousands of people in the UK alone could benefit from this, based on the trial’s patient population, she says. “It’s highly likely the US and Europe [including the UK] will approve it next year.” However, producing the vaccine is very expensive, and it may not be deemed cost-effective for use on the UK’s National Health Services (NHS), she says.

Advertisement

In August, drug-maker Moderna announced that the vaccine had positive results in a late-stage trial. More specific findings have now been released.

The trial recruited more than 1100 adults who had surgery to remove high-risk melanomas that were likely to recur or spread to distant sites. In the UK, 19,400 melanoma cases are diagnosed annually, of which about 25 per cent are deemed high risk.

Two-thirds of the participants were randomly assigned to receive a bespoke vaccine on top of standard immunotherapy, called pembrolizumab, which helps the immune system find and destroy cancer. Both were delivered every three weeks for up to a year. The remaining participants received placebo injections plus pembrolizumab.

The vaccine is made by genetically sequencing a small sample of a person’s cancer and comparing that sequence with the DNA in the individual’s healthy blood cells. This enables researchers to pinpoint mutations specific to the cancer.

Free newsletter

Based on the same technology used in covid-19 vaccines, the cancer vaccine contains mRNA molecules that encode for proteins with up to 34 of those mutations. “The jab contains a fingerprint of proteins specifically associated with the cancer,” says Lee. “This helps [immune] T-cells recognise the cancer better, and then pembrolizumab prevents those T-cells from becoming exhausted once they’ve started attacking the cancer cells.”

About two years after the start of treatment, 82 per cent of the participants who received the vaccine plus pembrolizumab were alive without their cancer recurring, on average, compared with 70 per cent among those on pembrolizumab alone. “It’s a really exciting result,” says Lee. Side effects were similar between the two groups.

The results combine cancer recurrence and death rates into one figure, but since a treated cancer has to recur for it to cause death, this combined measure should be interpreted mostly as a sign of the vaccine reducing recurrence, says Melcher. The participants haven’t been tracked for long enough to robustly determine whether the vaccine improves survival rates. These results should be available within a few years, says Lee.

We have long treated cancer based on its location in the body. But a whole new approach that analyses tumours differently is now helping people survive forms of cancer that were once considered a death sentence

But because the vaccine has to be tailored to and manufactured for each individual, it is expected to be very costly, which could affect NHS access. “If it was a cheap drug, I’d definitely say it will get approved [for NHS use], but it’s going to be expensive,” says Lee. In January, a report by Reuters suggested it would cost around $200,000 per treatment. Moderna and Merck (also known as MSD), which was also involved in the vaccine’s development, did not respond to a request about its cost.

Further research is needed to better understand who is mostly likely to benefit from the vaccine, says Melcher. Some people may have mutations included in their vaccine that fail to stimulate anti-cancer immunity as predicted, or pembrolizumab could work so well that the vaccine can’t lead to further improvement. “If we can find immune markers in the blood or tumour that predict patient responses, we could use those to determine who to give the jab to,” says Melcher.

James Larkin, also at the Institute of Cancer Research, says personalised vaccines could also work for other types of cancer, such as those affecting the lungs, bladder and kidneys, which are also routinely treated with immunotherapy. Body temperature may drive the higher risk of autoimmune conditions in women

New Scientist October 23, 2026

The menstrual cycle and menopause mean that women’s body temperature fluctuates more than men’s, which could help explain why they are much more likely to develop autoimmune conditions. Our body temperature influences our immune response, and frequent fluctuations in women could affect their immune cells’ ability to differentiate between a dangerous invader and healthy tissue.

“If women’s immune cells are experiencing more changes in temperature, they might be getting more overwhelmed and dysfunctional, which could contribute to an increased risk of autoimmunity,” says Elizabeth Maloney at the Pasteur Institute in Paris, who presented the findings at the Immunology of the Exposome conference at the Royal Society in London on 12 October. “It could be one piece of the puzzle in understanding sex differences in immunity.”

We may finally have a cure for many different autoimmune conditions

Women generally mount stronger immune responses than men, making them less prone to infections. But this comes at a cost: women are up to four times more likely to develop autoimmune conditions, such as lupus or rheumatoid arthritis, which occur when the immune system overreacts to healthy tissue.

Advertisement

Such differences are due to several factors, including the genetics that determine sex. Most women have two copies of the X chromosome, which carries many immune genes, whereas most men have one X and one Y chromosome. This means women have greater genetic variation, strengthening their immune response.

Hormonal differences also play a role. Oestrogen, the main sex hormone in women, generally bolsters immune system activity in those of reproductive age, while declining levels during perimenopause and menopause seem to accelerate inflammation, which plays a big role in autoimmunity. Men’s main sex hormone, testosterone, generally reduces inflammation.

Now, Maloney and her colleagues have looked at the role of body temperature. They measured the core body temperatures of more than 900 adults, aged between 20 and 69, via a thermometer in the inner ear. The group was made up of a roughly equal number of men and women, none of whom had a known autoimmune condition.

Free newsletter

The researchers also collected blood samples, which they exposed to a powerful immune-stimulating protein from Staphylococcus aureus bacteria in a test tube.

The one-off temperature readings were similar between the men and women. But among the women’s blood samples, a higher body temperature was linked to suppression of T-cells in response to the protein. T-cells are part of the adaptive immune system, which responds to threats like viruses or – inappropriately – to molecules in the body. The latter response can bring about autoimmune conditions.

Among the women’s samples, the researchers found that every 1°C (1.8°F) increase in body temperature was linked to a 36 per cent decrease in these cells’ ability to produce interferon-gamma. This is an inflammatory protein that enhances the ability of T-cells to attack target cells, whether they are healthy or infected.

“This may be counterintuitive because we generally think of fever as stimulating inflammation,” says team member Darragh Duffy, also at the Pasteur Institute. But it seems there is also a mechanism by which high temperature can dial down the immune response to stop it getting out of hand, he says.

One interpretation of the sex differences in the results is that the more frequent temperature fluctuations experienced by women caused their T-cells to switch between suppressed and activated states more often, says Maloney.

Antibodies mistakenly attacking the brain are linked with conditions including schizophrenia, dementia and OCD, prompting a revolution in how we think about mental health conditions

The core body temperature of premenopausal women rises by about 0.6°C (around 1°F), on average, after ovulation, then falls a day or two before menstruation. Perimenopause and menopause can also cause sudden increases in body temperature, manifesting as hot flushes. “Maybe the adaptive immune system is having to constantly change its set point, which sort of wears it out, and then that contributes to autoimmune risk,” says Maloney.

“The findings add another dimension to sex differences in immune function,” says Sabra Klein at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore. Future studies should examine whether body temperature affects immune responses between men and women independently of their hormonal differences, she says.

They could also track links between the menstrual cycle, body temperature and T-cell response, says Maloney. For now, the team is working with another group of researchers to implement body-temperature measurements in a vaccine trial starting next year, she says.

Why do mathematicians keep proving things they already know?

New Scientist October 23, 2026

Earlier this month, I wrote a story about how OpenAI had inadvertently produced two versions of its proof of the Navier-Stokes problem. You can read the details here, but one thing that has stuck with me is that some non-mathematically minded people I spoke to about the story struggled with the idea that two different proofs of the same problem could both be correct. It got me thinking about how and why mathematicians prove things multiple times – and what happens when it goes wrong.

One thing it’s important to grasp is that proofs are not homework problems. A couple of mathematicians have made this point to me recently: because most people’s experience of maths begins and ends at school, there is a perception that mathematicians are simply working down a big list of problems and writing answers to be ticked off by some sort of cosmic maths teacher. This is not the case – proofs are a way of organising and developing mathematical thinking. You can think of a proof as a journey, from statement to conclusion – and as with many journeys, there are many routes you can take to get from A to B. This is where we get multiple proofs of the same problem.

Terence Tao’s Six Maths Essentials opens his field to all of us

This act of reproving, of taking the mathematical road not yet travelled, dates back to antiquity. One of the earliest examples is the statement that an isosceles triangle always has two equal sides and two equal angles at the base. Writing around 350 BC, Aristotle describes a proof of this that involves drawing lines from the centre of a circle to its circumference – the original author of that proof is lost. Around 50 years later, Euclid described a proof that only requires triangles, not circles. This neatly avoided a mathematical disagreement about how to define angles formed between a straight line and a curved line – a question that wasn’t settled for thousands of years, as it happened.

Advertisement

Euclid also crops up in another example that shows how useful it is to keep attacking “solved” problems. He recorded a proof that there are infinitely many primes, and you may have learnt it at school. Suppose you have a finite list of primes. If you multiply them all together, you get a new number, P. Now, define q = P + 1. If q is prime, it can’t have been on the list, because it is bigger than P. If q isn’t, it must instead be divisible by a prime, as all non-primes are. If that prime we divide by had been on the list, it must also divide P, but that must also mean it divides q – P = 1, which is impossible. Either way, we have identified a prime not on the original list.

According to a 2023 survey, they are now 200 different proofs of Euclid’s theorem, as it is known. One that particularly added to mathematical knowledge at the time was published by Leonhard Euler in 1737, who found a formula that related the sum of all numbers to the product of all primes. He also used this to hint at the structure of the primes – not only that there are infinitely many, but that they become sparser as you go up the number line. Euler’s formula inspired Bernard Riemann over a century later to propose the Riemann hypothesis, a deep question about the structure of prime numbers that is considered one of the greatest unsolved mysteries in maths today – so it was well worth Euler having another crack at Euclid.

Perhaps surprisingly, there are even times when mathematicians have produced multiple proofs of the same theorem before revealing a flaw in the reasoning. In 1933, mathematician Wilhelm Grunwald published a proof showing that a number, a, with a certain property in relation to all prime numbers, must always be able to be written as some other number, x, raised to the nth power, so a = xn. A second mathematician, George Whaples, gave a new proof of this using slightly different maths in 1942. But then in 1948, Shianghao Wang found that actually, this isn’t true for 16, because 16 isn’t equal to x8 for any x. The correct result is now known as the Grunwald-Wang theorem.

Hannah Fry: How OpenAI has caused an existential crisis in mathematics

Pleasingly, researchers have even studied the idea of taking proof journeys mathematically. In a 2022 paper, Scott Viteri at Stanford University and Simon DeDeo at Carnegie Mellon University in Pennsylvania point out that if a mathematical proof is a sequence of logical steps, each with a tiny probability of a mistake, the odds are that a long enough proof is more likely to be wrong than not. Roll enough times, and the dice will be extremely likely to land on a 1. How then can mathematicians prove anything?

The pair show that a mathematical proof is structured like a network, with “truth” being transmitted along paths between each step, exactly like a journey. With the potential for error at each step, the strength of this truth diminishes along longer paths. But proofs aren’t random walks around a conceptual arena – they have structure, and claims are often reinforced by multiple routes. This structure allows truth to be transmitted along the strongest paths, even if it fails along other routes. Because of this, the network undergoes what the pair call an “epistemic phase transition”, a scenario under which you can be extremely certain the proof is correct.

This is just a model, and not necessarily something accepted by all mathematicians, but I find it appealing. It also fits with what you would naturally expect: the more proofs mathematicians have of a result, the more paths that are carved from A to B, the more certain you can be that it is true. In an age when AI is beginning to produce maths that humans don’t necessarily understand, we might find that having multiple routes to the truth, whether human or AI derived, can bring confidence where we might otherwise have uncertainty.

It came as Luxon and National have used the resignation of Labour candidate Kerrin Leoni over campaigning at a gang event to attack Labour’s record on law and order.

Labour is scheduling a visit to Starship children’s hospital to discuss staffing shortages, despite Hipkins saying such a visit would be inappropriate during an election campaign.

Luxon has introduced his 100 day plan of 26 actions a National-led government would prioritise.

“It's not exhaustive but it is very comprehensive,” Luxon said of his plan, saying the items were critical to safer and wealthier future for New Zealand.

Luxon then pitched to the roughly 100 people the alternative, being a Labour-led Government.

He went on the attack, focusing heavily on the controversy surrounding politicians like resigned Labour candidate Kerrin Leoni being captured campaigning at gang events.

Luxon referred to the matter several times, asking the crowd how they could trust Chris Hipkins on Labour’s promises being fully funded given he had been hit by such a saga.

Luxon confirmed he and wife Amanda will be voting tomorrow.

Christopher Luxon is now speaking, reiterating his comments that the election would be “incredibly tight”. He then went on to laud the Government’s economic record as well as its efforts in crime and education.

“Things haven't been easy but the plan is working.”

National East Coast Bays MP Erica Stanford spoke at her party rally at Northcross Intermediate School in Browns Bay, Auckland.

National leader Christopher Luxon is also speaking at the rally this morning.

Stanford was joined by an array of National candidates, including deputy leader Nicola Willis, Mark Mitchell, Emma Chatterton, Jess Rowe, Greg Fleming, Carlos Cheung, Rima Nahkle, Mahesh Muralidhar, Paul Goldsmith, Dan Bidois, Cameron Brewer as well as party president Sylvia Wood.

Stanford gave quite the speech, lauding the work of her National colleagues in Government, such as Mitchell’s efforts targeting gangs and Chris Bishop’s work in infrastructure and RMA. At one point, Willis stood up and proclaimed, “Here’s to Erica Stanford” as she spoke of education.

National has announced the 26 actions it will pursue in its first 100 days if re-elected to Government.

The plan includes introducing National’s Kiwisaver changes, locking in no new taxes, passing the rates cap, extending paid parental leave, widening access to 5% deposits for first home buyers, boosting Pharmac funding for cancer and life-changing medicines, and establishing an Auckland Transport Police Team.

National leader Christopher Luxon said the party has a plan "for a more secure future with a growing economy".

“Kiwis have done the hard yards over the past three years and our plan is working, with the economy growing faster than Australia and the UK, inflation and interest rates down from the record highs reached under Labour, kids back in school and learning the basics, and safer streets with fewer victims of crime," Luxon said.

He added that this is a "positive plan to grow the economy".

Act leader David Seymour thinks New Zealand is divided by race and that has put a strain on the country’s progress and productivity. He also has no issue with Māori customary rights in ‘specific instances’ and upholds property rights in general. Are these two stances compatible?

David Seymour has no issue with Māori customary rights - just ‘activist’ judges

New Zealand Herald October 24, 2026

Act leader David Seymour thinks New Zealand is divided by race and that has put a strain on the country’s progress and productivity. He also has no issue with Māori customary rights in ‘specific instances’ and upholds property rights in general. Are these two stances compatible?

It raised more than a few eyebrows during the second multiparty debate when David Seymour pushed his party’s policy on constitutional reform as his next big move.

Race relations, essentially. Not lower taxes, or a much smaller government, or a market freer from regulation, though these are also Act policies.

Asked why, Seymour told the Herald the question was framed around his success with legalising euthanasia, but added that he would give the same answer if he had another chance.

“If you look at the real challenges we have – passing knowledge from one generation to the next, raising productivity, building homes cheaper, getting more infrastructure built – a lot of the challenges stem from this insecurity about who we are as a country.

“If you look at the resource management law, one of the most frequent challenges we run into is that the Crown would not be upholding its obligations to the Treaty [of Waitangi].”

Consider what would happen if the Crown claimed that it owned water, he said.

“Immediately there would be a dispute of whether the Crown has the right to assert that. If you can’t have secure property rights over who owns the thing, then it’s very difficult for people to plan or invest in that thing.”

The same issue might arise over genetic modification, he said.

“Are these genetics a taonga [treasure/resource] according to the Treaty? We’re talking not just about whether this is good for people in general, but whether it’s somehow good for a different type of people.

“Almost every topic, you run into these issues.”

Scrapping this approach is one of the aims of Act’s “one law for all” policy, which would:

This is Seymour’s follow-up to the Treaty Principles Bill, which was defeated this term at the second reading.

He believes the policy package would entrench universal rights and legal certainty in a way that, thanks to “judicial activism”, doesn’t exist. This would help tear down those barriers, for example in resource management or genetic modification, and ultimately help boost productivity.

The counter to this is that Māori rights to taonga are a property right Act should be upholding, while Māori engagement in decisions that affect them is guaranteed under the Treaty.

The former is a matter of British colonial common law, while the latter is the application of article two of the Treaty: tino rangatiratanga (self-determination).

“The Treaty recognises property, but any property rights that Māori may have, such as foreshore and seabed or the looming question over freshwater, those are questions of common law property ownership,” University of Otago law professor Andrew Geddis said.

“The common law position in 1840 was that the laws of that country continue to exist and apply: ‘We will continue to recognise the property of the people who were here beforehand and won’t just take it off them’.”

The application of tino rangatiratanga has been a matter for Parliament, rather than the courts, he said.

“The courts didn’t order the Crown to put rights to consultation into the Resource Management Act. The courts may have recognised that, under the Treaty, there are certain rights for Māori to be engaged with.

“But giving legal force to those rights has been a choice by governments to include in legislation.”

Seymour said he had no issue with indigenous customary rights, pointing to the Ngāti Apa court case in 2003 that sparked the foreshore and seabed furore.

“That was under an English legal system that those rights were discovered. I don’t have a problem with that,” he said.

“I do have a problem with the way that [the] Ngāti Apa [issue], through the Foreshore and Seabed Act and then the Marine and Coastal Area Act [Maca], has metastasised and been interpreted incredibly widely by the courts.

“We’re into the common law and property rights. But that’s not what the courts have been doing for the last 20 years or so.”

Perceived judicial overreach is why the coalition Government made changes to the Maca, supposedly restoring it to its original intent; this is vehemently disputed by the National minister behind the 2011 law, Chris Finlayson, who said the Government has undermined it.

Any government can, of course, change the law if it doesn’t like a court’s ruling, or how Treaty principles are being applied, or the common law regarding customary rights.

This is what Act tried, and failed, to do with the Treaty Principles Bill, and what the coalition Government has done with its changes to the Maca, as well as to Treaty references in dozens of laws.

Act wants to go further by requiring any Treaty reference in a new law to be explicit about the obligations it creates, and for whom. This is effectively a block on what it deems “vague” references – such as “having regard to Treaty principles” – where the door is more open to judges filling in the gaps.

This is the potential for judicial activism Seymour wants to minimise.

So what would New Zealand look like if Act’s proposals were implemented, compared to today?

Seymour thinks it would be a step towards no generic Māori interests in genetics or resource management or education or health, or even new plants under the Plant Variety Rights Act.

“That’s very different from certain property owners who happen to be Māori to be able to go to court and claim rights in specific instances,” he said, which would be how a pathway for customary title would be maintained.

“What is the underlying cause of where New Zealand is today? The last 20 years of basically saying there are two categories of New Zealander and trying to work out how they interrelate.”

Seymour pointed to the Peter Ellis case as an example of judicial activism, where the Supreme Court made a tikanga ruling in a case that had no Māori element.

This has also been highlighted by Emeritus Professor Peter Watts, KC, who described the court decision as a “revolution ... welcome or not”, and by Deborah Chambers, KC.

“Before Ellis, the role of tikanga Māori (Māori customary law and values) in the common law was limited and reasonably settled,” Chambers said in a Herald article.

“It was recognised mainly in cases involving customary Māori property rights or matters closely connected to Māori affairs, particularly certain family law issues. In Ellis, the court went much further. It effectively declared that tikanga is potentially relevant to any question of common law or statutory interpretation that might come before the courts.”

Chambers cited the Fonterra climate case as well as a three-strikes Supreme Court decision as further examples of the judiciary overstepping its bounds.

“These cases are frequently cited as the court advancing particular policy outcomes on Māori rights and tikanga, climate change, and a more cautious approach to criminal sentencing – outcomes that align with a broadly liberal, insulated Wellington-Beltway centric worldview,” she said.

“Legitimate questions remain about the clarity of the court’s judgments and the proper limits of its role. Without sensible but vigilant criticism, judicial activism risks becoming normalised. When that happens, we risk moving from the rule of law toward something closer to the rule of judges.”

Where the line should be drawn when it comes to judicial boundaries is a point of contention and where some legal experts disagree with Seymour. The courts can already set legal principles, for example.

“The entire legal principle of negligence law, that people owe duties of care to other people in society, was made up by the courts,” Geddis said.

“Every time you have a car accident, your ability to sue the person who caused that accident is a result of the court saying there’s a general duty in law to look out for the interests of other people. So the courts have always had a role in developing and widening the laws of the country without Parliament.”

Former Act MP Deborah Coddington has also made this point in a Herald article, where she said Act’s policy would “interfere in the judiciary’s role by screwing tight the judiciary’s boundaries”.

Act was “tying itself in constitutional knots”, she said, and blurring the lines between the separation of powers: the legislature, the executive and the judiciary.

Geddis said an inevitable outcome from that separation is that sometimes a court decision will land that a lawmaker doesn’t like.

“Act effectively seems to be upset that, on occasion, the courts have given meaning to Acts of Parliament different from what Act itself would like the outcome to be.

“That’s just what you get when you divide power up so that you don’t have one group in charge of all aspects of how the country runs, being able to do what they want, how they want, whenever they want.”

He derided Act’s proposed changes to the Constitution Act as the “constitutional equivalent of making English an official language”.

“It would change absolutely nothing whatsoever in terms of the actual practice of how New Zealand’s constitution works. And it wouldn’t change an iota as to how any institution within our constitution works.”

The Constitution Act already says: “The Parliament of New Zealand continues to have full power to make laws.”

As a package, Geddis said the policy sought to embed Act’s particular view of how the constitution ought to operate. That is, of course, what you would expect from a party’s policy platform.

“But it’s full of ironies. For example, putting in place instructions to the judiciary as to how they should interpret statutes goes against the Regulatory Standards Act [which Seymour secured in the National-Act coalition agreement].”

That law says: “Legislation should preserve the court’s constitutional role of ascertaining the meaning of legislation.”

“And now they want to change various bits of our constitution to say the courts must do what Parliament says when interpreting legislation,” Geddis said.

“So which is it?”

Derek Cheng is a senior journalist who started at the Herald in 2004. He has worked several stints in the press gallery team and is a former deputy political editor.
