Karla Cardno’s stepfather dies before her killer is denied parole for the 19th time

New Zealand Herald October 24, 2026

Mark Middleton fought to keep the man who murdered his stepdaughter, Karla Cardno (inset), behind bars. Photo / Mark Mitchell

Warning: Disturbing content

For decades, Mark Middleton fought to keep the man who murdered his stepdaughter, Karla Cardno, behind bars.

But two weeks before Paul Joseph Dally’s recent appearance before the Parole Board, where he was denied parole for a 19th time, Middleton died.

The 69-year-old died in the early hours of September 27 at Manor Park Private Hospital in Lower Hutt.

Family, friends and his lawyer gathered in Martinborough last Sunday for a private farewell.

His eldest brother, George Middleton, 79, told the Herald that Mark suffered a severe stroke six years ago that left him incapacitated.

“After his first stroke, they thought he was going to die, but he recovered,” George said.

“He was in a psychogeriatric hospital and always seemed on the verge of dying. He couldn’t move and his brain was gone.

“He had an excellent doctor and terrific nurses. The care was first-rate.”

George, a retired schoolteacher, remembered his younger brother as a handsome, talented charmer with a good sense of humour.

“Mark was tall, blond and handsome – the best-looking in the family, after me.

“He was musical, a gifted artist and talented at just about everything. He had two sons and loved Karla as his own daughter.”

But Karla’s murder was something he never recovered from.

“Karla’s death had a deep effect on him. He never forgave Dally and he never forgot Karla. She was a lovely girl.”

On May 26, 1989, Dally kidnapped 13-year-old Karla in Lower Hutt before raping and torturing her over 22 hours.

The teenager had borrowed her brother’s BMX and cycled to the Taita dairy for a drink, three Jelly Tip ice creams and a newspaper.

Dally spotted her, pursued her around a shopping centre and snatched her as she rode home.

When Karla failed to return, her mother went searching and found only her daughter’s abandoned bike.

Police cordoned off Churton Rd, where Karla lived just metres from Dally.

As police and family searched the neighbourhood, Dally watched from his window while raping Karla in the upstairs bedroom he had shared with his partner.

Middleton’s father unknowingly knocked on Dally’s door. There was no answer.

The following day, Dally bundled Karla – naked, bound and gagged – into the boot of his car and drove to Pencarrow, near Wellington, where he buried her alive in a shallow grave.

Almost six weeks later, Dally confessed to police and led them to the remote beach where he had buried her body.

In 1990, he pleaded guilty to murder and was sentenced to life imprisonment.

At a Parole Board hearing in 2014, Dally admitted to the board he had enjoyed committing the crime.

His latest unsuccessful bid for parole was heard on October 14.

Keith Jefferies, 78, Middleton’s lawyer and friend of more than 30 years, described him as a “likeable rogue with a huge heart”.

“Mark was a colourful character – charming, talented, with a swagger like Clint Eastwood. He could have been a Hollywood star.

“He was a swashbuckler – daring and adventurous, but with a softer, compassionate side.

“He owned a house painting business and took young people under his wing, teaching them the trade, and helped troubled teenagers at a centre on the Kāpiti Coast. Some struggled at school; others had got into minor crimes.”

Jefferies said youth “connected” with Middleton, with some seeing him as a father figure.

“He loved his kids and never got over losing Karla. Mark had a strong sense of justice.”

Jefferies first represented Middleton after he was charged with threatening to hunt down and crucify Dally.

The charges followed comments Middleton made to journalists and police in August 1999, when Dally first became eligible for parole.

“Mark threatened to hang Dally upside down and cut his balls off.

“He said, ‘If they let this guy out, I’ll kill him. I’ll nail him upside down to a tree, cut his balls off and shove them down his throat. I’ll sew his mouth shut and kill him over three days’.

“He was a robust guy. A few inmates offered to kill Dally for him, but Mark said, ‘No, I’ll do it myself’.”

Middleton was furious that Dally had previously been released from prison after serving a nine-month sentence for attacking an elderly Auckland woman.

About a month before Karla’s murder, Dally’s partner had taken their three children to a Women’s Refuge.

In February 2001, Middleton was found guilty of threatening to kill.

The verdict sparked nationwide outrage. Talkback radio lines ran hot, protesters gathered outside courthouses, and the Sensible Sentencing Trust emerged.

The late Judge Michael Lance, KC, sentenced Middleton to nine months’ imprisonment, suspended for two years, after a psychiatrist diagnosed him with “chronic hypertrophic grief” – a form of prolonged grief disorder.

The diagnosis helped persuade the judge to suspend the sentence so Middleton could receive professional help.

“At the time, Mark was living in Whanganui, where he had become something of a local folk hero. The trial was moved to Auckland,” Jefferies said.

“He was tough and resilient. He never complained about the prospect of prison. He had a strong sense of justice and integrity.”

Jefferies said Middleton was also fiercely loyal, standing by him when the lawyer faced his own criminal charges.

In 2015, Jefferies was convicted of drug offences after police found illicit substances, including methamphetamine, during a search of his car.

He pleaded guilty to charges including possession of utensils for smoking methamphetamine and possession of a psychoactive substance.

Jefferies sought a discharge without conviction, but Judge David Ruth declined the application and fined him a total of $1300.

He said the case had been “blown out of proportion” and claimed police went after him because he was a lawyer.

Through it all, Middleton remained a loyal friend.

“Mark was always there for me. He wasn’t a fair-weather friend.

“He was a good chap, with a real sense of decency. I’ll miss him.”

Karla’s mother, Veronica Cardno, declined to comment to the Herald.

Jefferies said there was one rule at Middleton’s private farewell: no one was to mention Karla.

“Veronica is a strong woman, but the grief is still raw and real.”

Dally, now in his 60s, is set to next appear before the Parole Board in September 2028.

In June, the Parole Board issued a ruling that current photos of the notorious killer could not be published.

It also issued a non-publication order relating to the location he would be released to if a parole bid was successful.

Carolyne Meng-Yee is an Auckland-based investigative journalist who won Best Documentary at the Voyager Media Awards. This year she was a finalist for Best Current Affairs. She worked for the Herald on Sunday from 2007-2011 and rejoined the Herald in 2016 after working as an award-winning current affairs producer at TVNZ’s 60 Minutes, 20/20 and Sunday.

Memoir from Ardern’s press secretary Andrew Campbell amplifies what the Chrises lack – Kiri Allan

New Zealand Herald October 24, 2026

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

Close to midnight on December 9, 2019, hours after Whakaari erupted, Jacinda Ardern walked into the Civil Defence centre in Whakatāne. She arrived well briefed and prepared, then sat down and listened to every piece of advice from the local responders. She took it all in and worked with the people in the room to make deliberate decisions on the nature and scale of the tragedy as it unfolded.

In the days that followed I watched her hold families who had lost loved ones, then turn to her team, me included, and make her expectations plain: be on the ground, and do anything and everything a government could do to respond. She was empathetic and she was clear. When she asked for action, people moved.

I thought about that night often while reading In the Room, Andrew Campbell’s account of five years as Ardern’s chief press secretary. I thought about it even more while watching the two men who want her old job.

Campbell coined “the team of five million”. He was also the adviser who told Ardern, in the back of a Crown car, that her Government was trying to do too much. His book is built on that tension between loyalty and argument, and it is better for it. He is generous about Ardern without being starry-eyed, and he names where he and the Government got it wrong: mandates that ran too long, an economic pivot that came too late, a retreat from international media he now regrets.

I sat at the Cabinet table through some of those years, and his account rings true. The mosque attacks, Whakaari and a pandemic arrived one on top of another, and for me they arrived alongside a cancer diagnosis, which I have written about in my own memoir, Go Hard or Go Home. Those years taught me what leadership under pressure looks like. Campbell’s book is a reminder of how rare it is.

His central insight is one he admits he reached late. For years he advised Ardern as though her job was to manage the status quo. She was a conviction politician set on changing it, and he believes his advice would have been different had he seen that sooner.

Her warmth, he insists, was real and her communication drove her Government. Speeches he thought were finished came back covered in her red ink. People make hard changes only when they feel the reason for them, he argues; a list of numbers will not move them.

He is just as clear about the price. Winning against the virus burned enormous political capital. Death threats against her more than tripled. He watched casual sexism play out in rooms where people addressed him instead of her, and where business leaders praised Chris Hipkins for finally listening, months after dismissing Ardern across the same table.

More than three years after she left, Ardern still out-rates everyone in the game. A Freshwater poll for the Post puts her net favourability at +10, ahead of a field of current leaders who are all underwater. Campbell says those are numbers either Chris would kill for. In this past week’s 1News Verian poll, 20% of voters picked Christopher Luxon as preferred Prime Minister and 17% picked Hipkins. Between them, the two men who could lead the next Government cannot win over two voters in five.

This week’s final debate showed how much room remains to grow. Both leaders appeared to read their vision statements from an autocue, which left voters with polished lines and little of the thinking behind them. Seventeen days out, the country is still waiting for a clear picture, in each leader’s own voice, of where he wants to take it. Charisma is the smallest part of that gap.

Both Chrises are managers, and both are good at it. Luxon came from the boardroom and governs like a chief executive reporting against targets. His line this week was that National’s plan is working, while seven in 10 voters tell pollsters the health system is in crisis. Hipkins was the minister Ardern trusted with the hardest logistics of Covid, and he delivered. When he took over, he steadied a Government that needed steadying, clearing the policy “bonfire” and returning to bread-and-butter issues. Campbell thinks he should have paired that reset with an early election while the change was still fresh. Hipkins now has the chance to show the conviction the reset made room for.

Competence matters, and both men have it. Competence is also the minimum. Voters follow leaders who tell them where they are going and why the trip is worth it. Ardern did that in a single press conference in 2017, an appearance Campbell credits with reviving Labour overnight. Neither Chris has had that moment yet.

To be fair to both, Ardern’s leadership was forged in crises neither has faced as Prime Minister and conviction cost her. It made her a global target and a polarising figure. Popularity is a poor measure of a good Prime Minister. Still, voters give their trust to leaders who say plainly what they stand for, and both men have time to do that.

In place of vision, we have been handed venom from both podiums. Campbell calls this a very negative campaign that makes politics feel small-minded. Wednesday night’s leadership debate proved him right. Luxon called Hipkins the most abysmal Education Minister the country has ever had, and Hipkins hit back. Ardern’s 2017 message was “let’s do this”. This campaign has given voters nothing so simple and nothing so hopeful.

The line on Campbell’s cover is Ardern’s farewell to him: “Every Prime Minister needs someone who will challenge them – and that was you”. In an election, that job belongs to all of us.

It belongs to the media and our leaders are making that harder. Ardern stopped doing Mike Hosking’s show because Campbell judged the interviews had become disrespectful. Since then Luxon has dropped his weekly TVNZ Breakfast slot, and David Seymour and Winston Peters have, for periods, kept away from RNZ programmes. Every leader who picks the friendly microphone over the hard one denies voters the chance to see what they believe under pressure.

It belongs to coalition partners. With smaller parties likely to decide who governs again, the next Prime Minister will need to say no to his partners as readily as he says yes. Hipkins accused Luxon this week of letting Peters and Seymour run circles around him. Whoever wins will face the same test.

Most of all, it belongs to voters. Over the next two weeks, ask both men the question a scripted format cannot easily answer: what do you actually want to do with this job?

In the Room is essential reading for anyone who wants to understand the Ardern years, and for anyone who wants to lead. Its lesson for Luxon and Hipkins fits in a single sentence: know what you believe, say it like you mean it, and when the moment comes, walk into the room and lead. I saw what that looks like in Whakatāne at midnight. We deserve no less from whoever leads us next.

Kiri Allan is a former Labour Party minister who held the portfolios of justice, regional development, conservation and emergency management. She was the lead minister for the Cyclone Gabrielle response in Tairāwhiti. She is the founder of renewable energy company Four Directions Fund and runs KLA consultancy firm.

Firefighters will return to the scene of a scrub fire on Auckland’s North Shore this morning, after it burned last night.

Crews were called to Kauri Point in Chatswood shortly after midnight.

The fire was 600m from where trucks could reach, so firefighters walked with hoses to put out the blaze, Fire and Emergency said.

It was extinguished, but crews will return to the site to check for hotspots this morning.

Labour setting up Starship visit despite Chris Hipkins saying it would be inappropriate amid election campaign

Labour is scheduling a visit to Starship children’s hospital to discuss staffing shortages, despite leader Chris Hipkins saying such a visit would be inappropriate during an election campaign.

However, the party has since clarified Hipkins’ comments, saying the Labour leader supported visiting Starship and claimed his remarks were intended to convey how Labour wouldn’t be “offering to fix the situation from Opposition”.

On Thursday, Hipkins told media in Taradale a Labour-led government would move “heaven and earth” to ensure Starship had the necessary funding and support following reports of staffing shortages impacting scheduled cancer treatment in the hospital’s oncology ward.

Hipkins wasn’t able to specify what level of support a future government he led would give Starship, saying he would meet with hospital leaders within the first 100 days after the election but not before.

“It would be inappropriate for them to meet with us while we’re out on the campaign trail and I’m not going to put them in that position.

“They have to be above the political process. As soon as a government is formed though, I’d be sitting down talking to them.”

The Herald has seen correspondence between Hipkins’ office and Health New Zealand showing Hipkins’ team had asked on Monday if Hipkins and health spokeswoman Dr Ayesha Verrall could visit Starship on Tuesday, two days before Hipkins made his comments to media.

The request from Labour referenced “concerns about staffing pressures at the hospital”.

“We are looking to better understand these issues and what can be done to address them,” the email read.

A member of Health NZ’s executive team wrote back, informing Hipkins’ office a Tuesday visit was not possible but was happy to discuss other dates.

A reply from Hipkins’ office, which was sent less than an hour prior to Hipkins making his comments on Thursday, requested a visit on Tuesday next week. Health NZ also said that date was not possible but later suggested times later in the week.

Asked yesterday if Labour had expressed interest in visiting Starship, a party spokesperson said Verrall’s office had approached Starship requesting a visit but it was declined so Verrall and Hipkins “met oncology nurses offsite”. They acknowledged Starship had offered other times to visit.

Following further questions about the meaning of Hipkins’ comments, the spokesperson acknowledged they could have been clearer.

“While it could have been clearer, Chris Hipkins was responding to questions regarding what fix a Labour government would put in place with Starship.

“While it is common and appropriate for politicians to visit hospitals in a campaign to hear of the day-to-day workings and pressure points, it would not be appropriate to engage with Starship staff offering to fix the situation from Opposition.”

The spokesperson said Labour had contacted Health Minister Simeon Brown’s office about visiting Starship to hear about reported issues. Brown’s office referred the request to Health NZ, the spokesperson said, and it’s understood Labour still intends to visit during the campaign.

Also in Thursday’s stand-up, Hipkins said he was motivated to sufficiently resource Starship after hearing impactful stories from staff who worked there.

“I’m just not going to accept that kids who are receiving cancer treatment should be being treated in hallways, in waiting rooms, because there aren’t enough staff, it’s just not OK,” Hipkins said on Thursday.

Labour clarified Hipkins had been told of “children being administered chemotherapy in a waiting room” in his offsite discussions with oncology nurses.

The Herald asked Labour whether Hipkins was also told of treatment in “hallways” as he claimed on Thursday but did not get a response.

In response to Hipkins’ claims, Health NZ said in a statement: “We can confirm no children are being treated in corridors at Starship Hospital.”

The Herald asked whether such treatment had occurred previously but was told by Health NZ a response wasn’t likely to come until Tuesday.

It comes after Timaru dad Shaun Todd accused Brown and other politicians of politicising child cancer this week following revelations that treatments had been delayed by up to a week on the oncology ward at Starship due to severe nursing shortages.

Brown agreed to meet parents whose children were receiving cancer treatment on Friday after one mother posted on Facebook about her family’s experience.

Adam Pearse is the Deputy Political Editor and part of the NZ Herald’s Press Gallery team based at Parliament in Wellington. He has worked for NZME since 2018, reporting for the Northern Advocate in Whangārei and the Herald in Auckland.

University of Auckland survey finds 30% of students experienced sexual harm

New Zealand Herald October 24, 2026

Almost one in three students surveyed at Auckland University claim they have experienced sexual harm while at the tertiary institution.

The anonymous Auckland University Students’ Association Te Rōpū Kahikatea (AUSA) survey was conducted last year and completed by 183 students.

The results, released last week, found 30% of respondents reported having experienced some form of sexual harm during their time at the university.

Students reported incidents of sexual assault, sexual harassment, stalking and inappropriate comments and contact.

The incidents typically took place at external social events involving students, though incidents in residential halls represented almost a quarter of responses.

“The findings are disappointing, but unfortunately they are not surprising,” said author Emelia Martin Moses.

The Attitudes Towards Sexual Injustice in the University Environment report defined sexual harm as “any non-consensual, unwanted sexual behaviour, act, or attempt”.

More than half of those surveyed said they didn’t report incidents because they didn’t think it would be taken seriously, didn’t feel it was significant enough, didn’t trust the system, or found the process too complicated.

Many students reported that the reporting processes involved procedures that some found distressing or retraumatising, the report said.

Concerns about inadequate follow-up, a perceived lack of investigation, and fears of retaliation further undermined confidence in how the matter would be dealt with, the report read.

“From my own experience as a student, and through conversations I have had with others, there has often been a lack of trust in institutional processes for addressing sexual harm,” Moses said.

While it was confronting to see these violations reflected in the data, the report reinforced what many survivors, advocates, and researchers have highlighted for years, Moses said.

The AUSA report proposed several changes the university could adopt to reduce sexual harm.

Its recommendations included increased communication to students regarding what defines sexual harm and available support, extending existing support services, mandatory consent training for staff, and reviewing the university’s policy on staff–student intimate relationships.

The university has commissioned an independent review, currently underway, to examine how it handles sexual harassment complaints raised against staff.

The institution made the announcement after it came under scrutiny for how it handled an investigation into chemistry professor Jonathan Sperry.

The review began in September and is expected to take up to six months.

Kai Creighton is a journalism student at Waikato Institute of Technology.

AI in education: Tauranga experts weigh the benefits and risks

New Zealand Herald October 24, 2026

Revision Village chief executive Tim Vaughan says AI should help students learn, not think for them.

A Tauranga man who helped build an education platform into a global learning tool believes artificial intelligence could make personalised learning possible at scale.

But Tim Vaughan says the challenge is ensuring AI supports learning without removing the thinking and struggle that comes with it.

That is a concern shared by Steam-Ed Tauranga lead educator Barbara Cook, who questions what children could lose if AI does too much of the thinking for them.

Vaughan is chief executive of Revision Village, a study platform used by about 85% of International Baccalaureate students at more than 700 schools globally.

The IB Diploma Programme is a two-year pre-university curriculum for students aged 16 to 19 that offers an internationally recognised alternative to NCEA and Cambridge qualifications.

About 20 schools in New Zealand offer one or more IB programmes; 93% of those students use Revision Village.

Vaughan said the company was increasingly focused on using artificial intelligence to personalise learning and reduce teachers’ administrative workloads.

His focus on education technology was shaped by years growing Education Perfect, which reached more than one million users before being sold in a deal valuing the company at up to $455 million.

Vaughan first connected with one of Education Perfect’s co-founders, Craig Smith, while studying at the University of Otago.

At the time, the company was known as Language Perfect, and Vaughan was developing his own financial literacy platform.

He was invited to return and join the company after spending several years working on his own projects overseas.

He agreed on the condition that he could help expand the platform beyond language learning.

Language Perfect evolved into Education Perfect, broadening its reach into other subjects through gamification, spaced repetition, and a focus on improving the user experience.

Vaughan attributed the company’s growth to listening closely to students and teachers and making constant improvements.

Revision Village was acquired by Crimson Education in 2023 and Vaughan was shoulder-tapped by chief executive Jamie Beaton to become Revision Village’s chief executive.

The platform provides IB students with question banks, practice material, worked solutions and videos from experienced educators and examiners.

Vaughan said the aim was to give students a way to work through the curriculum at their own pace.

“It’s really designed as a bespoke, one-stop sort of solution for an IB student.”

The company has developed its own AI marking tool, which has graded almost half a million questions and produced tens of thousands of hours of personalised feedback.

For teachers, the aim is to reduce repetitive marking so they can spend more time supporting students who need extra help.

“No teacher entered their profession to primarily deal with the plethora of administrative tasks demanding their time.

“It’s very, very powerful in terms of closing the loop there.”

Vaughan said he was cautious about presenting AI as an uncomplicated win for education, and said it could risk removing too much of the struggle that drives learning.

“Learning is about kind of wrestling with ideas,” he said. Hedescribed the “cognitive friction” needed to master something.

The challenge was using AI to support learning rather than simply produce an outcome, he said.

Vaughan said AI could make personalised education a reality, something the sector has long struggled to deliver at scale.

“Rather than a one-size-fits-all kind of way of learning, it has to be dynamic, it has to be personalised, it has to be at the appropriate level for every single student.

“And that’s never actually been possible before.”

Vaughan said schools would need to rethink how they taught and assessed students as AI became more widespread.

Banning the technology was unrealistic, he said, particularly as students entered workplaces where AI was increasingly embedded.

Instead, schools would need clear guidelines around when AI could be used, with oral and practical assessments likely to play a greater role in learning.

Steam-Ed Tauranga lead educator Barbara Cook said educators needed to think carefully about how AI was used in the classroom.

Steam-Ed Tauranga provides specialist science, technology, engineering, arts and mathematics classes.

“You’ve got to ask the question of which parts do we want to outsource to AI and which parts are important for both ourselves and our students to sort of struggle with?”

Cook said an experiment using AI to write scripts for a holiday movie-making programme showed what could be lost when technology removed too much of the challenge.

Students had written their own scripts, but when AI was used to speed up the process, the resulting films were less creative and engaging, she said.

“We went, ‘Wow, never again will we do that.’”

Cook said AI also helped students in a recent robotics workshop generate code and build functioning robots without years of programming experience.

She said she wanted children to learn how to use AI, but not at the expense of learning how to think without it.

That ability to struggle through an imperfect first attempt, she said, was part of developing the skills children would need later in life.

Zoe Blake is a multimedia journalist at the Bay of Plenty Times and Rotorua Daily Post.

Letters: Majorities, falsehoods and herding cats – the art of voting in an MMP world

New Zealand Herald October 24, 2026

Labour leader Chris Hipkins (left) and his National counterpart Christopher Luxon may have to make significant policy concessions to minor players in coalition negotiations after the election.

Letter of the week: Clear majorities, falsehoods and herding cats

Having run a few political campaigns in my time, I have a better-than-average understanding of the mathematics of MMP.

It’s simple: if you want a Labour-led Government you have to vote Labour. If you want a National-led Government, you have to give your party vote to National.

Why? Because it’s important that whichever major party wins the most votes, they need to be in a strong negotiating position when dealing with potential coalition partners.

Otherwise, a weak major party will have to give the minor players greater policy concessions.

Hence, we could possibly see Chlöe Swarbrick as Finance Minister in a left-wing Government. The voodoo economics of the Green Party would put New Zealand into a fiscal hole from which it would take a decade or more to recover.

Or David Seymour could be Finance Minister in a centre-right Government. In which case we could see radical and unwelcome change to the social fabric that is important to most New Zealanders.

We’re looking at the possibility of a party that has 5% of popular support choosing the next Government. That’s not what should happen.

The leader of the Opportunity Party is an intelligent and articulate woman, who no doubt would make a good Member of Parliament, but we know nothing about those who stand behind her on its party list.

On current polling, they could have as many as 10 MPs in the next Parliament, all of them politically inexperienced and of unknown political worth.

It was evident in the last Government that a three-way coalition could be fractious and not always acting in the country’s best interests.

A government coalition of four parties – Labour, Greens, Te Pāti Māori, and Opportunity – would be like herding cats. It could result in the sort of political inertia that would be disastrous for New Zealand right now when we need a Government that is prepared to challenge the problems with insight, vigour and determination.

The same is true of a four-way patchwork of National, Act, New Zealand First and Opportunity.

It is critical that voters are not gulled into the falsehood of “tactical” voting. Let’s give one or other of the major parties a clear mandate to get on with the job, unhindered by the tails that would otherwise wag the dog.

David Morris, Hillsborough.

Thank you to your correspondent Reg Dempster (Oct 18) for raising the very concerning issue of joblessness in New Zealand and the consequences thereof.

One of the many consequences is child poverty, an issue that the current coalition appears to find a little embarrassing.

When asked recently about the horrific current child poverty statistics, Louise Upston, Minister for Child Poverty Reduction, gave an interesting response. She agreed that the statistics are concerning but stated that the answer to child poverty is not (as recent advice recommended) to increase benefits, but to “get parents into paid work, reducing the cost of living, and improving health and education outcomes”.

This is a minister who, in her own words, is “comfortable” to receive $1000 per week from the Remuneration Authority in order to live in her own mortgage-free home in Wellington.

All I can say is, roll on November 7.

Jackie Evans, Pukehangi.

Thanks so much NZ Herald for your in-depth articles on “how can we stop an overhang from stealing the election” and former SAS officer Guy Haddleton on business success and “New Zealand’s lack of vision”.

It was so good to see the flip side of the latest idea to manipulate the election, or as Nick Clark said “the 2026 election campaign is the first to see deliberate attempts to engineer an overhang and is that what we really want?”

Secondly, Guy Haddleton on what the SAS taught him was that it was all about people. He “always surrounds himself with people far better than him” and “there is always someone better than him”.

It seemed to me it was about the team rather than the leader and that is not something we hear about under our current political system.

So thanks for some of the best reporting I have read so far in this election.

Robin Harrison, Takapuna.

Destiny Church’s Brian Tamaki mouths off like New Zealand First MPs and gets kicked out of Australia at the border. In Aotearoa New Zealand, racist comments are treated as acceptable by Luxon. Could we get some Aussie ethics in New Zealand or is that too “woke”?

What a revelation to hear this.

Steve Russell, Hillcrest.

‘National suicide’: The election issue tearing Israelis apart

Sydney Morning Herald October 25, 2026

A row over whether a Jerusalem coffee shop could open on the Sabbath escalated into an epic culture war. For modern Israel, it could be the shape of things to come.

Jerusalem/ Bnei Brak: Almost anywhere else in the world, a cafe opening for business on Saturday would not be an inflammatory act. But in downtown Jerusalem, Cafe Basimta’s decision to sell coffee and pastries on the Sabbath ignited an almighty culture war between the Holy City’s ultra-Orthodox and secular residents.

Soon after the coffee shop opened in a quiet alley in May, dozens of ultra-Orthodox teenage boys wearing black suits and fedoras showed up to block its entrance while chanting “Whoever breaks the Sabbath has no part in the world to come”.

Ultra-Orthodox Jews believe in resting on the Sabbath, the frequent study of religious texts, strict gender segregation and eating kosher, pitting them against the less devout, who favour a more relaxed approach.

As the demonstrations grew each week, so did counter-protests. Hundreds of non-religious activists locked arms to protect the entrance to the café, and prominent politicians from the right and left joined in.

The fact that the cafe’s owners – the messianic and controversial Jews for Jesus organisation – were hardly secular was a wrinkle in the narrative. But it didn’t deter most of the counter-protesters, who believed they were fighting for an important principle.

“We see it as our right to be able to drink coffee on the Sabbath in the centre of Jerusalem,” says deputy Jerusalem mayor Adir Schwarz, a champion of the city’s secular population. “Our capital is supposed to unite all Israelis, and if any Jew is being pushed out of Jerusalem, that is a bad forewarning for the rest of the state of Israel.”

While the havoc was a boon for business, the owners ultimately decided it wasn’t worth the pain. In September, the cafe announced it would no longer open on Saturdays. “The cafe has become, over the past several months, a focal point of friction and danger,” Jews for Jesus chief executive Eli Birnbaum said.

Disappointed by the decision, secular activists mostly abandoned the cafe and business plummeted. When we visited last week, the coffee was excellent, but only a handful of customers were there.

Schwarz says the backdown was just the latest blow to secular Jerusalemites, who feel increasingly marginalised and disempowered. Ultra-Orthodox residents are rising in number and moving into secular suburbs, sparking heated battles over resources and cultural norms.

“A territorial battle is playing out in certain neighbourhoods as their identity changes and becomes more religious,” Schwarz says.

Schwarz cites strict ultra-Orthodox modesty laws which can expose female pedestrians to harassment and intimidation for wearing jeans. “The fact a secular woman cannot walk in pants through the neighbourhood she grew up in is a big problem,” Schwarz argues.

Israel’s ultra-Orthodox community – known as the Haredim – makes up 14 per cent of the national population. That figure is exploding, reflecting the fact that the birth rate for ultra-Orthodox women (6.5 children per woman) is vastly higher than for other Jewish women (2.2 children). By 2065, the Haredim are projected to comprise a third of Israeli society, a figure unimaginable when Israel was founded in 1948. Such rapid growth equals more political power but also greater scrutiny about ultra-Orthodox Jews’ contribution to Israeli society.

The fight over Cafe Basimta is emblematic of a deeper battle being waged in Israel ahead of national elections on Tuesday. Topics that foreigners may expect to be front-of-centre – like how Israel waged its war on Gaza or the possibility of a two-state solution with the Palestinians – are almost entirely absent from the public discourse. Meanwhile, the concessions provided to ultra-Orthodox Israelis are tearing the nation apart and dominating the campaign.

Bnei Brak is a mere 20-minute drive from the gay bars and non-kosher restaurants of Tel Aviv, but it might as well be on a different planet. “We live in separate worlds, and those worlds are getting further apart,” Rabbi Yisrael Goldwasser says of the two cities, which serve as avatars for Israel’s ultra-Orthodox and secular tribes. Here there is none of the clashing and intermingling you find in more integrated Jerusalem.

Bnei Brak is one of the world’s most densely populated cities: 230,000 people, almost all of them Haredi, crammed into just seven square kilometres of land. “It’s a terrible city, it’s dirty, it’s more crowded than Gaza,” Goldwasser says as he slurps a bowl of matzo ball soup. His kosher phone, which blocks internet access, sits on the table. On the plus side, he says it is a self-contained society packed with restaurants, yeshivas, shops and medical facilities where the streets remain lively until the early hours of the morning.

In Hebrew, the Haredim means those who tremble before God. To be ultra-Orthodox is to be on edge. But Goldwasser says the community’s naturally high anxiety has spiked to intolerable levels because of an all-out campaign to force them to serve in the military.

The dilemma of ultra-Orthodox army service has existed before the founding of Israel in 1948. To ensure as broad support as possible for the creation of a Jewish state, founding prime minister David Ben-Gurion granted 400 yeshiva students exemptions from compulsory military service. This reflected the ultra-Orthodox community’s fraught relationship with Zionism (many believe establishing a sovereign Jewish state before the arrival of the Messiah violates divine law).

A decade later, with thousands of students now exempt, Ben-Gurion questioned his decision. Today, court filings by Israel’s attorney-general estimate that about 80,000 are avoiding military service. This became a source of fury as Israel fought a multi-front war against its enemies after the October 7 attacks of 2023. The burdens of service – time spent away from family and the risk of dying on the battlefield – have not been distributed evenly across society.

Reflecting the new era Israel entered after October 7, the Supreme Court ruled in 2024 that the longstanding blanket exemption for yeshiva students was unlawful. Fierce resistance has followed. Last year, chief rabbi Yitzhak Yosef used his weekly sermon to warn that the ultra-Orthodox community “will all board planes and leave Israel” if they are forced to serve in the army.

Attempts to force Haredi men to enlist, including through arrests, have sparked riots and blockades of major highways. In June, ultra-Orthodox rioters smashed windows, damaged flowerpots, and vandalised a car parked at the home of the Supreme Court’s deputy president.

“As far as they’re concerned, it’s life or death. Religion comes first,” Wasserman says, explaining why the issue arouses such passion. Bnei Brak yeshiva student Yakov, 20, says he has no intention of enlisting. “Prison, sanctions, nothing can break us,” he declares. His dream is to be a rabbi.

Protests and arrests have accelerated in the lead-up to the October 27 election, raising the temperature. The military arrested 40 ultra-Orthodox men returning from the United States on Tuesday at Tel Aviv airport on suspicion of draft dodging.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whose conservative coalition is reliant on ultra-Orthodox parties, criticised the arrests. “We need to preserve the world of Torah study because it has preserved us,” he said in a radio interview.

On the other side of the debate, the four main Jewish parties running against Netanyahu are all campaigning to end sweeping exemptions from military service. They are convinced they are onto a vote winner. An overwhelming 72 per cent of Israelis want to see the Haredim drafted alongside other Israelis eligible for military service, according to a September poll by the Israel Democracy Institute.

Heightening the anger over draft dodging is the ultra-Orthodox community’s dependence on the Israeli state. The employment rate for Haredi men is only around 50 per cent, and more than half live in poverty, making them reliant on government subsidies. Ultra-Orthodox schools typically devote little time to subjects such as maths and science, leaving graduates poorly equipped for the modern workforce. Critics argue this is a time bomb threatening the viability of Israel’s advanced, high-tech economy.

“There’s a million-and-a-half Haredis; in one generation there is going to be four million,” former prime minister Naftali Bennett, who is running to unseat Netanyahu, told podcast host Eylon Levy last week. “Right now, they don’t serve in the army, they barely work and barely pay taxes, but we have to fund them ... It’s a machine of national suicide.”

Rabbi Goldwasser says the military enlistment drive is encouraging hatred in a populist bid to win votes. “We take care of the poor, we look after the unfortunate. That’s why it hurts so much,” he says of being labelled shirkers and draft dodgers.

While he believes trying to force resistant Haredis into the army by arresting them will be disastrous, he says making the military a welcoming environment for the ultra-Orthodox could boost recruitment numbers.

Elchanan Wasserman is on a mission to prove it can be done. At 18, Wasserman did something normal for secular Israelis, but remarkable for a young Haredi man like himself – especially one raised in a fervent anti-Zionist household. He enlisted in the army. A troubled childhood convinced him yeshiva life wasn’t for him, prompting a search for an alternative source of structure and meaning. “I didn’t know what to do with myself,” he says from Syria, where he is currently serving. “I joined the military to help my country, and it saved me.”

Wasserman, 27, heads recruitment for the newly formed Hasmonean Brigade, created to accommodate ultra-Orthodox soldiers. The soldiers only serve alongside men, are given time to study the Torah, are allowed to wear black-and-white on the Sabbath and eat the highest level of kosher food. Before October 7, 2023, only around 1800 Haredi men enlisted each year. That jumped to 4300 last year, a substantial rise off a small base.

Wasserman’s work has come at a cost: he was cut off from the community he grew up in and had to be evacuated with police protection in January when violent riots broke out at a conference for ultra-Orthodox recruits. But he says he will encourage his children to serve when they turn 18. “If I didn’t enlist, I think I would be in jail or dead,” he says.

Like Goldwasser, Jerusalem deputy mayor Adir Schwarz is alarmed by the sight of ultra-Orthodox men being arrested. He prefers the use of economic incentives, and sanctions, to encourage enlistment. “Everyone knows the current situation of having this society within a society can’t continue,” he says. “People have simply had enough.”

‘Without you the union is gone’: Mick Gatto’s secret support for John Setka

Sydney Morning Herald October 25, 2026

Leaked texts reveal how John Setka raged, survived and stayed at the top of the CFMEU through a domestic violence scandal, with unwavering support from his gangland friend and some Labor insiders.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

The sky was a blanket of unrelenting grey and large droplets clung to the leaves of the red flowering gums lining the road in Melbourne’s west as a thickset man with thinning hair scrolled through his mobile phone. Australia’s most powerful union leader wanted advice. If anyone knew how to navigate bad press and criminal allegations it was Domenic “Mick” Gatto.

Any other union or political leader facing criminal accusations of stalking and terrorising their wife would have been penning their resignation letter. But not the towering trade union chief now focused on his phone. As usual, the boss of Australia’s construction union, a division of the CFMEU, was defiant.

And why wouldn’t he be? He was John Setka, son of a blue-collar worker who in 1970, when John was only six, had survived one of Australia’s worst industrial accidents. John’s dad had ridden a slab of the West Gate Bridge as it plummeted through nearly 50 metres of icy Melbourne air. The same slab of concrete and iron had claimed the lives of 35 others.

Forty years after his father’s escape from death, John Setka had led tens of thousands of chanting protesters through Melbourne’s CBD, unfazed by the cops on horseback or those sweating on foot in their riot gear.

In 2018, he had stormed out of the national conference of Australia’s oldest political party having labelled its former leader Kevin Rudd a “f---ing dog” and a “maggot” as the ex-prime minister was awarded his Labor Party life membership.

The rain was still falling, the sky growing ever greyer. Setka knew his so-called union comrades were now judging him. F--- ’em. Setka tapped furiously on his phone. “F--- these prim and proper people have never done it hard in the [sic] whole lives,” Setka texted his mate. “I’m sick of all these squareheads trying to micro manage me and tell me who I can be seen with or who I can talk to. Yet when the shit hits the fan they’re nowhere to be seen.”

Setka was finding his rhythm. It is hard not to conclude he felt comfortable when he was raging which, of late, was more often than not. He continued his message to Gatto: “F--- these people who should probably look up in the dictionary what mateship means.”

Setka’s fury had begun building days before when someone, probably a dirty cop or a grubby lawyer, leaked the details of the domestic violence case in early 2019 that had been lodged against him in the Melbourne Magistrates’ Court. One of the police witnesses, a former female judicial officer who was friends with Emma Walters, Setka’s wife, had given a sworn statement describing how John’s “anger” toward Walters had left her feeling “extremely distressed”. Walters had been repeatedly harassed and intimidated by Setka, the witness had said.

The evidence extracted earlier from the phone Setka was now using to text Gatto was similarly damning. Police analysis had revealed that, on a single evening, he had rung Emma 25 times and sent her 45 text messages, calling her a “weak f---en piece of shit”, a “treacherous Aussie f---en c---” and a “f---en dog”.

When the police case had been splashed all over the front page of The Age, along with leaked disparaging comments Setka had made about anti-domestic violence campaigner Rosie Batty, the pile-on had begun. It included Australian Council of Trade Unions (ACTU) secretary Sally McManus, who had publicly called for Setka to resign, asking him to consider that ‘no one is bigger than the movement’. She opined: “While John is elected by his members, he also needs to consider the interests of working people and the wider union movement.” According to McManus, Setka had left “the union movement’s reputation damaged”.

Australia’s largest unions, including those representing teachers, nurses and truck drivers, had publicly agreed and piled on too. Senior Labor figures Anthony Albanese and then-Victorian premier Daniel Andrews weighed in, criticising Setka.

And yet, behind the scenes, it wasn’t all bad for Setka. He was also fielding support, and not only from Mick Gatto. It said something of Setka’s power and reach that it wasn’t just several of his male comrades offering him backroom support, but women too. Even when Albanese was the newly installed opposition leader and moved to turf Setka from the party, Setka’s phone had lit up with text messages from female federal and state Labor politicians and union figures.

Victorian MP Bronwyn Halfpenny had assured Setka she was “thinking of you and hope everything will be OK”. She had texted: “You are a great comrade to working people so the establishment will always want to bring u down. Hope to see you soon. Xxx.”

Rail, Tram and Bus Union secretary Luba Grigorovitch (now a state Labor MP and minister) had repeatedly sent messages of support, vowing to direct her union to back Setka. “We will get through this John xx,” she had promised.

Grigorovitch advised Setka to rely on the behind-the-scenes advice of communications expert and Labor political adviser Tanja Kovac, who also headed EMILY’s List, a group devoted to promoting ALP women into parliament. Kovac had also texted Setka, telling him to craft his public messaging carefully. Setka had decided to plead guilty to a charge of harassment and breaching a family violence order, but Kovac warned Setka that he not only had to survive the Magistrates’ Court but the court of public opinion as well.

It was vital that Setka be seen to publicly champion “the need to talk about family and gendered violence”, texted Kovac. “Be strong, genuine, sorry & the leader I know you are,” she had advised, finishing her text with the words: “Thinking of you.” Kovac also suggested that Setka find supporters willing to support him publicly.

Mick Gatto required no cajoling. Of all Setka’s backers, he had been the most unflinching. Gatto was, in underworld parlance, staunch. Where Kovac urged Setka to display contrition, Gatto urged him to fight. “Sorry you are going through all this nonsense. If I was you I would reconsider pleading guilty,” Gatto advised.

Governments and the “establishment” had also come after him, Gatto told Setka. They had changed the law to stop him from running his boxing promotion company. Now they were coming after Setka because of all he had done for the hundreds of thousands of building workers around the country. Gatto wasn’t having any of it. “Thanks john for publicly defending our friendship,” he texted. “I do love ya. Without you the union is gone.”

Setka hadn’t bothered to respond to some of his other supporters, but for Gatto he had only love. “Thanks brother. I really appreciate the support and I’ll never forget it,” he told his ally.

Setka’s union would also not forget Gatto’s support. A month after Setka took to the steps of the Melbourne Magistrates’ Court, with Emma by his side, to publicly “take responsibility” for the criminal harassment and intimidation of his wife, another man appeared on the steps of the neighbouring Supreme Court.

Gangland identity Faruk Orman had just been released from prison, his murder conviction quashed after a court had found he’d been denied a fair trial because his lawyer engaged in serious misconduct.

Before being jailed for 12 years, Orman had worked as Mick Gatto’s driver. But it was the accusation that he had acted as the wheelman for an underworld hitman that had landed Orman in prison. Orman had entered prison with a boyish face and a skinny frame; he’d left with jowls, a slight paunch, and no desire to drive any more gangland figures around town.

The criminal cases of Setka and Orman had little in common save for two things: both men had a close connection to Gatto, and both would leave their respective court ordeals with the assured future support of the CFMEU.

After his sentencing, Setka was welcomed back to union headquarters as the CFMEU’s most powerful official, as if nothing had ever happened. Orman’s visit to the union would come in time. And when it did, it would sow the seeds of one of the biggest corruption scandals in recent Australian history.

This is an edited extract from Building Bad: The explosive inside story of the CFMEU by Nick McKenzie and Ben Schneiders (Hachette), out on Tuesday.

Anthony LaPaglia: ‘There is not a role I didn’t get that I ever gave more than four hours of grievance to – even Tony Soprano’

The Guardian Sat, 24 Oct 2026 19:00:42 GMT

The actor on surviving 2000s network television in Without a Trace, the role that made him take Brad Pitt seriously, and leaving the US to ‘ride out Trump’

Get our weekend culture and lifestyle email

I didn’t know before reading your new memoir that you were almost Tony Soprano. Is there a role that you really wanted that you didn’t end up getting?

It’s not Tony Soprano. There is not a role that I didn’t get that I ever gave more than four hours of grievance to. When I don’t get something, I move on. Because there’s no point. I’m very pragmatic that way. It’s for your own mental health. Once it’s gone, it’s gone.

The thing you have to understand is if you don’t get something, it’s not personal. It can be as simple as the director has already got three brunettes or three male actors and they don’t need a fourth. It’s never personally about you. It’s about the picture they have in their head … Or sometimes a role is already out to another actor and they’re just waiting for them to say yes. That is one thing I wish they wouldn’t do, because that’s a waste of my time. If you’ve got an offer out to Ben Affleck or whoever, don’t put me on the revolving wheel of possibility. Because if I find out, I’m not doing it. Not that they care! [laughs]

If you were casting your dream project with three actors you’ve already worked with, plus one new face, who would be on your team?

Allison Janney. Kerry Armstrong. Alison Whyte. And a new face … I just saw Moneyball and I don’t think I ever took Brad Pitt that seriously but that guy is phenomenal. Great movie.

Acting opposite Janney in A View from the Bridge on Broadway sounds as though it was a transcendental experience for you.

It was. That’s the thing about Arthur Miller’s plays: the women are the glue. The women make the plays work. My performance is not going to be enough to make it work – I’ve been so lucky to have two phenomenal women [Janney and Whyte in Death of a Salesman] play the lead roles with me. Without them, you have no play.

Your account of your years working on Without a Trace is really fascinating – that era of network television where they were making 24, 25, 26 episodes a season feels like a bygone time. Would you ever do a show like that again?

If I did, I would approach it completely differently. I would not get involved in quality control. I would figure out the lines that didn’t work for me, change them and get on with it …

When I wrote an episode it totally transformed relationship with the writers because I suddenly realised how difficult it was to write a story that gets chopped into four pieces, where you have to pause for five minutes of commercials then come back and re-engage your audience. Very difficult. When I wrote the first one [LaPaglia wrote two episodes], I went, “Oh god, I need to go and apologise to some of these guys!”

The workload on Without a Trace was counterproductive to doing good work. I would find myself acting on autopilot. I’d have the new episode that we were shooting next week sitting in my chair. The minute I finished doing a take, I’d go, “Right, bring in the writers, I’m going to talk to them for a minute.” Then we’d go back and do another take. Then they’d come in and I’d start talking about the next episode and what I think they should fix. It was like being schizophrenic … And at the end of it, I realised the show would have been successful whether I did that or not. So annoying. I wish I’d known that when I started.

Which role has been most personally fulfilling for you, and why?

Lantana. From the minute that I read it, I was in love with it. There wasn’t a single word in that script that I wanted to change, which is so unusual for me. Andrew Bovell wrote an absolutely lean, suspenseful script and we basically shot it exactly as he wrote it – that’s very rare. The preparation I got to do [to play a Sydney police detective] was incredible. It was some of the funniest stuff and some of the most heartbreaking stuff, in a way. I ended up being placed with these two Sydney detectives who were themselves under investigation. They were eventually found guilty, of course. They were the funniest guys, though. I remember they took me to Leichhardt once and everybody knew them. They didn’t pay for a single meal, ever, when I was there.

As someone who is also from Adelaide, I laughed out loud at your descriptions of the city, like: “There’s a bad energy running through it. Whenever I go back, I feel the same low-frequency unease that used to spook me as a kid.” Have your feelings about it changed at all?

A little bit. Not drastically. Remember, I’m talking about an Adelaide that I left a very long time ago. I was there recently working [on Death of a Salesman] and the Adelaide audiences were amazing. I didn’t feel Adelaide had changed all that much itself but I was greatly appreciative of the audiences. They were some of the most raucous. They laughed much more than other audiences did. Because there’s a dark streak in Adelaide, which I appreciated.

If a biopic was made about your life, who would play you?

God, that’s such an awkward question. Channing Tatum!

You write about ageing into playing Willy Loman. Are there any theatre roles that loom large for you as you grow older?

Anyone who’s written for a 67-year-old. There’s not many! I’m not a big wishlist guy. I’m much more in the moment. I’m a gun for hire. I’ve tried to self-generate projects and I found that to be an incredibly difficult and boring experience. I have no capacity to raise money. I can’t ask somebody to put money into a project that I know they’re going to lose money on. And they will! I’ve been the person that’s lost money. I’ve done the cardinal sin of investing in my own projects and I’ve lost so much money! And it doesn’t matter what contract you sign, either. You can sign a contract that says first dollar repayment, then they lie and cook the books. It’s happened to me more than once. Mostly with Australian films.

It is so much harder to get anything financed in Australia, right?

Well, they’re better at cooking the books. [laughs]

What is the best piece of advice you have ever received?

“Know your lines and don’t hit the furniture.” That is Spencer Tracy’s acting advice. I’ve always thought, dead on.

What has been your most memorable interaction with a fan?

This one was at a distance, which I liked. It was quite early in my career. I was walking down Sixth Avenue in New York, which is quite a wide avenue, and I hear from the other side: “Hey, LaPaglia!” I went, “Yeah?” And the guy says, “I hate you! I hate every movie that you’re in!” And I went, “Good for you. You have taste!” He laughed, I laughed and on we went.

That’s what I liked about New York back then. People just had no filter. My daughter lives there now and I always thought I’d end up back there. But having gone back to see my daughter a few times in New York, there’s only three good months a year in New York. Summer’s too hot. Winter’s miserable. I like California now.

But also I’m pretty sure I’m going to move to Mexico shortly. It is more to ride out Trump than anything. There’s no way that he’s going to let an election happen. I think you’re going to see some significant outbreaks of civil unrest. And do you know what? I’d just rather not be there for that.

I don’t like Trump but he’s quite old and he won’t be around much longer. That’s the saving grace. Once he goes, that whole party falls to pieces. The only thing that keeps it together is the cult of Trump. There’s all these people behind Trump that actually run the country and they won’t have that cover any more. They’re not very brave, they don’t want to put themselves out in the open – but Trump keeps outing them! [laughs] That’s one thing I like about him: he has no filter. He has no loyalty to anyone but himself. The idea that he thinks his son is going to run and win is a joke. His son is one of the most dislikable humans on Earth. Even more dislikable than Donald. At least Donald’s funny!

Do you have a nemesis? (And based on your memoir: is it John Landis?)

As you get older, those things count less. I don’t have the energy for that any more. I don’t think I would have considered John Landis a nemesis. I just did not understand him. I still don’t understand him! I’m not the only person that’s clashed with him but there are other people who swear by him. I just can’t respond to screaming. He screams a lot and that bothers me. It’s unnecessary and off-putting on a set. He may not do that any more, it was a long time ago. But I have read things where he said, “I don’t understand why he doesn’t like me” and I found it remarkable that he doesn’t understand. Maybe he doesn’t register that stuff. I’ll certainly won’t forget it! I’m just waiting for the lawsuit.

The Life We Choose by Anthony LaPaglia is published on 27 October (HarperCollins)

The moment I knew: I admitted I had a crush on her. She replied, ‘Well, that’s good. Isn’t it?’

The Guardian Sat, 24 Oct 2026 19:00:41 GMT

Actors Peter Houghton and Anne Browning played lovers onstage, but a shared sense of humour and a magazine horoscope flipped the script on their real-life relationship

Find more stories from the moment I knew series

Anne and I met in Melbourne in 1997 when we were cast in a production of Hamlet. We were both single and playing onstage lovers. The first time I saw her in the Melbourne Theatre Company cafeteria, she had a sleepy, grumpy face. I still recall those intense, slightly scary green eyes looking at me. I thought to myself: she is very attractive, but also quite formidable.

At first it was a little awkward, but humour was the key. We’d sit on the dusty rehearsal room floor in our tracksuits while the director was working with another actor. Instead of practising our lines, we’d flip through the faded 70s magazines left in the corner and make jokes about what the models in flares or with chopped beards might be saying as they shot the images.

One day by chance I flipped to the horoscopes. I asked Anne what the stars could have in store for us in 1972. She told me her sign was Scorpio – the same as mine. My aim was just to laugh at the bullshit of horoscopes but when I read it out, it stopped me cold: “You have met someone now through work who will be one of the most important people in your life, perhaps a partner and soulmate.”

It was weird and uncanny but we just laughed it off. I felt embarrassed because it sounded like some kind of calculated romantic ploy. I quickly flicked to the next page but somewhere in my brain I knew it was the truth.

Later, when the show was well under way, we were walking along St Kilda Road after a performance. We stopped at the lights and I summoned the courage to say: “I think I’ve got one of those crushes on you.” She looked at me and said: “Well, that’s good. Isn’t it?”

I took her cryptic and understated response as confirmation she felt the same way. It is very much her style – and I liked that it had a question mark on the end of it.

After the show closed our connection grew and we officially became a couple, filling our days and nights with dinner and theatre dates. She was living with her sister and I was living in this big groovy warehouse in Richmond with other actors. I liked that when she’d come to my place, the bohemian setting made me look a bit more impressive and artistic than I was.

Early on, we went on a hiking trip to Wilsons Prom. We were massively overpacked and it quickly emerged that neither of us was good at camping. As soon as we got back to the car we made a beeline to KFC and gorged ourselves on fried chicken after days of miserable camping stodge, secretly thankful we weren’t in nature any more.

Anne was violently ill all the way back – all that rich food after rehydrated dust! We both exposed ourselves as kind of daggy on that trip, and that was OK.

Anne and I share a clown-like heart that over the decades has helped us through hard times. Big life events like losing a parent have been somewhat easier because there’s a levity and lightness Anne brings – never letting me go into the dark places or stay there for too long.

Since meeting in that rehearsal room we’ve spent almost 30 years together, had two children and performed all over the world. Romantic love has its seasons, but really loving someone also has to do with trust. I trust her implicitly, she trusts me, and we don’t let each other down. We always show up for each other when it matters. We help each other realise our own dreams. That’s the thing about having a teammate you can rely on – it’s priceless.

We met working with each other as theatre artists, which we’re still doing now after all these years. A magazine from the 70s with an out-of-date horoscope written by a charlatan brought us together. I don’t believe in horoscopes … but I do believe in that one.

Peter Houghton, Anne Browning and Tom Gutteridge perform in the world premiere of Crapbox, showing from 27 October to 7 November at the Explosives Factory in St Kilda, Melbourne.

Why Stanley Matthews’ Ballon d’Or triumph echoes down the years for Harry Kane

The Guardian Sat, 24 Oct 2026 19:00:41 GMT

In 1956, the Blackpool great was recognised for his force of individual will, the very thing that makes the Bayern and England striker the standout candiate

Systems football began in 1963 – on the hallowed turf of Wembley – with the impact of a cynical foul by Gino Pivatelli.

At that moment in the European Cup final, when the hard-working Milan forward, brought in to combat Benfica’s Mário Coluna, caught the great playmaker, football of the individual came to an end. The foul not only checked a promising break, but broke a bone in Coluna’s foot. Without substitutes, he hobbled on, diminished, and Milan won 2-1 to lift the trophy and register the first victory for a team that prioritised the system over the individual. Modern football was born.

There are degrees, of course. The success of Zinedine Zidane’s Real Madrid was far more predicated on individuals than that of, say, Thomas Tuchel’s Chelsea or Pep Guardiola’s Manchester City. But, fundamentally, since that first success for catenaccio, football has been resolutely a team game.

Which is what always makes individual awards in the game such an oddity. Even in successful teams there is often a tension between the individual and the collective. That can be productive – sparks of friction are often creative. In sides that disappoint, though, the issue, whether the result of his own ego or the shortcomings of his teammates, is often an overreliance on one individual.

When the Ballon d’Or launched in 1956, that paradox was less pronounced. If the decision back then was less contentious than Monday’s award will assuredly be, though, it can only have been because there was no social media on which the furious could vent.

That the Hungarian vote was split between Ferenc Puskás, József Bozsik and Sándor Kocsis immediately highlighted a problem that successful teams still face, although given the award was made a month after the uprising was crushed by and Soviet tanks entering Budapest, with two of the three players in the process of defecting, it was probably just as well for the magazine France Football that none of the Hungarians did triumph.

Still, the choice of Stanley Matthews, from today’s perspective, looks odd. While it is true Blackpool had finished second in the First Division in 1956, but they were 11 points behind Manchester United and had gone out of the FA Cup in the third round. Was there not a case for Duncan Edwards or Tommy Taylor? Or for Bert Trautmann, the goalkeeper who won the Football Writers’ player of the year in 1956 after playing on with a broken neck in the final as Manchester City lifted the Cup?

Looking beyond England, what of Alfredo Di Stéfano, who had inspired Real Madrid to the inaugural European Cup? Or one of the Athletic Bilbao players who had just won La Liga? Or Pivatelli, who had been top-scorer in Serie A? Or Giuliano Sarti, the goalkeeper who had won the Scudetto with Fiorentina? Or Nikita Simonyan, whose goals had powered Spartak Moscow to the Soviet title? Matthews was 38, and there’s a clear sense that the inaugural Ballon d’Or was something of a lifetime achievement award.

Perhaps that is fine. Maybe the award should recognise longevity. What, after all, is it for? It’s certainly not just about how much a player wins in a given year. If it were, Fabián Ruiz would be a hot favourite on Monday, having won the World Cup, the Champions League and Ligue 1 this season.

Yet fine player though the midfielder undoubtedly is, he would be neither Paris Saint-Germain nor Spain’s player of the season. Besides, an award for winning lots of other awards is the definition of gilding the lily. There’s perhaps even an argument that individual awards represent an opportunity to acknowledge those who strive and delight but rarely win medals.

According to its website, the Ballon d’Or is “awarded based on three essential pillars … individual performance, team achievements, and class combined with fair play.” The “complete” winner will be defined by a “combination of talent, sportsmanship and competitive excellence”.

Team achievement is perhaps easiest to isolate. PSG have largely ditched their egos as Luis Enrique has led them to back-to-back Champions Leagues, but how do you tease out which of their exceptional front three has been the most important? Ousmane Dembélé won that battle last year. Khvicha Kvaratskhelia was arguably the standout this year, but, in a World Cup year, can a player whose country didn’t qualify be regarded as the best individual? And neither Dembélé nor the other member of the trio, Desiré Doué, had an especially notable World Cup.

Given the relative level of the French league and the fact PSG can rest players for domestic games to keep them fresh for Europe, it’s arguable the greatest achievement by a European club last season came from Arsenal, as they won the Premier League and reached the Champions League final. But their strength is the collective, and only three of the 30-man shortlist are Arsenal players, but none of Gabriel, William Saliba or Declan Rice had stellar World Cups.

What then of Spain? They too are a team short on star quality, certainly when Lamine Yamal is carrying an injury as he did for the first few months of this year. They won the World Cup, ultimately, because of the collective strength of their midfield. Rodri is the embodiment of their approach, but his involvement at Manchester City in the second half of last season was restricted.

Real Madrid have just endured one of only five trophyless seasons this century, which weakens the claims of Kylian Mbappé and Jude Bellingham and Vinícius. Lionel Messi had great moments at the World Cup but playing in MLS reduces his chances. Which perhaps means it’s time again to reward somebody who has had a good year, even if he went out of the World Cup in the semis and the Champions League in the quarters: Harry Kane.

Goals in the Bundesliga may not quite have the currency they did when Karl-Heinz Rummenigge was scoring them, but 61 in 51 club games last season represents a remarkable record, and he also got six at the World Cup, winning the game against the Democratic Republic of the Congo almost by force of individual will.

In a season without an obvious outstanding candidate, there seems a strong possibility that the panel, just as it did in 1956, will reward consistency and longevity.

Winds of change are coming for Australia as selection storm brews in South Africa

The Guardian Sat, 24 Oct 2026 19:00:41 GMT

Crushing defeat in second Test raises fresh questions about fragile batting lineup before Cape Town decider

The old adage that it is harder to get out of the Australia cricket team than into it is about to be put to the test. The horror show against South Africa in the second Test that ended in defeat for Australia by an innings and 31 runs exposed familiar fractures in the lineup that have less than a week between matches to be repaired.

The Australian selectors have shown in South Africa they are prepared to change a winning formula with the ball, while they have long been reluctant to cut ties with proven performers with the bat. But the first innings capitulation as Australia were all out for 99 in Gqeberha could force their hand to make a tough call or two – or perhaps more – as a selection storm brews before the series decider in Cape Town.

Marnus Labuschagne remains a persistent problem though arguably not the most pressing concern with Australia forced to consider other selection dilemmas. Even with three scores in the 30s from four innings in this series against South Africa, Labuschagne’s numbers are damning. So was his decision to loft off-spinner Simon Harmer into a stiff breeze and toward the long on fence when time at the crease was Australia’s only hope of escaping St George’s Park with a series lead.

The 32-year-old’s barren spell without a Test century has now extended well beyond three years and he has averaged 22.09 in 47 innings since last raising the bat against England at Old Trafford. He has not averaged more than 40 in a Test series since compiling 207 runs with three half-centuries on home turf against Pakistan in 2023-24. A Test average that sat above 61 in late 2022 has now dropped to 43.36.

Labuschagne had been clinging on to his spot since long before he was left out of the side for three Tests against West Indies that followed the 2025 World Test Championship final. Even with the numbers stacked against him, Labuschagne could still be handed one more last chance with a vacancy widely expected to open at the top of the order to partner Travis Head. The most likely route to another Test lifeline could therefore be for Labuschagne to open the innings in Cape Town, just as he did in the WTC final defeat last year.

Cameron Green and Josh Inglis are expected to be available for the third Test after recovering from injuries sustained during the one-day leg of the tour of South Africa. Green is nearing a return after suffering an abdominal strain in the third ODI and spent time batting in the nets as the second Test played out at St George’s Park. The 27-year-old once rivalled Labuschagne as the batter most under pressure, until he earned some credits with a defiant ton and a half-century from No 5 in the drawn series against Bangladesh. Head coach Andrew McDonald has said Green is unlikely to bowl in the Test series against South Africa but his batting alone should be enough to ensure selection, if fit, with Australia needing reinforcements to help fill the top six.

Inglis, on the other hand, remains far from a walk-up starter. The keeper-batter has become a mainstay of Australia’s white ball sides but has been unable to make the most of his opportunities in the longest format since a century on debut against Sri Lanka. Cooper Connolly is also back in the frame though the spin-bowling all-rounder’s hopes of adding to his one Test could rest on whether selectors are prepared to back the versatile but underperforming Beau Webster as well as the conditions at Newlands.

The three batters forming a queue just as Australia weigh up their options are all best suited to the middle order, just as gaps appear to be forming at the top. The selection gamble to recall Nic Maddinson after almost a decade in the Test wilderness and more than 18 months without first-class cricket, in part while recovering from testicular cancer, has shown few signs of paying off.

The 34-year-old looked out of his depth as he returned with a 33-ball duck and even a quick-fire 48 in the second innings in Durban only left a glimmer of hope that better was to come. Kagiso Rabada has troubled more established batters than Maddinson but the manner in which he was dismissed by the South Africa quick for another duck and eight in Gqeberha is likely to bring an abrupt end to the left-handed batter’s shock selection.

Shifting Matt Renshaw back to the top order and letting him settle in a position where he has been comfortable at domestic level could resolve the most glaring issue. It would also open up a spot for Green to return in the middle order while leaving the door ajar to perhaps call in Inglis or Connolly for the third Test against South Africa.

Australia have not lost a bilateral Test series since early 2023. They have not been defeated by a side other than India since Pakistan claimed a 1-0 series victory in the wake of “sandpapergate” in the UAE in 2018. The natural flow state of the side under captain Pat Cummins has been to ride out the highs and the lows. But the long journey through the top end of Australia, a tour of South Africa and home series against New Zealand, then the renewal of the tensest of rivalries in India and England already looks like being blown off course. Winds of change are finally coming for the Australia Test team. And this time, even Cummins’ unwavering calm might not be enough to weather the storm.
