Tottenham stun Chelsea for second league win in a week as Cole Palmer is sent off

The Guardian Sat, 24 Oct 2026 18:32:03 GMT

There are days when Tottenham go into these big games and find ways to beat themselves. This time, though, they held their nerve at a ground where they have mostly only known doom. Spurs played with control, stayed patient and won at Stamford Bridge for the first time since 2018 after waiting for Chelsea to press the self-destruct button during a calamitous and comical ending to a cagey game.

Chelsea were meant to have grown. Xabi Alonso had even praised his side’s emotional control and ability to manage awkward spells during the buildup, but perhaps that was asking for trouble. Chelsea, short of poise on and off the pitch, deserved to be beaten at home for the first time this season and there was plenty of blame to go around after Alonso got his tactics wrong, Mike Penders scored a ridiculous own goal and Cole Palmer was sent off after a lunge on Conor Gallagher when he was already on a booking.

Alonso suggested this could be a learning moment for Palmer. He could have been sent off when he earned his first booking for bumping into the excellent Mateus Fernandes and the frustration is that Chelsea still had time to find an equaliser before their No 10 suffered his rush of blood to the head.

It summed up a haphazard display, bringing an abrupt end to talk of Chelsea’s improved discipline. There was a collective loss of nerve from Alonso’s edgy side and Spurs made them pay by pressing at an obvious weakness. Fernandes targeted Penders with a corner and the young goalkeeper ruined his full Premier League debut by punching the ball into his own net.

It would be harsh to pin the defeat on Penders, who started only because Emi Martínez is out with a broken jaw. Palmer was foolish and Alonso was culpable. Chelsea were muted without the injured João Pedro but their manager’s setup did not help. Playing without a recognised striker and giving Geovany Quenda his first start at this level was a mistake from Alonso, as was his failure to bring on Danny Welbeck until it was too late and Spurs were already coasting towards only their second win in 35 attempts in this fixture.

Chelsea lacked punch and balance without João Pedro up front. They need the Brazilian back soon. Palmer and Morgan Rogers were ineffective as false nines and Spurs had the tactical edge. De Zerbi was delighted with his side’s poise in possession and raced from his technical area to celebrate when Mathys Tel capped off a thrusting display by making it 2-0 in the 87th minute.

Spurs are a work in progress. They were bottom at the start of the week but have something resembling momentum now. Two consecutive wins have lifted them into 12th place and allowed De Zerbi to focus on some fine performances from his youngsters. Fernandes, who has had a slow start since joining from West Ham, was outstanding in a deep-lying role in midfield and Archie Gray was impressive in both full-back positions.

• Spurs gained just their second away win in 35 attempts against Chelsea in the Premier League (D11 L22) and their first since April 2018 (3-1).

• Spurs have beaten Chelsea in all competitions at Stamford Bridge while keeping a clean sheet for the first time since December 1986 (also 2-0).

• Chelsea’s Mike Penders (21yrs 85d) is the second-youngest goalkeeper to score an own goal (pictured) in the Premier League, after Illan Meslier (20yrs 354d) for Leeds against Wolves in February 2021.

• Cole Palmer’s sending-off was the 100th red card Chelsea have been shown in the Premier League (excluding rescinded cards), becoming the third team to reach this milestone after Everton (113) and Arsenal (110).

Tel was also positive on the left-wing and it was not hard for the Spurs back four to contain Chelsea. The hosts usually fly out of the traps but struggled to assert themselves during a tepid first half. Chelsea had nobody to hold the ball up and only threatened when Palmer and Jordan Henderson tested Antonin Kinsky from long range.

Spurs built confidence, their midfield of Fernandes, Sandro Tonali and James Maddison outplaying Moisés Caicedo and Henderson. As ever the challenge was finding a clinical touch. Mohammed Kudus and Tonali sent hopeful efforts off target. Omar Marmoush met Andy Robertson’s cutback but shot straight at Penders.

The game was there to be won. Fernandes kept making interceptions and moved the ball quickly. Spurs were comfortable. Too comfortable? Their luck was out at the start of the second half. Maddison, who was a doubt before the game, had played well before making way for Gallagher.

Not that there was a response from Chelsea. They played in random bursts and Pedro Neto drew another save from Kinsky but they had no focal point without João Pedro and it was strange that Alonso brought Estêvão Willian on before turning to Welbeck.

Estêvão at least made an impact, driving in from the right to shoot wide. Spurs responded, Solanke and Pedro Porro for Marmoush and Robertson positive moves, and the opener followed.

Austin MacPhee, Chelsea’s set-piece coach, was busy telling four home players to stay high when Spurs won a corner. The box emptied out, Fernandes delivered from the left and Penders got his angles horribly wrong. The 21-year-old, who struggled in the air when Chelsea beat Leeds in the Carabao Cup last month, was thrown by a challenge from Van Hecke and watched in horror when his weak punch sailed over the line.

Chelsea were still coming to their senses when Palmer’s exit ended any hope of a comeback. It was Chelsea’s first red card of the season and was followed by Tel skipping in from the left to clinch a precious win for Spurs with a crisp shot from 20 yards.

Leicester turn up the hostility as Steward caps old-time beating of Northampton

The Guardian Sat, 24 Oct 2026 18:13:50 GMT

Leicester 28-7 Northampton

Hosts score four unanswered tries after interval

We have seen this before. It is easy to forget, amid all the tries and sunshine, that rugby has a darker side too: a wet, windy, deafening ferocity that not even the most twinkle-toed can transcend. And they practically invented it here.

This is not the first time Leicester have welcomed their beloved neighbours to the lair as champions and disabused them of any notions of grandeur. It took the Tigers 40 minutes to whip themselves into the necessary fervour, but when they did, all else followed: the rocking stadium at capacity, the win, the bonus point, the obliterated opposition.

“The crowd was brilliant,” said Geoff Parling, Leicester’s head coach. “The crowd is outstanding. This stadium is iconic. It’s rustic, I know it is. I’ve said it before. It’s old. But I wouldn’t change it for the world.”

It was not just the 40 minutes of directionless fumbling by the home team, but a mass fracas with a number of those visiting friends, which spilled into the stand, that sparked them into life, pretty much from the moment they re-emerged from the break.

The second-half Tigers showed the first-half version how a lineout and drive is executed, when Jamie Blamire scored their first try within four minutes of the restart. That earned them a one-point lead and normal service was resumed.

Half-time’s highlights analysis probably centred on that, well, we can’t really call them fights these days – this is the age of the camera, after all – but certainly pushing and shoving long after the referee had brought the first half to a close.

There were Alex Coles and Freddie Steward at each other’s throats. On it went, up the steps of the Crumbie Stand, where Henry Pollock, obviously, seemed more interested in tying his shoelace than getting in for an orange. Ollie Chessum and Steward, his England teammates, did not find it funny, shoving him all the way to the changing room.

“These games are going to be hostile,” said Phil Dowson, the Northampton coach. “In the current game, you can’t throw anything. It’s just push and shove and talk crap. That happens every derby. So I don’t think that had any impact. It’s not as if anyone got filled in. Well, you just can’t any more.”

Bristol moved into third place in the Prem table with a hard-fought 20-7 win over Exeter in appalling conditions at Ashton Gate.

It was their fifth successive league victory over Rob Baxter’s men after an old-style-rugby war of attrition in heavy rain and strong winds.

Bristol took the lead when a long pass by England scrum-half Harry Randall found Gabriel Ibitoye in space on the left wing to cross in the corner.

Centre James Williams slotted an excellent touchline conversion and he was also on target with a 35m penalty three minutes later.

Exeter got back into the game when they kicked a penalty to the corner and Greg Fisilau was driven over in emphatic style. Henry Slade converted to make it 10-7 and the visitors chances to draw level in the last 10 minutes when they turned down two kickable penalties inside the 22. Bristol made sure of victory three minutes from time when Williams kicked his second penalty and Luka Ivanishvili added some gloss when he forced his way over moments later.

On Friday night, Gloucester continued their resurgence to remain at the top of the Prem table with a hard-fought 23-5 victory over Bath at Kingsholm.

The win looked unlikely when Bath dominated for most of the first half, but Gloucester survived for a morale-boosting victory.

For Bath, it was a disappointing night as they fell to their third consecutive defeat and lost both Santiago Carreras and Guy Pepper to injuries. Freddie Thomas and Max Llewellyn scored Gloucester’s tries with George Barton converting both and adding three penalties. A try from Kepueli Tuipulotu was Bath’s sole response.

Christian Wade equalled Chris Ashton’s top-flight try record to inspire Newcastle to their first win of the season in the Prem. Wade made it 101 tries when he sprinted over in the 49th minute as Newcastle recovered from a 3-0 interval deficit to blow Sale away 17-3 in a gale at Kingston Park. It drew the 35-year-old winger, capped once by England, level with former Sale wing Ashton, who was inside the stadium.

The Newcastle captain, George McGuigan, grabbed the other home try with Josh Hodge adding seven points with the boot. There was little to cheer for Sale, who only had a George Ford penalty to show for their visit to the North East. Press Association

Such discord was in keeping with a first half in which neither side could quite find their feet on the slippery turf. Saints seemed more in tune with the kind of rugby that has prevailed before the rains came. Theirs was the only try of the first half, early on, when Finn Smith, with an advantage, chipped in behind, where Billy Searle spilled and James Pater gathered to score.

Leicester could not make anything of a stream of penalties in the first half, sending four of them to the corner in the first quarter and spilling or, often, not even securing the subsequent possession. How that was going to change.

Once Blamire’s try had restored order, the Tigers tore through the Saints at set piece and high ball. The champions deteriorated in the swirling rain.

Cameron Henderson was next to rise to take a lineout, after a ferocious scrum had earned the penalty. Henderson then finished in the corner like a winger, sent away by Gabriel Hamer-Webb. That put Leicester six ahead and five minutes later they were more than a score clear, this time Finn Carnduff finishing after another attacking lineout.

Leicester Steward (Pearson 79); Radwan, Wand (Bailey 73), Kata, Hamer-Webb; Searle, Van Poortvliet (Whiteley 73); Van der Flier (Haffar 73), Blamire (Asiata 79), Heyes (Hurd 73), Henderson (Thompson 79), O Chessum (capt), Wainwright, Carnduff, Cracknell (Moro 73). Tries Blamire, Henderson, Carnduff, Steward. Pens Steward, Searle. Con Searle.

Northampton Pater (Sleightholme 76); Freeman, Hutchinson, Dingwall (capt), Hendy; F Smith, Mitchell (McParland 58); Iyogun (Fischetti 63), Langdon (R Smith 63), Kundiona (Necolai 54), Coles, Prowse (Van der Mescht 63), Kemeny, Pearson (Lockett 58), Pollock (Chick 54). Yellow card Lockett 70. Try Pater. Con F Smith.

Referee Craig Maxwell-Keys.

The bonus point came in the final 10 minutes after one of the more bizarre swings of fortune. Smith’s cross-kick had sent George Hendy away from his own 22, Adam Radwan’s slap-down earned him a yellow card. But way back earlier in the move Tom Lockett’s head had collided with Solomone Kata’s. It was another totally innocent accident, Kata not only changing direction, but rising sharply to clash with the covering Lockett.

Even by rugby’s standards, the yellow card was absurd punishment. But it also meant Radwan’s was rescinded. On he came, off Lockett went, and over strolled Steward for the bonus point from the subsequent lineout.

When it is not your day, it is not your day, Saints must have rued. But when it is your day, especially at this grand stadium in the wet and windy twilight, it really is.

Tens of thousands of Lula supporters rally on eve of Brazilian election runoff

The Guardian Sat, 24 Oct 2026 18:11:44 GMT

Nearly 159 million people to head to polls on Sunday in battle between leftwing incumbent and Flávio Bolsonaro

Tens of thousands of supporters of Brazil’s leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, have streamed on to Rio’s most famous beach for a giant protest they hope will propel him towards a historic election fightback against his far-right rival, Flávio Bolsonaro.

Nearly 159m Brazilians will vote in the election’s runoff on Sunday, with the pair tied in the polls after Bolsonaro won the first round on 4 October by 47% to 45%.

On Saturday, under a fierce sun, red-clad crowds packed the 2.5-mile Copacabana beach in an attempt to help Lula clinch a dramatic and unprecedented comeback. Never since the return of democracy to Brazil in the 1980s has the first-round loser managed to bounce back.

Josias Silva, a 61-year-old truck driver, voiced confidence that his 80-year-old president would win a fourth non-consecutive term. He carried a homemade sign to the carnival-like procession reading: “Lula re-elected. Tomorrow will be a new day.”

“The people have woken up,” Silva said of the large pro-Lula street protests that have swept Brazil since the leftist’s first-round defeat, many led by students.

“Young people know we need this victory because otherwise we will have dictatorship again – and we don’t want dictatorship. We don’t want hatred. We don’t want guns. We want a country of love,” added Silva, celebrating the large number of people who came to witness one of the final presidential campaign rallies in Lula’s storied 50-year political career.

“There’s never been a demonstration like this one. This is the biggest protest in the history of Brazil. And we are going to win tomorrow with more than 60% of the votes,” Silva claimed.

Polls suggest a far tighter margin and most analysts see Bolsonaro, whose father, Jair Bolsonaro, was president from 2019 to 2022, as the slight favourite, having sold himself to voters as someone who will tackle chronic levels of violent crime with an iron fist.

However, in recent days Lula has appeared to regain the initiative and climb in the polls, amid a succession of scandals involving his rightwing foe. Last week the Brazilian magazine Piauí claimed that at the height of Brazil’s 2020 coronavirus outbreak, Flávio Bolsonaro attended a boat party attended by sex workers and vaccine lobbyists hoping to strike a deal with the government of his father.

Some experts speculate a Lula comeback may be possible. At the Copacabana rally, activists unfurled an enormous yellow and green banner declaring: “WE ARE GOING TO TURN THIS AROUND!”

“I’m super excited. Lula’s going to win,” said Marta Moraes, a 59-year-old restaurateur, as she joined Saturday’s demo.

Moraes said the election was not about left versus right. “We’ve nothing against the right … what we’re against is Bolsonarismo,” she said, tears filling her eyes as she recalled how Flávio Bolsonaro’s father botched the response to Covid during his chaotic 2019-2022 administration.

“I lost four members of my family because of Bolsonaro’s neglect,” Moraes said.

Jair Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year prison sentence for plotting a coup after he lost the 2022 election to Lula. Many Brazilian democrats fear he will be released – and could even return to government – if his son wins. Reports in the Brazilian press suggest several of Bolsonaro’s fellow plotters – who are now in prison or hiding in exile – may be given top military and police jobs in a Bolsonaro administration.

Cammy Marinho, a 49-year-old DJ and activist, said: “I’m here to prevent democracy becoming extinct – which is what the Bolsonaro family wants”.

Marinho said she had spent the past fortnight fighting to persuade people who voted for Bolsonaro, or did not vote in the first round, to back Lula.

“It’s non-stop work: in the bakery, in the supermarket, on the underground – whenever you feel there is an opening to talk to someone and show to them the reality, everything that Lula has done and is doing for the people and everything that this [Bolsonaro] family has done against the people,” she said.

Many marchers were part of the so-called “Lula’s Army” – a 10 million-member WhatsApp group that was created after the first round in the hope of turning the election around.

“Being a soldier in Lula’s army … means fighting for Brazilian democracy. This isn’t a normal election,” said Isabella Gaze, 64, a retired teacher and one of the group’s members.

“They constantly claim Lula is corrupt. But the truth is that they represent the most rotten and worst part of Brazilian politics. This is what we are fighting against now,” Gaze said of the Bolsonaros.

Many of the faces on Copacabana beach were teenagers, including 14-year-old Heitor Lopes da Silva. Silva had come from the city of Duque de Caxias in his wheelchair, with a placard that said: “Lula, I’m a person with a disability and I’m here to support you.”

“My whole life I’ve believed Lula was a good president. [Bolsonaro] represents the destruction of Brazil …. he represents sadness and death,” he said of the Bolsonaro-era Covid catastrophe.

Large crowds of Bolsonaro supporters also hit the streets, including in Belo Horizonte, the capital of Minas Gerais state, which has Brazil’s second-largest electorate after São Paulo, and is a key bellwether. No presidential candidate has ever won the presidency without securing Minas Gerais, where Bolsonaro led by just under 5% in the first round.

Thousands of Bolsonaristas gathered to see their candidate in a palm-lined plaza called Praça da Liberdade. To the booming sound of AI-generated funk carioca tracks praising Bolsonaro, a sea of supporters dressed in Brazil’s yellow football jersey waved Brazilian flags – and many of the United States too.

“The US is a great nation. Who wouldn’t want to be aligned with them?” said 56-year-old cosmetics entrepreneur Marcos Antonio, holding a flag that merged the emblems of both countries.

“I don’t want an alliance with Cuba or Venezuela. I want to move forward,” Antonio added. When reminded that Venezuela was currently aligned with the US after Donald Trump’s January invasion, he said: “True. But for now, a fully right-wing government hasn’t been installed yet. It’s in transition.”

Antonio Carlos Costa Jr, the 59-year-old owner of a shooting club, complained: “Lula did nothing for the country.”

Jair Bolsonaro relaxed gun ownership and buying laws – which security experts agree ended up diverting many firearms to criminal gangs – whereas Lula tightened regulations once again. “Jair Bolsonaro simply gave citizens the right to defend themselves, and his son will do the same,” said Costa Jr.

Lula supporters scoff at the idea that Bolsonaro, who has a history of well-documented ties with members of Rio’s paramilitary “militia” groups, could rid Brazil of criminality.

“If we vote the militias into power, we will be living in a dictatorship,” said Erika Cavalcante, 43, an architect who came to the march with a sign reading: “Don’t let the mobsters win.”

Hundreds of thousands march across France in protests over schools and policing

The Guardian Sat, 24 Oct 2026 17:54:41 GMT

Almost 1,000 arrested as police charge crowd in Paris and teargas used to stop protesters reaching other city centres

Hundreds of thousands marched in cities across France on Saturday in largely peaceful protests to support schoolchildren’s demands for more teachers and repairs to dilapidated buildings, as Emmanuel Macron faces a social and political crisis in his final months as president.

In Paris, at least 110,000 people marched along the eastern edge of the city, according to government estimates. They supported high schoolers but also complained of the high cost of living and the government’s heavy policing, saying riot police had been sent to target school protesters over the past month, instead of the government offering political solutions.

The mood in Paris on Saturday afternoon was peaceful and lighthearted, with brass bands playing and children and grandchildren present. Some people carried banners critical of the government’s policing, saying: “Oppression breeds rebellion” and “The right to protest”.

But at the end of the Paris demonstration, at Porte de Vincennes on the city’s eastern edge, different groups of masked men dressed in black emerged who had not appeared to have taken part in the peaceful march. Some groups of masked men threw glass bottles and stones at police, who responded with teargas, water cannon and stun grenades. A bin was set alight and fireworks were set off towards police.

Riot police also charged a larger crowd of protesters at the end of the Paris march, using batons against them.

Police fired teargas to prevent protesters in Lyon, Lille, Montpellier, Nantes and Toulouse from reaching city centres. In Marseille, some bin fires were lit amid clashes with police. At least two people were seriously injured, one in Clermont-Ferrand and another in Toulouse, who reportedly had fingers blown off.

The government estimated that at least 400,000 people had marched across France. Trade unions estimated the number at double that. The interior ministry said there had been almost 1,000 arrests.

Laurent Nuñez, the interior minister, said that at various street marches across France there were what he called “high-risk groups” who “broke away from the main body and sought to commit acts of violence”.

More than 70,000 police were on the streets of French cities, with shops boarded up and many museums closed. The government had feared a repeat of last Saturday, when, despite peaceful protests taking place, France saw one of the most violent days of unrest in years, with public buildings burned, hundreds of shops destroyed and looted and at least 2,700 people arrested in cities across the country.

At Saturday’s protests, there was widespread anger at Macron for banning non-union demonstrations that his government deemed “illegitimate” and for keeping all protesters away from city centres.

At the Paris march, Nadège, a 43-year-old communications worker, said she had been teargassed last weekend at a peaceful demonstration. “I’m out again peacefully today to support everyone who is brave enough to demonstrate. It does take courage. People are afraid now. We have to keep our rights alive … In France, it’s our legal right to protest in the street and I’m here to defend that.”

A 21-year-old student from a Paris science faculty that is now blockaded by demonstrators said: “We feel in France that we are increasingly living in an authoritarian regime that is trying to stop our democratic right to protest in the street.”

The radical left presidential candidate, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who took part in the Paris rally, said Macron must “give in” and address France’s social malaise or face repeated protests. “Given the current situation, I think he will come to understand that this will happen again every week,” Mélenchon said.

The government has been facing a crisis since the start of high school demonstrations in mid-September, when children aged between 15 and 18 began protesting against staff shortages at their schools, leaking and crumbling buildings, and a lack of chairs in overcrowded classrooms. It grew into the biggest youth movement in years, with trade unions, teachers and parents joining. Police investigations are under way after some children and protesters were maimed and injured by explosive police weaponry.

At Saturday’s march there were some people dressed in yellow vests who had taken part in the gilets jaunes anti-government protests of 2018 and 2019. Standing amid demonstrators, Jérôme Rodrigues, a key figure from the gilets jaunes protest, said: “Today the government is afraid; that is why they are pushing demonstrators to the edge of the city, away from places of power. It’s not police shields that will provide an answer to French people struggling and unable to make ends meet.” He said it was likely that demonstrations would continue.

Pierre, 60, a retired banking consultant, said he was demonstrating in support of school students. “I have an eight-year-old granddaughter. I want her to have a brighter future than the sombre times we are facing today. There is a complete refusal by the government to listen to people’s demands.”

Jesse, 40, a charity worker from the north of Paris, carrying a sign saying “Free Hugs”, said: “I’m so angry. I’m here to support schoolchildren’s demands for better conditions. I’m so proud of them, and we have to stand together.”

She said: “I know I’m not going to war by coming out to demonstrate peacefully. But at times it really does feel like a war … This is the first time I’ve prepared so carefully for a peaceful march, wearing old clothes in case they are gassed or torn.”

In Orléans, thousands shouting anti-fascist slogans marched against a congress held by Marine Le Pen’s far-right anti-immigration National Rally party. Protesters criticised Le Pen, a frontrunner in next year’s presidential election, as well as Macron, who steps down from power next year. “Macron, resign. Le Pen in prison,” the crowd shouted.

Scottish Premiership: Kelsy fires Rangers to emphatic win; Dundee United pip Aberdeen

The Guardian Sat, 24 Oct 2026 16:52:06 GMT

Rangers 4-0 St Johnstone; Dundee United 3-2 Aberdeen

Kevin Kelsy scores two to sink 10-man Saints

Derek McInnes asked his Rangers side to be “brilliant” against St Johnstone and was rewarded with a 4-0 Premiership win at Ibrox. After dropping two points at Dundee last Saturday, the Light Blues dominated the first half but only led at the interval through a goal in the 29th minute from the Venezuela forward Kevin Kelsy.

Saints started the second half brightly but goals from the Gers striker Ryan Naderi in the 61st minute and Kelsy again five minutes later had the home side cruising. The Saints substitute Kai Fotheringham was shown a straight red card by Chris Graham in the 74th minute for his high challenge on the midfielder Nico Raskin, before the substitute Tochi Chukwuani added a fourth for the hosts with three minutes remaining.

McInnes said: “It’s quite ironic in the sense that we were so good and so brilliant at times in the first half and create so many opportunities, that we were only a goal to the good at half-time. And obviously, we don’t want to let the frustration of those missed opportunities and dominance filter into the second half.

“I think half-time came at a bad time for us because, despite the conditions, some of the play was really good. I asked the players to be brilliant today, not just win the game, can we really commit to being the best we can be, as good as we can be? And I thought we were in the first half. Everything was brilliant except the result at half-time because we should have been more in in front.”

Celtic can restore their four-point advantage over Rangers at the top when they travel to Hibernian, the bottom side, at noon GMT on Sunday.

Dundee United won a rollercoaster game 3-2 against Aberdeen at Tannadice. Zidane Iqbal scored for the hosts before the visitors equalised through Nesta Guinness-Walker – both players scoring their first goals for their clubs.

United took the lead once more thanks to a Dylan Tait strike, with Connor Ronan drawing Aberdeen level after the break. Zac Sapsford secured all three points for his side, with the win moving United up to fourth – one point behind Hearts, who are at Motherwell on Sunday – while Aberdeen dropped to ninth.

Two own goals helped Falkirk climb to seventh with a 3-0 victory over Kilmarnock. The Guardian Sat, 24 Oct 2026 16:40:21 GMT

Woman alleging frat-house rape has privacy and safety issues outweighing need to publicly identify her, judge says

The woman at the center ⁠of rape allegations against students at Cornell University can continue using a pseudonym in ⁠her lawsuit, a ⁠judge ​has ruled.

The New York state judge Phaedra Perry-Bond ruled on Friday that the woman’s ⁠privacy interests – particularly concerns for her safety – outweighed any need to publicly disclose her identity ⁠in court proceedings.

The woman alleges she ​was drugged and ‌raped by students at the elite Ivy League university in upstate New York in 2024.

She has become the target of threats, ‌her lawyer, Thomas Giuffra, said earlier this month.

The defendants in the lawsuit have not opposed the request for anonymity, as the woman continues to go by a generic placeholder name “Jane Doe” used in many legal or official situations, especially when a woman’s identity is protected.

But Perry-Bond wrote in a ruling released on Friday that “some members of the public have made it their ‌mission to try and identify Jane Doe”.

The judge warned that “cyberstalking and engaging in ​or encouraging threats across state lines, whether it be of Jane Doe, of any of the named defendants, or their attorneys, can be considered a federal ⁠crime and perpetrators of those acts may be subjecting ​themselves ​to prosecution”.

The woman in the Cornell case was 20 at the time ​of the ‌alleged gang-rape at a fraternity house at the university. She filed her ​suit on 16 September, prompting prosecutors to reopen a criminal investigation they had initially closed without charges.

Mass protests erupted on Cornell’s Ithaca campus earlier this month, with students criticizing officials’ handling of Jane Doe’s gang-rape allegations, demanding the university president’s resignation and painting “SMASH THE PATRIARCHY” on an administration building.

Protesters shouted “Ban the frats” and held signs saying “At Cornell, rapists are safer than women” and “Stop rape culture.” Some demonstrators directed their anger at Michael Kotlikoff, Cornell’s president, arguing he had failed to keep students safe and chanting, “Kotlikoff, resign!”

Clinical Arsenal earn precious win against Everton thanks to Konsa and Gabriel

The Guardian Sat, 24 Oct 2026 16:03:49 GMT

The wait goes on for David Moyes. The 63-year-old Scot must have been hoping that on his 14th visit to this stadium as Everton’s manager, his luck would change. Yet from the moment Ezri Konsa slammed home his first goal for Arsenal as the Premier League champions rediscovered their knack of scoring from set pieces, the writing was on the wall.

While it took until midway through the second half for Gabriel Magalhães to make sure of the victory, Arsenal were never going to let slip the chance of moving level on points at the top with Manchester City after their defeat by Aston Villa earlier in the day.

Asked whether it was strange that his side are again going toe-to-toe with their great rivals but with the added uncertainty of what punishment City will receive after being found guilty of 115 charges by the Premier League, Mikel Arteta said: “[We are] just focusing on what we can do. We are very pleased with 90% of the results and performances that we have.”

This was hardly a vintage performance from the clinical home side after a testing week but it did not need to be against opponents who offered precious little in attack, even if they defended for their lives at times.

Having gone six matches without defeat to start the season, a second in succession will only add to Everton’s concerns after confirmation that the club’s American owners want out.

“It was always going to be hard after conceding the early goal,” said Moyes, whose solitary victory at the Emirates was as West Ham’s manager in 2023. “I want us to challenge the top teams but it’s difficult when you see the strength of their bench.”

Everton’s record at this stadium is almost as bad as their manager’s. They arrived in north London having won twice in 35 matches here and had to do without Jarrad Branthwaite and Jack Grealish, who was ruled out with illness. It did not bode well for them when Arsenal took the lead in the seventh minute with a third corner in succession.

Gabriel made the crucial first contact at the near post and Jordan Pickford tipped the ball on to the crossbar, only for Vitaliy Mykolenko’s failed clearance under pressure from Viktor Gyökeres to allow Konsa to ram home from close range. After a record-breaking 25 goals from set pieces last season, it was their first of this campaign.

It was a measure of Arsenal’s exertions against Bayern Munich on Wednesday that Arteta rotated his side more than usual for a Premier League match, making five changes.

Eberechi Eze and Noni Madueke spurned good opportunities to extend the lead in front of the watching England head coach, Thomas Tuchel. The latter was left out of the last squad, but could well benefit from Bukayo Saka’s expected long absence due to a thigh injury. He was inches away with an instinctive effort with his right foot from the edge of the area on the half-hour mark and was consistently Arsenal’s most dangerous threat.

Everton must have feared the worst as yet another Arsenal corner – 10 during the first half – was launched into the area. Yet the defence just about stood firm.

A moment’s lapse of concentration from Ben White just before half-time almost gave Everton an equaliser but Thierno Barry could not get enough on his attempt to flick the ball past David Raya in their clearest opening.

Gyökeres looked determined to make an impression on his first Premier League start of the season but the Sweden striker, who has yet to score for his club this term, looked laboured.

• With both Arsenal and Manchester City doing so this season, this is just the third top-flight campaign to have two teams win at least seven of their opening eight matches after 1892-93 (Preston and Sunderland) and 1913-14 (Blackburn and Manchester United).

• This was David Moyes’s 400th defeat across all competitions in his managerial career with all clubs. 31 of these have come against Arsenal, more than against any other opponent.

• The opener from Ezri Konsa (pictured celebrating) was Arsenal’s first set piece goal (excluding penalties) since May against Crystal Palace, ending a run of 13 games without one. Opta

He could not believe it when Tony Harrington penalised him for a foul on James Tarkowski and a sheepish Arteta earned himself a booking for protesting. Unsurprisingly, Gyökeres’ number was up soon after as Arsenal turned to their bench.

It took less than 60 seconds for Gabriel to head in at the back post as White offered Tuchel a timely reminder of his qualities with a brilliant cross.

Moyes’ frustration meant he joined Arteta in the referee’s notebook. Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall could have made things interesting but his header fizzed just wide of a post.

Arsenal are now breathing down City’s necks, although whether this title race lasts the course remains unknown.

Ukraine’s military says Starlink satellite connection stable after recent restrictions

The Guardian Sat, 24 Oct 2026 15:47:20 GMT

Volodymyr Zelenskyy offers thanks to US allies for restoring system key to air defence and ‘frontline logistics’

Ukraine’s military has a “stable connection to Starlink”, the Ukrainian government has said, 10 days after its ability to use the satellite communications system was suddenly restricted.

The Starlink satellite terminals, which are produced by Elon Musk’s SpaceX but managed by the US government, are a key component of Ukraine’s military operations. Sudden speed restrictions on the terminals, which capped operations at speeds of 160km/h (99mph), led to the failure of several Ukrainian combat missions earlier this month.

The military’s ability to intercept Russian attack drones was hampered and some Ukrainian operations to strike behind enemy frontlines were cancelled. Russia was able to launch ballistic missiles at Ukraine without any advance warning from the US.

The speed restrictions coincided with the announcement by Donald Trump of a US deal to buy Russian diesel, although the US president initially denied that his administration was behind the decision to cut intelligence sharing with Ukraine.

“I don’t know if it was anybody, but it wasn’t me, and I don’t think it was Elon,” Trump said, referring to Musk, SpaceX’s chief executive.

However, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, appeared to throw suspicion on Musk when he defended Trump last Wednesday. “The president has nothing to do with the decisions that are made by Starlink and Starshield and by Mr Musk,” Rubio said. “That’s a private company. The president doesn’t run that company and can’t direct that company to do anything.”

Musk was quick to blame the limits on Starshield on the Trump administration, writing on X last week that the systems were “owned and controlled by the US government”. “Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately Potus [president of the United States],” he wrote.

The US vice-president, JD Vance, backed Musk on Thursday, saying the billionaire “doesn’t want to get in the middle of what is a war between two state actors without the United States government effectively directing him on what to do”.

Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, blamed both parties: “It was a message from [the] American government to limit the speed … And technically, SpaceX did it.”

There were no similar restrictions on Starshield terminals in EU countries and that they applied only to Ukraine, he added. “In other words, this is a planned operation.”

He said the decision would “bring a lot of human losses … of course people would die”.

Maisie Symonds’ first-half stunner sent Brighton on their way to a 3-0 win against West Ham at the Amex Stadium. Meghan and Prince Harry recently moved back to the UK from the US.

“The letter was reviewed and a decision was made that it should be passed to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex for their awareness. The details of the allegations in the letter were not shared with other law enforcement agencies.

In a statement on Friday, issued through her spokesperson, the duchess said: “I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed.

‘Bolso shows all signs of fascism’: the journalist who predicted Brazil’s future – and paid the ultimate price

The Guardian Sat, 24 Oct 2026 12:00:33 GMT

Dom Phillips warned that Jair Bolsonaro would make life more dangerous for reporters and the Amazon rainforest, and that his sons were even more extreme

“Bolso shows all signs of fascism, as do his supporters,” the murdered British journalist Dom Phillips told me before his death. “His sons are all more extreme if anything.”

These words were written in 2018 by the Guardian contributor shortly before the election of the far-right former army captain Jair Bolsonaro as president of Brazil – a prospect that Dom viewed with dread.

As he predicted back then, this would lead to more mortalities, more destruction of the Amazon rainforest and more danger for journalists. His own life and death were to prove the prescience of this foresight.

Dom was killed four years ago alongside the Brazilian indigenous expert Bruno Pereira, but his views feel alarmingly relevant once more as Brazil braces for a presidential runoff this Sunday in which a member of the far-right Bolsonaro clan is once more a favourite to win – despite all the dangers that poses to the environment and those who seek to protect it.

Polls suggest Flávio Bolsonaro – the son of Jair Bolsonaro – is narrowly ahead of the Workers party incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Although the difference between them is within the margin of error and Lula appears to have gained momentum, the possibility of another Bolsonaro administration is likely to fill any friends of Dom and Bruno with alarm.

Dom was no diehard political leftist. In an earlier election, he shocked me by expressing support for the centre-right challenger Aécio Neves because he felt the then Workers party administration had become too entangled in corruption. But while Dom eschewed ideology, he had clear ideas about the importance of sound, considerate government in the interests of people and the planet.

He saw the Bolsonaro family as a menace to both. Looking back through our exchanges of WhatsApp messages, I am struck by the prescience of his observations.

Some may be inclined to normalise Flávio as just another candidate, or to assume that all politicians are as bad as each other. That was certainly not how Dom saw things – and he came to pay the ultimate price for his efforts to address those concerns.

“I don’t think I have ever been so negative about Brazil’s future. Spent a week in Manaus, everyone seemed to be voting for Bolsonaro,” he wrote ahead of the first-round vote in 2018. “ If he wins, what would it be like living here? It’s like a ‘carte blanche’ to attack anyone his mob disagrees with.”

Two weeks later, he observed the creeping hostility towards the media at a Bolsonaro press conference, which he said was packed with rightwing supporters who loudly booed a journalist that they considered unfriendly.

This followed a physical attack on the organiser of an anti-Bolsonaro women’s group. “Chilling times here,” he wrote on 12 October of that year.

“I agree that Bolso shows all signs of fascism, as do his supporters.

“This is a very dark and worrying period and it is only going to get worse. My sense if [sic] that it is also going to become more dangerous for journalists.”

He detailed the changes he was already seeing – the proliferation of lies, a hardening of discourse online and a rising sense that violence was acceptable. He predicted more people would die as a result of Bolsonaro’s policies, and the wider environment would also pay a heavy price.

Over the following years, Dom’s reports for the Guardian confirmed his worst fears. Bolsonaro’s mismanaged response to the Covid crisis contributed to more than 704,000 deaths – the second highest toll in the world after the US.

His four years in power saw the highest level of Amazon deforestation of any presidential terms. Orwellian misinformation campaignsincluded efforts to blame environmental groups for forest fires and to boast – contrary to all the evidence – that his government was saving the Amazon.

In August 2019, Dom told me these claims were “staggering even by Bolsonaro standards, especially given Flávio Bolsonaro’s bill to get rid of legal reserves”, the latter a reference to a proposal by the then president’s son – and now presidential candidate – to remove one of the greatest protections for the rainforest.

Dom also came under social media attack after he politely asked the president about Amazon deforestation at a press conference. Bolsonaro snapped back, “the Amazon is Brazil’s, not yours, OK?” – a reply that was instantly spread across networks to suggest the nationalist had bested the foreigner.

Dom felt he had been set up. “The smile doesn’t last for long,” he observed. “Wonder how much of the Amazon will be gone by the end of Bolsonaro’s first term?”

That answer to that question would be 45,000 sq km (17,400 sq miles) over Bolsonaro’s 2019-2022 period in office, roughly equivalent to the loss of more than a million trees a day, and 59.5% higher than the previous four years.

Dom never got to report on that. He too was cut down, murdered alongside Bruno on 5 May 2022 close to the Javari Valley indigenous territory while he was researching a book titled How to Save the Amazon.

The man who confessed to their killing was a fisher named Amarildo da Costa de Oliveira, who is now on trial. He apparently resented Bruno’s efforts to prevent him invading the indigenous territory, incursions that were illegal but encouraged by the president’s weakening of protections, rhetoric against environmental groups and tacit acceptance of lawlessness. As Dom had foreseen, Bolsonaro had made life more dangerous for journalists and the forest.

Jair Bolsonaro lost office later that year and was then convicted for attempting a military coup to overturn the election results. Dom had also anticipated this: “He is a criminal and I sincerely hope one day I see him being arrested by those federal police guys in the balaclavas in black,” he wrote in 2021.

I am sure Dom would have been cheered by last week’s government announcement of record low deforestation in the Amazon and the neighbouring Cerrado savanna thanks to strong enforcement during Lula’s current four-year term.

Such gains look precarious now that one of Bolsonaro’s “more extreme” sons is frontrunner in the presidential runoff and has promised, if he wins, to free his father and give him any job of his choice in the government.

Is there time for Lula to turn this around? How much worse could a second Bolsonaro family administration be? How much life – people, trees and other species – will die if they return to power?

I wish Dom were still around to discuss that.

My mother donated her body to science. I really wasn’t prepared for what came next

The Guardian Sat, 24 Oct 2026 12:00:33 GMT

The process included a gala featuring medical students doing aerial yoga and singing Taylor Swift to donors’ families. In some way, it was absolutely perfect

When my mother, Erin O’Connell, was diagnosed with a rare and aggressive cancer in late 2022, one of her first thoughts was: “What will I do if I can’t work?”

At the time, she was 62 years old and working as a physical therapist in Portland, Oregon, where she had recently moved to live closer to me and my family. Reluctantly, she filed for short-term disability from her job and paused her training to become a volunteer search and rescue EMT.

My mom was 40 when she started physical therapy school. I was already a teenager. Despite her newfound stress, I remember how deeply it affected me to watch her fall in love with her work. The year she took anatomy lab she told my sister and me – and anyone who would listen – that dissecting a real human body was the coolest thing she had ever gotten to do, and when she died, she wanted to donate her body to science, too.

I spent so much of my childhood wanting nothing more than my mother’s hard-earned approval, and here she was, utterly devoted to a dead body. On some level, I was jealous of that cadaver.

Now here I was, 25 years later, with my mom’s illness progressing, printing out the paperwork from the nearest med school: “Enrollment Form To Bequeath a Body On Behalf of an Individual”. And all I could think was how jealous I would be of the students who would dissect my mother – who would get to do what I never could, crack her open and peek inside.

This paperwork, though, was its own form of clarity. My mom was going to die, too young and against her will, but we had a plan – an easy, free, meaningful one at that.

Of course, the reality ended up being more complicated and more absurd than I imagined.

After her death, my mom’s body was transported to Oregon Health & Science University (OHSU), just across the river from where we had both lived in Portland.

I worried that, in my grief, I might drive to campus to find out where she was. Would I be tempted to wander the halls, looking for her? Better not to dwell on it, I decided. Instead, I imagined she had been shipped elsewhere, used for something vaguely embarrassing like rectal science or dentistry.

Every year, roughly 25,000 Americans sign up to donate their bodies to science after death. But demand far outstrips supply. According to Tamara Ostervoss, director of OHSU’s body donation program, “it remains an unpopular choice,” partly because so few people even know it’s an option. In Oregon, she told me, only about 1% of people choose to donate their bodies.

For my mom, the registration process was simple: a two-page consent form, signed in front of two witnesses. My mom agreed that her family would not profit from the donation or any discoveries that resulted from it, and that we would have no say in how her body was used. She chose to have her remains cremated and mailed back to us. Eighteen months later, they arrived in a red, white and blue US Postal Service box marked “HUMAN REMAINS”, with an illustration of an urn on the side.

By the time I spoke to Ostervoss, the remains were safely in my closet – and I had a darkly funny story about my awkward visit to the post office to prove it.

Still, talking to the woman who had overseen my mom’s donation was emotionally fraught. As Ostervoss likes to say, your life dictates how you go on to teach others. Thanks to the progression of her cancer, my mom was missing so many internal organs by the end that I joked she would have given some poor anatomy student a pretty limited education.

It’s a credit to Ostervoss’s professional, respectful demeanor that she didn’t laugh so much as smile warmly, with pity in her eyes.

I didn’t tell her that, when my mom was still alive, I had asked her how she would feel if she ended up sold to one of those Bodies exhibits from China. Would my kids recognize her without her skin on?

She laughed, then shrugged. “What do I care? I won’t be there.”

But I will be, I wanted to say.

You can decide what happens to your body after you die, if you’re willing to plan ahead. But that doesn’t necessarily mean that, once you’re no longer there to insist, your family will follow through with your plans.

If your loved ones are firmly opposed to body donation, they can simply call a funeral home instead. Which is why, if you’re considering donating your body to science, it’s a conversation worth having while you’re still alive.

Most families, though, fall somewhere in the squeamish-but-accepting middle. “We’ve had families where they might not choose it for themselves, but they really want to honor and support their loved ones’ wishes,” Ostervoss said. “So they’re more along the lines of, “I don’t want to hear anything about it, I don’t want to know about it. I just want to support my mom.”

For me, the mild unease of never knowing exactly what happened to my mom’s corpse at the university was peanuts compared with the prospect of being upsold a coffin by a funeral director while I waded through grief. According to the National Funeral Directors Association, the average cost of burial in our home state of Oregon is $7,895 and the average cost of cremation is $5,812 – numbers that don’t even include a funeral or memorial service.

With body donation, you can always do a memorial later, but in the meantime there are no grief-stricken decisions about embalming or viewings. No deciding what goes on the gravestone, no grave. What does happen is a brief phone screening (in our case, by a hospice nurse), followed by a brief, in-person physical assessment. Then, voilà, off my mom went to fulfill her destiny as, in the language of the body program, someone’s first patient.

The reality is that about 25% of registered donors don’t meet the eligibility requirements at the time of death, per Ostervoss’ estimate. “It’s like medical school,” she said, “Not everyone gets in.”

A common disqualifier is high or low body weight, and privately my sister and I feared my mom had lost too much to be accepted. When she was, I found myself literally jumping up in the air to cheer. “She passed her final test!” I wrote to her sibling group chat, triumphantly. “PTL!” her sister wrote back. Praise the Lord!

Was it odd to feel jubilant on the same day I watched my mother take her final breath? Absolutely, but it was also a gift. It really did feel like her version of a med school acceptance, I told Ostervoss.

Those 150 bodies who do “get in” are able to go on to teach approximately 5,000 learners across the state of Oregon, encompassing not just the first-year medical students you might think of, but surgical residents and practicing doctors, dentists and other healthcare workers.

For students, the benefits of learning about human anatomy and practicing procedures on the real thing, with no risk of hurting them, are intuitive and obvious – the difference between a flight simulator and piloting an airplane. Think of all the variation in vasculature and body size. In reality, no surgeon would see the same internal organs twice. It’s the kind of thing that can’t be replicated, not even with advanced 3D models with haptic feedback.

The emotional side of the student experience is another story. Facing your cadaver for the first time as a new med student has always been a rite of passage, but as western life expectancy increases and our end-of-life rituals become more and more sanitized, anatomy lab is more and more often students’ first encounter with a dead person.

Historically, med school programs have dealt with this by cultivating what the writer Mary Roach calls “a sort of sink or swim mentality about dealing with death”, a kind of future doctor hazing ritual that encouraged future providers to desensitize themselves.

Roach talked to the director of the medical anatomy program at Vanderbilt University, Art Dalley, who says that, “There was a time not all that long ago when students were taught to be insensitive, as a coping mechanism.” In the past, she writes: “Humor – at the cadaver’s expense – was tolerated, condoned, even.”

Not so in our current era. Instead, I received an invitation to a gala in the mail.

At OHSU, the anatomy class culminates in what Ostervoss calls, “the body ceremony”, a 25-year tradition where students plan a memorial to honor the donors and families who have made their education possible.

The service was created to honor the donors, but it’s also important emotionally for the students who are encouraged to have conversations with the families at the reception afterward.

After a year of almost willful dissociation on my part, it was a bizarre experience to be welcomed in. The invite explained that the service would include a slideshow of the 100 or so donors who had given their bodies that year. Students would show their gratitude through performances and reflections they had programmed themselves.

It sounded bizarre but earnest, like a talent show for death. I was thrilled.

Once we were in the auditorium, my eyes darted over to the section of nervous future doctors in new blazers and kitten heels. There was a kind of aura of promise about them, and I felt almost maternally proud. It was clear that families and students had a wild interest in each other and my heart raced as I scanned the rows, looking, as I imagine they did, for some glint of recognition.

I leaned over to whisper to my sister, a note of hope in my voice. “Do you think they’ll recognize us?”

“Meaghan,” she shushed me. “No.”

“But maybe our height?” (My mother, like us, was around 5ft tall with shoes on.)

Lauren just gave me a look and I went back to studying the program.

In accordance with HIPAA laws, no one would tell us who dissected whom. It was clear what a bizarre human exchange we had been party to, despite never having met. It had to be acknowledged, ritualized. Otherwise, it made no sense.

Not that a collective death talent show made a whole lot of sense either. As the students took the stage to share their talents – someone played Taylor Swift’s Bigger Than The Whole Sky, a member of the school of dentistry’s class of 2028 sang Sweet Creature by Harry Styles – I wanted to feel something like closure, but all I could muster was affectionate bemusement.

Who were these children, I wondered, and what did they know about death?

When two svelte near-adults took the stage in spandex (their leggings a respectful shade of black) and did what I can only assume was aerial yoga accompanied by Debussy, I had to avoid eye contact with my sister to avoid laughing. Still, as they balanced on each other’s shoulders and knees in midair, I had the urge to text my mom, to tell her how weird it was. I wished I believed she could see it. I know she would have thought it was cool.

When a chaplain got to the podium. “We know that your loved one’s participation in this program has probably complicated your grief, and prolonged it.” She talked about how when someone dies, there is a human need for closure, and we families probably hadn’t quite gotten it yet. They wanted to acknowledge the sacrifice we had made.

Truthfully, I hadn’t thought of it as a sacrifice at the time, more like a “get out of jail free” card, but I was beginning to understand. The chaplain’s words reminded me of the recurring dreams I had had after the two polite, somber men had taken my mom’s body away in a sprinter van. In real life, my sister and I had watched her take her last breath. When it happened it was so obvious, on an almost existential level, that to check her pulse would have been absurd. We didn’t need a nurse to come out. We declared her dead ourselves.

In sleep, though, my subconscious had its say. In recurring dreams, my mom would show up, back from the morgue and on her doorstep again, a little worse for the wear. She would push past us to get inside, clearly miffed we had sent her away prematurely.

After enough of these dreams, I came to understand why we bury our dead. Sure, no one wants the finality of loss but maybe the brain has a hard time moving on without it. It wasn’t until the chaplain alluded to this that that I realized that the lack of closure was exactly what I wanted. I didn’t want to move on. The ambiguity, the mystery even, meant the story of my mother wasn’t over yet.

Near the end of the ceremony, families were invited up to speak. When it was my turn, I gripped the podium, shaky-voiced but not crying. I remember knowing for certain what my mom would want me to say.

I told the students about my mom’s own experience in anatomy lab, all those years ago. The way our dining room had been overtaken by her schoolwork – the table strewn with flash cards and textbooks, colored-pencil anatomical drawings papering the walls. Those years we would find candy corn and York peppermint patty wrappers in the couch cushions – Mom’s study snack of choice.

She was more scatterbrained and short-tempered than ever, but I loved watching her find something she loved, something that was only hers. She learned a kind of devotion, then, an awe that would stay with her even in the darkest days of her illness.

I told them that they would have this, too.

A few weeks ago, after getting up the nerve to ask Ostervoss, I signed a HIPAA form and a media release to find out how my mom’s body came to be of use after she died. Five days later, a media relations specialist from the university forwarded me the answer in the body of an email. It read:

During her time with us, Erin played a crucial role in teaching spine anatomy, associated surgical techniques, and stereotactic and functional neurosurgery skills at OHSU. Through these educational experiences, neurosurgery and neurology trainees gained greater foundational knowledge that will inform their patient care throughout their careers.

After supporting these learners, she went on to teach in several orthopedic residency training courses.

In total, 121 learners directly benefited from your mother’s gift. Her legacy will live on through countless patients cared for by the healthcare professionals she helped educate.

Reading it, I felt the thrill of new information, of something happening in the world of my mother.

Then came the pang of loss, knowing that the one person who would truly appreciate this information was necessarily not available to receive it.

She would think it was so cool. She would have loved to know all of it.

Which supermarket pots are ambrosial heaven and which are a gummy disaster?

The best supermarket double cream

It was only when I sat down to taste 10 custards that I realised this was a dangerous test to judge on my own. I tried a range of ready-made offerings, from cans to cartons to tubs of fresh custard from the supermarket chiller section, some of which I found hard not to drink by the pint.

I analysed each custard for aroma, texture and taste, and awarded extra points for minimal processing and the use of free-range eggs; I deducted points for the inclusion of palm oil, modified maize starches and colourings, all of which are often used to replace the colour, fat and thickening ability of eggs. It was, however, the long-life cartons that most provoked nostalgic memories of bananas and custard as a child.

My main take-home is that cans and cartons are great for when you need a quick dessert, but if you want the real thing – a proper crème anglaise made with hot, vanilla-infused cream and milk, egg yolks and sugar – go for the fresh stuff and check the label for additives.

★★★☆☆

Attention LaMelo Ball: only losers boast about avoiding diaper duty

The Guardian Sat, 24 Oct 2026 12:00:32 GMT

The basketball star seems proud to leave the job to his partner. That’s so last century

Nobody can accuse the basketball star LaMelo Ball of being bad at his job. That said, the Minnesota Timberwolves point guard doesn’t seem to be a huge fan of dribbling.

Ball has a nine-month-old son, LaOne, with his partner Ana Montana (real name: Analicia Chaves) and is apparently uninterested in dealing with all the body fluids that come with a baby.

“You’re a dad now,” the sportscaster Ernie Johnson Jr said to Ball during an ESPN interview on Wednesday. “Are you a diaper changer?”

“Nah, my girl do all that,” Ball replied. “We got a good gameplan going on. So I know what I gotta do, bring to the table, she know what she gotta do, bring to the table.”

Johnson, to his credit, seemed disappointed by this answer. “Oh man, you don’t know what you’re missing, I’m telling you that.”

“I did it before, you feel me? I’ve definitely did it before, [but] it’s just not my job,” Ball clarified. “You know what I’m saying? It’s not my job.”

Well, actually, excuse me while I mumsplain here, but it very much is your job. A baby doesn’t care that you signed a five-year contract extension worth up to $260m in 2023. Parenting is a 24/7 commitment no matter how much money you make.

Ball and Montana (and, presumably, a team of hired help) are obviously free to share domestic duties however suits them. Nobody expects a professional athlete to be as hands-on as a parent with a more flexible schedule.

But going on TV and boasting about how you don’t change diapers? That’s an extremely outdated look. A 1982 study based on fathers in Britain found 43% of fathers had never changed a nappy (as diapers are called in the UK). By 2000, that figure had dropped to 3%. Meanwhile, the average time US dads spend caring for their offspring daily has quadrupled over the past 50 years and about 85% of dads say parenthood is one of the most important aspects of their identity. Being a hands-off dad is now very last century.

Still, even though modern fathers are doing a lot more, they’re still held to different standards than mothers. Imagine if a female athlete said changing diapers wasn’t her job: the rightwing pitchforks would be instantly out for her.

It doesn’t matter how accomplished a woman is in her career; there’s still an expectation that her identity as a mother comes first. Particularly under the Trump administration, which is trying to foster a whole new generation of tradwives.

Ball is only 25, so I’ll give him some grace. But I hope the backlash to his comments makes him realize that only complete losers boast about not changing diapers. A case in point: Donald Trump.

“I would never ask to change [Barron],” the president told the New York Post in 2006. “Melania probably wouldn’t let me. I’d just do it wrong.” Asked whether he’d ever changed the diapers of his four other children, he said he probably had, but couldn’t remember.

There’s a phrase frequently applied to men who pretend they’re incapable of doing basic domestic chores in order to wriggle out of them: weaponized (or strategic) incompetence. In Trump’s case, however, it may not actually be weaponized incompetence. It may just be incompetence.

Which leads me to present a modest proposal. In the future, we should apply the Diaper Test™ to any man in the running for a high-powered job. If he can’t clean up his own child’s mess, he’s sure to make a mess of the job.

‘Cuts mean jobs’: Skydance staff brace for shake-up after $110bn megamerger

The Guardian Sat, 24 Oct 2026 12:00:32 GMT

Battle far from over after Paramount and Warner Bros deal creates new global entertainment powerhouse

“It feels like the calm before the storm,” says an executive at Skydance, the newly minted media empire formed from the megamerger of Paramount and Warner Bros Discovery (WBD). “David has got what he wanted, but now there is a price to pay.”

Earlier this month, David Ellison, Skydance’s chief executive, sealed the $110bn (£82bn) deal, creating a global powerhouse spanning two Hollywood studios each more than a century old, the TV networks HBO, MTV and Discovery, and news outlets CBS and CNN.

Having seen off a rival bid from Netflix and faced significant political and industry opposition, in a process Ellison told employees was at times “downright ugly”, the battle is far from over for Hollywood’s newest magnate.

With an aggressive target of reducing an eyewatering debt load of more than $80bn in just three years, it is what is going to be cut, sold and restructured that will be uppermost in the minds of Skydance’s more than 53,000 employees.

Ellison, 43, who studied film and acted in the 2006 film Flyboys before moving into producing, is targeting $6bn in savings within three years. Executives and financial backers are steering away from the need for swingeing job losses, but a memo from management earlier this month warned that there would be “difficult decisions that affect our workforce”.

“It is business as usual but, to be honest, everyone is worried about what happens next,” says another Skydance executive. “Cuts inevitably mean jobs.”

There are also concerns about the political direction of the new entity, given Ellison’s closeness to Donald Trump – a longtime friend of his father, Larry, who co-founded the software company Oracle. David Ellison has pushed back at such framing, stating: “We do not want to politicise the company.”

Nevertheless, fears in the news division have been stoked by events at Paramount before the merger. It came under fire for cancelling the long-running Late Show with Stephen Colbert after its host said it had paid a “big fat bribe” for settling a $16m lawsuit with Trump.

Days later, US regulators agreed the $8.4bn merger of Paramount with Ellison’s Skydance Media, with Trump ally Kenneth Weinstein’s appointment as ombudsman at CBS News to root out “complaints of bias” as one of the conditions to get regulatory approval.

Christiane Amanpour, CNN’s international anchor, criticised the “ideological realignment of CBS” and warned that changes and cuts could lead to the potential “destruction” of flagship news show 60 Minutes. This week, she announced she was leaving CNN after 43 years, although her exit is not thought to be tied to the new ownership.

CNN staff were relieved at Skydance’s decision shortly after closing the deal to keep Mark Thompson, the former New York Times boss and BBC director general, as chair and chief executive.

Many had feared that the network, which alongside MS Now and Politico had faced a now-lifted White House media ban in apparent retaliation for critical coverage of Trump, might face a sweeping overhaul that could have seen the divisive Bari Weiss, the editor in chief of CBS News, installed at the top.

While Thompson has said that Skydance supports CNN’s independence, fresh concerns over rightwing influence emerged this week when it was reported that Elon Musk, a Trump ally and supporter of far-right causes through his X platform, has invested $1bn for a stake in the media conglomerate.

“The preservation of editorial independence is a growing concern among media consumers,” said Mike Proulx, an analyst at Forrester. “Private wealth is getting a greater foothold on public information channels.”

In terms of creative television output, star performers such as HBO will be left to keep churning out the all-important hits the business needs.

Ellison immediately extended the soon-to-expire contract of Casey Bloys, promoting the HBO boss to also oversee streaming services Paramount+ and HBO Max, to ensure the golden goose keeps making must-watch dramas such as The White Lotus, Game of Thrones, The Pitt, Succession and The Sopranos.

However, there are longer-term questions over some of the group’s cable and TV channels – such as MTV, Nickelodeon, the UK’s Channel 5 and Network 10 in Australia – which are in decline but still account for 70% of profits, according to CreditSights.

“In a world where the majority of consumers can access content through a smart TV, it should be a natural consideration to sell physical broadcast assets,” said Brian Wieser, chief executive of consultancy Madison and Wall.

“At a Skydance level they have made the choice to go all in on streaming. But the problem you have is maybe you don’t get offered enough to sell it, and, given the cashflow we know they make, they might be better served to hold on.”

Newly filed accounts for Channel 5 show the broadcaster paid a £215m dividend to Paramount last year. In the UK, the culture secretary only cleared the takeover after Ellison made commitments including pledging to keep Channel 5 operating as a free-to-air, public service broadcaster until at least the end of 2034. However, according to sources, these agreements do not preclude any potential sale of Channel 5 in the future.

Last month, Paramount moved its £300m TV advertising sales business from Sky’s sales team to Channel 4. That came after WBD extended its deal for Sky to handle its £90m-£100m ad sales business from January, covering TNT Sports, Discovery, Animal Planet and streaming service HBO Max. However, multiple media sources believe now the Skydance deal is done the business will eventually also move to Channel 4.

The megamerger also paves the way for BT to exit its joint venture with WBD – TNT Sports – which would finally end the telecoms company’s costly foray into pay-TV sport after almost 15 years.

Last year, Paramount outbid WBD for the rights to Champions League football, the flagship rights owned by TNT Sports. That blow prompted BT to write off the entire value of its stake in the joint venture.

However, with Ellison intending to merge Paramount+ with HBO Max, the rights will effectively be retained, and viewers will not have to sign up to yet another streaming or pay-TV service to watch all top-flight football.

Skydance says it will spend an estimated $30bn a year on content across all divisions, and as part of the takeover Ellison promised to release at least 30 major films a year until 2031.

This promises to be a boon for the UK production industry, especially for WBD’s studio at Leavesden, which is home to all of its DC superhero franchises and the forthcoming Harry Potter TV series destined for HBO Max this Christmas.

However, Warner is enduring one of its worst box office showings for years, the most recent flop being Tom Cruise’s Digger, prompting Ellison to put Paramount’s leadership in charge of both studios.

Analysts point out that Ellison is unlikely to maintain that level of moviemaking beyond the five-year pledge, as it goes against the grain of a Hollywood trend towards fewer films and lessons from past takeovers.

Since Disney’s acquisition of Rupert Murdoch’s entertainment assets in 2019, which included the then 20th Century Fox and Fox Searchlight studios, the number of film releases has broadly halved.

“After the 2031 deal ends there will be fewer films, obviously,” says Tom Harrington, a media analyst at Enders. “It has never happened before when there has been a takeover that more have ended up being made.”

Skydance declined to comment.

The Stone Roses showed me the power of being an introvert

The Guardian Sat, 24 Oct 2026 11:00:32 GMT

At boarding school in the early 90s, quietness was seen as weakness. But then I saw the band’s guitarist John Squire making a vast noise while hiding behind a fringe – and learned the strength of understatement

In September 1991, I had just been thrown into the meat-grinder of a Midlands boarding school. In this bear pit, there were predators and there was prey. You were either the swaggering rugby alpha, whipping a wet towel at pale bodies in the eight-boy dormitory; or the homesick ghost, keeping your guard up, endlessly braced for your toilet cubicle to be kicked open or your washbag chucked off the fire escape.

My mind had always been loud, racing with opinions, stories, jokes. But by the time I adequately considered a thought, the conversation had raced on without me. Suddenly, under 24/7 social scrutiny in a world where bullhorn confidence is king, I felt dismissed.

Up to that point, music hadn’t helped. Every rock star I had ever seen – Elton John, Freddie Mercury, Mick Jagger – was a showboating peacock, all hips, handclaps and absurd glasses, seeming to whisper in my ear: “This isn’t for you, bookworm.” But that September, I stumbled across the Stone Roses’ self-titled 1989 debut album. I must have seen John Squire’s genius before I heard it, on his paint-splashed, lemon-drizzled sleeve art.

Hearing his cascading, iridescent guitar solos, I assumed Squire must be an extrovert axe hero: foot on the monitor, diamante codpiece, the works. But there he was on the CD inlay: pipecleaner-skinny, dressed in Manchester streetwear and inscrutable beneath a bird’s-nest fringe (until the mid-90s, I genuinely wasn’t sure if Squire had eyes), slinging a Gretsch Country Gentleman guitar but not treating it like a penis extension.

Years before YouTube, it wasn’t easy to find out more. But when I dug up back issues of NME, I went from fan to disciple. A sometime model-maker who once worked on The Wind in the Willows – but also a child of 70s punk – Squire was enigmatic and otherworldly, softly spoken yet intense as a laser-cutter. Asked by one interviewer what the Roses were all about, his answer was the perfect collision of sky-scraping ambition and bone-dry Britishness: “Love and hate. War and peace. Morecambe and Wise …”

In those formative weeks, for the first time, I realised that “quiet” could also mean charismatic, insolent, snarky, simmering with latent attitude and temperamentally suited for a life in the arts. Through Squire, I discovered painting (Jackson Pollock’s “drip and splash” influence was all over his sleeves and guitars), modern history (the Paris riots of May 68 referenced on Bye Bye Badman), fashion and even religion (you only had to read his lyric to 1994’s Love Spreads, a take on the Passion, with Jesus imagined as a Black woman, to sense the iconoclast claws below the still waters).

Hearing the Roses at school, meanwhile, was my ticket into a secret society of indie kids that I hadn’t known existed, all swapping albums, making mixtapes, easy in each other’s company, building each other’s confidence. I picked up the guitar that same year, too, went on to write about it for the music press – and now play so loud in my own band that I can drown out a thousand braying show-offs.

Squire doesn’t do many interviews, and when I drove to his Cheshire farmhouse for Guitarist Magazine, I was worried he wouldn’t actually speak. But perhaps he recognised a kindred spirit. Over an hour’s encounter in his studio, the musician who had meant so much to me proved thoughtful, witty and profound, signed the schoolboy-era guitar I’d flecked Pollock-style with paint, and even gave me a parting hug.

Sign up to The Guide

Get our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every Friday

after newsletter promotion

John Squire didn’t change me; he stopped me fighting myself. Under his influence, I stopped trying to turn up the volume, accepted being an introvert and held him in mind whenever anyone equated quietness with dullness. Fast-forward 35 years – to a time when influencers squeal and preen, flogging every last grain of themselves to the attention economy – and the Roses guitarist seems a few degrees cooler for existing on his own terms, leaving something to the imagination, and treating Jonathan Ross with chilly disdain. Perhaps we could all stand to be a little more Squire?
