The sexual assault scandal rocked gymnastics – but has pace of change in the sport been too slow?

The Guardian Sat, 24 Oct 2026 05:00:25 GMT

Former USA team doctor Larry Nassar’s 2018 conviction sparked a global reckoning in gymnastics, yet gymnasts say they are still being let down

It has been 10 years since the Indianapolis Star published allegations of sexual abuse by Larry Nassar, the former team doctor for USA Gymnastics, setting off a chain of events that would lead to a reckoning for the sport. Hundreds of women came forward with their own allegations against Nassar, who also worked at Michigan State University, leading to his conviction and jailing.

The exposure of his crimes sparked a wider investigation into how gymnastics had allowed predators to abuse young athletes around the world. While Nassar was the worst recorded case, it emerged many other countries had questions to answer about the failure to protect victims from not only sexual but physical and emotional abuse. But a decade later, on a large houseboat moored in Rotterdam three tram stops away from the Ahoy Arena, where the World Gymnastics Championships are taking place this week, survivors and advocates raised fears about the slow pace of change.

The impact of the Nassar case was seismic, not least because of the decision of Judge Rosemarie Aquilina, on agreeing to Nassar’s plea deal, to allow his victims to have their say in her courtroom. People tuned into Aquilina’s courtroom from all over the world to watch as 169 people took to the stand across seven days, delivering blistering, emotionally charged and brave testimonies of Nassar’s abuse and the impact of that abuse. Aquilina sentenced him to up to 175 years in jail with other convictions, federal and state, making a total of 300 years to life.

“I know, dealing with so many victims, that when they speak publicly you see them shed their pain and get taller. You see them have a relief, an automatic release,” says Aquilina, perched on a seat in the helm of the boat. “The most interesting thing was that at first I had a list of maybe a dozen names who wanted to speak, then it was 20, then it was 30, and then it got up to 80, 100, etc.

“What happened was that one girl empowered the next, who empowered the next. It was the beginning of their healing because they felt finally heard and believed, in a safe space, and they got to tell him to his face, eyeball to eyeball: ‘You hurt me. I am not a number, I am a name, how dare you?’”

“Nassar constantly wanted control. He wanted to continue to control me, to control the girls, and to say: ‘Look what I’ve done. I took the plea for you’. That was constant … Did he deserve my respect? No. Did he give me respect? No. Did he give any of the victims respect? No. He never owned it. That infuriated me. It should infuriate everyone.”

Among the victims motivated to speak after hearing others’ statements was the Olympic gold medallist Aly Raisman, who was excoriating in blaming USA Gymnastics for enabling Nassar. She was joined by fellow gold medallist Jordyn Wieber, Olympic bronze medallist Jamie Dantzscher and former US national champion Mattie Larson. The mother of the athlete who first complained about Nassar, Maggie Nichols, read out a powerful statement on her behalf. Simone Biles, the most famous gymnast of her generation, revealed she was a victim on social media and later testified publicly in front of the US Senate Judiciary Committee.

Two years after Nassar’s sentencing, a documentary film named after Nichols, called Athlete A, was released, shining a spotlight on the traditional coaching system of compliance, fear and silence and how it allowed Nassar to operate. The documentary opened the global floodgates.

Kim Shore, who was a gymnast in Canada in the 1980s and “experienced all forms of abuse, but also all forms of joy”, was then on the board of directors of Gymnastics Canada, the national governing body, after stepping into governance when her own experiences and direct intervention had failed to prevent the cycle of mistreatment repeating with a family member.

“I absolutely love the sport. I love how it feels in my body. I love so many aspects of it. And yet I spent most of my time surviving it,” she says.

Shore, who is an independent safe sport advocate, says of the impact of the Nassar case: “I was floored, understanding: ‘OK, I wasn’t a bad kid, I wasn’t a bad gymnast, this is why I was treated that way, it’s endemic.’”

Yet the reaction from the organisation was “absolutely lacking”, says Shore. “I remember I sat and watched those girls tell their story in the courtroom and I just bawled. I encouraged the board members that I was associated with to watch it as well.” She does not believe any of them did.

Eloise Jotischky, 23, who in 2022 won the first civil case against British Gymnastics for the abuses she suffered in the sport, says the impact of the film was being able “to articulate what you’ve been through and find the terms to understand and talk about your experience”.

“It’s very hard to explain it to people who are not within that culture, that sport,” she says. “The only way I can really describe it is that it’s sort of like a cult in a lot of ways. It’s a very closed system, you’re very isolated, in a lot of cases you’re pulled out of school, you’re removed from your friends, you’re travelling to competitions all the time and you’re deprived of a normal social life. I’d say it’s very similar to a coercively controlling relationship in a domestic setting, there’s a lot of parallels there, but you’re a child, so there’s the duty of care issue as well.”

Jotischky stopped training at 14. “By the end, it wasn’t joyous. I think I hated it. You just blame yourself and you think that you’re the problem, until Athlete A comes out. That was about sexual abuse, but the underlying themes of Athlete A are about the physical and emotional abuse, the non-contact physical abuse, which made it get to that point. That’s what all resonated.”

At the same time, the life of former British gymnast and athlete Claire Heafford was in transition. She was splitting from her husband, leaving her dream job and taking up wrestling. “Those major changes were partly taking place because I hadn’t yet realised I’d been so badly abused and that I had some psychiatric issues,” she says.

“I got into professional wrestling when I saw it and felt very drawn to it. I didn’t really understand why, but it’s a performance art that is largely about the performance of masculinity and the violence is clear and obvious. I was really attracted to that being the inverse of my own experiences. I couldn’t understand that at the time. I was like: ‘I’ve gone mad, I’m 36, I’m learning to be a Mexican wrestler. I’m splitting up with my husband. What the fuck’s gone wrong in my life?’

“It was only when Athlete A came out that the penny dropped.”

The documentary made Heafford want to act; she decided to set up Gymnasts for Change, an alliance to bring about safer sport. As the head of Gymnasts for Change International, she brought together the advocates and survivors in Rotterdam.

“Athlete A was seismic. It came out just as Me Too had started,” she says. “On the one hand, Athlete A showed how awful the sexual abuse was and on the other it demonstrated to everybody in the world that gymnastics was a coercively controlling environment built on control and power. It showed that was just what the sport was, that everybody in it had experienced it and that they almost believed that it was necessary.”

The Nassar case triggered a series of reports and new measures in the US including the FBI acknowledging its handling of the case was “inexcusable” and Congress establishing the US Center for SafeSport. That organisation has since faced heavy criticism. USAG went through four presidents in less than two years, said it would adopt 70 of the recommendations in an independent report into preventing sexual abuse and set up an Athlete Bill of Rights. USAG now says athlete safety has been its “top priority since establishing a new board of directors and leadership team in 2018-2019”. It emphasises that “a culture of safety is something that has to be worked on every day, at every level”, requiring all adult USAG members to be trained in safeguarding. Eight members of the board are former elite athletes and one seat is dedicated to that of a survivor.

The case also inspired athletes around the world to speak up about their own experiences of abuse, including in Australia, Brazil and Britain. In Britain, an independent review led by Anne Whyte QC found that physical and emotional abuse were systemic, leading British Gymnastics to launch a 40-point plan aimed at changing the sport. That included a zero tolerance approach to abuse and a gymnast-coach led environment where “both feel empowered to create safe, positive and fair experiences at every level”.

Such an environment is something Aimee Boorman, who is Simone Biles’ former coach, has spent her career advocating for. Boorman channelled her anger at her own experience of negative coaching as a child gymnast into her coaching philosophy. “I knew that I never wanted to make another child feel the way that I felt as a child. So, that was the basis of everything,” she says. “So many times I was told that I wouldn’t be successful because I was too nice. I was like: ‘Well, then I guess I’m not going to be successful by your metrics, your standard, your qualifier for success’. For me, success is having happy, healthy athletes who want to put their children in gymnastics because they have such a good experience.

“Then, I went from being too nice to just being lucky that I had Simone, she’s successful and I’m successful because I was lucky that I had her. No, the reality is that Simone never would have gotten to where Simone is without the training she had from me and the other coaches that she had growing up. So, I’ve just had to hold on to my core beliefs.”

Across Europe, too, gymnasts have spoken out to force change. Former Dutch gymnast Petra Witjes and Germany’s Adina Hausch document falling out of love with the sport because of their experiences.

Sign up to The Recap

The best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s action

after newsletter promotion

“At the elite club in the city I moved to it wasn’t fun anymore,” says Witjes, whose book, Silenced for Gold, is a memoir about the systemic abuses within sport and her battle to expose it. “My dad taught me to let my voice be heard but in the gym it was the opposite.”

Witjes was terrified of speaking to her parents, she was taught not to trust them. “I didn’t feel safe at first, because my coach always said that parents don’t understand elite gymnastics,” she says. “They push your parents away from you. We were in total isolation.”

Hausch says an injury that forced her from the sport was a relief. “I was on beam and I slipped with one leg and fell with the other on to the beam and then crashed down,” she says. “The leg was pushed sideways so much that it broke. From the age of 13 I don’t think there was a week without training through pain. When I left after the injury, the worst injury I’ve ever had, I was really happy that I didn’t have to go to the gym anymore.”

In Rotterdam, survivors vary in age from their 50s to their teens; it is hard not to view the issues as systemic and global. And ongoing. Charlotte Jacobs, who is only 18, quit the sport after suffering emotional abuse when training in the UK.

“It got to a point where I was like: ‘I can’t do it anymore’,” she says. “My experience was strange because it wasn’t physical, it wasn’t sexual, but it was emotional. You were ridiculed all the time, constantly. You weren’t allowed to cry, you weren’t allowed to talk, you weren’t allowed to sit down, if you were caught leaning on anything you’d have to run, you needed permission to go to the toilet, you needed permission to drink, and it’s that sort of really controlling, consistent and dismissive behaviour so that no one really felt safe that was prevalent.”

Shore, who is a member of G4C Canada, argues that if a big list of cultural reforms comes from the top, that is then normalised within the national federations and then the clubs “all the way down to grassroots, then I think we would see faster reform and less resistance”.

“The more I learn that the stories are consistent internationally the more it says something about the need for World Gymnastics to take a leadership role,” she says “The treatment across the world is pervasive and coaches are moving from space to space, country to country, more frequently now or they’re not even staying in this sport, they’re moving into other sports, especially if they’ve come into trouble.”

World Gymnastics has moved to address the cross-border issue within the sport at least, publishing a new safeguarding policy last week which notes that the Gymnastics Ethics Foundation, which it launched in 2019 and has handled nearly 500 reports, has the power to extend sanctions imposed by member federations providing they are compatible with the rules of the governing body and general principles of law.

Among the efforts of World Gymnastics to address safeguarding concerns was the launch of the 10 Golden Rules of Gymnastics in 2021, the establishment of a safeguarding commission in 2022 and, this year, the launch of a safeguarding newsletter and the appointment of a full-time Safeguarding Manager.

Shore believes the pace of governing bodies fully engaging with the change needed has been slow, however, “because to admit that there is harm going on in the sport puts organisations into a liability risk. Also, they have been able to deflect responsibility for so long. They don’t know how to solve it and they are getting pressure from all sides. By putting their head in the sand for literally 50 years we’ve now got to a crisis.”

A statement from World Gymnastics said: “Creating a safe environment for current and future generations of gymnasts is a responsibility that World Gymnastics takes extremely seriously and shares with all stakeholders across the sport. The priority for World Gymnastics is not only to strengthen safeguarding rules and policies, but to ensure that they lead to meaningful changes in everyday practice.”

Heafford alleges that British Gymnastics isn’t entering into meaningful engagement and collaboration with Gymnasts for Change and other survivors in the sport and says that she finds that “extremely frustrating”. She is also hugely critical of the processes gymnasts have to go through in raising a complaint against a coach or gym and what resolution looks like, saying: “In six years, we haven’t had one outcome that we can stand by and say that was a good outcome.”

British Gymnastics, however, insists it has engaged with the organisation regularly which has “helped shape its approach”, including a meeting with G4CI and others in Rotterdam as well as introducting a new complaints and disciplinary process “to improve transparency and fairness” .

Minky Worden, of Human Rights Watch, fears the situation could worsen. “Sport is getting younger. There’s a youth Olympics about to launch in Senegal. There’s going to be thousands of athletes, every one of them 18 or younger. They’re all children and they’re at a very elite level,” she says. “These children are being monetised and they are not protected because we know the systems are not in place to protect them.”

Hausch wants to see “measurable boundaries, for example increasing the competition age to 18,” she says. “I would root for Germany not to join youth international competitions. Having a 13-year-old do youth European championships is the same as doing it as an adult, it’s the same amount of work you have to put in, the same amount of pressure, it’s not a softer version, it’s the full version, and it doesn’t make sense.”

All agree there needs to be more done to help athletes advocate for themselves and others. Jacobs says: “There needs to be a sort of package of what to look out for. I think there needs to be more training for coaches in terms of mental wellbeing, disability, neurodiversity, all that, alongside what are and are not best practices.

“We need more regulation,” she adds of the British landscape. “Look at the new guidance that’s come out about keeping children safe in education. That’s all been updated. Where’s the guidance for anything sports-wise, extracurriculars, whether it’s swimming, gymnastics, dancing, anything like that?”

British Gymnastics says that it “recognises there is always more to do” but that prevention is “at the heart of our work. We have overhauled learning and development … and set clearer policies and guidance to drive meaningful change.” It says a coach developer network, regional teams and safeguarding and welfare officers in every club support communities.

Jotischky, who is now studying law off the back of her experience, says there are changes needed there too. “The legislative gap that exists is astonishing. You have the 2015 Serious Crime Act section 76, which talks about coercive control, but it’s limited to domestic and familial relationships. Then you have the 2021 Domestic Abuse Act which lists personally connected individuals as only being family members. In a coach-to-athlete relationship where you spend 30 hours a week in the gym with your coach, and some gymnasts even go and live with their coach because they’ve formed such a close relationship, of course coercive control and emotional abuse can happen but it’s not recognised within the law. So, we have very little legislative ground to deal with the most serious cases in particular.”

Listening to this group of women in Rotterdam, what becomes clearer is that while federations, to differing degrees, make changes in the name of athlete safety, survivors are still being failed. Meanwhile, these survivors and knowledgeable advocates remain isolated from the very structures that should be embracing them and channelling their knowledge and understanding of their experiences into the changes necessary to ensure the future health of the sport.

Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organisations. In the UK, Rape Crisis offers support on 0808 500 2222 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 in Scotland, or 0800 0246 991 in Northern Ireland. In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found at ibiblio. org/rcip/internl. html

As a divided Israel prepares to go to the polls, can Netanyahu pull off his greatest political trick yet?

The Guardian Sat, 24 Oct 2026 05:00:24 GMT

The prime minister has defined and dominated his country’s politics for three decades and is putting his rivals on the defensive before Tuesday’s general election

They chant his name, they cheer and clap – and yet he is not the most dominant person in the room. Looming over the crowd that has gathered to hear Gadi Eisenkot, the former general who is the lead opposition challenger in Tuesday’s Israeli election, is a man who is not there. It is the man Eisenkot seeks to replace as prime minister, the man who first served in that role three decades ago and who has held it, on and off, for 19 of the past 30 years. It is Benjamin Netanyahu.

Naturally, the warm-up speakers at this evening rally in the modest city of Modi’in, halfway between Tel Aviv and Jerusalem, stress the virtues of Eisenkot, a son of working-class Moroccan Jews who rose through the ranks to become chief of staff of the Israel Defense Forces and entered politics only four years ago. But every sentence might as well end with two words that go unspoken: unlike Bibi.

Even the name of Eisenkot’s party, Yashar, meaning straight or direct, carries the implied contrast with Netanyahu, who is regarded by friends and enemies alike as a maestro of the darkest political arts. When Eisenkot calls for “a country without lies”, when he calls for “responsibility and leading by example”, when he suggests US-style term limits for the role of prime minister, “because power corrupts”, everyone knows what – and who – he means.

None of this comes with rhetorical fire or theatrical panache. But the lack of charisma serves only to emphasise that Eisenkot is every inch the un-Bibi. “I think that’s an advantage,” Noa Sadeh, 56, told me after Wednesday night’s rally. “I’m fed up with people who know how to talk – like Bibi. We need someone who will do the doing part.”

Spotting a journalist with a notebook, David Nadler, 74, a retired colonel who served under Eisenkot, insisted I write down the word “integrity”, meaning “he says something, he means it, he will do it”. Another sentence ending with those silent words: unlike Bibi.

It’s hard to overstate Netanyahu’s dominance not only over this campaign but over Israeli politics and political culture. The two blocs in this election are not left and right but Bibi and anti-Bibi. The latter camp includes at least two figures – the former PM Naftali Bennett and the Moldova-born Avigdor Lieberman – whose natural home is on the nationalist right and who both once worked closely with Netanyahu, only to fall out with him spectacularly.

Almost every political figure is defined, or defines themselves, in relation to Netanyahu. Eisenkot offers himself as the antidote, but listen to the pitch made by the far right and it too is all about the prime minister.

Netanyahu is like a shopping trolley, says Yishai Fleisher, of Itamar Ben-Gvir’s Otzma Yehudit (Jewish Power) party, to a group of about 30 orthodox voters in a study hall in Bet Shemesh on Thursday evening. “He has a tendency to go left, so you have to pull him to the right.” Fleischer makes the case for yet more Jewish settlements in the West Bank, to say nothing of settling Gaza; for a “ministry of emigration” that will encourage the “voluntary” departure of Palestinians; for the death penalty; for ever harsher treatment of Palestinian prisoners; for putting more guns and more ammunition into the hands of Jewish Israeli civilians – but all in the context of strengthening the resolve of a new Netanyahu-led coalition. On the right, Ben-Gvir is a moon that is rising, but Netanyahu is still the sun.

Partly, that’s a function of sheer longevity. But it’s also down to Netanyahu’s undimmed ability to set the political agenda. Even in this election, he has demarcated the terrain on which battle is fought. His latest poster campaign offers voters a rhyming choice of Yamin, meaning the right, or Falastin, meaning Palestine. On the right side is, of course, his own face and the Israeli flag; on the other, the leaders of the opposition parties, including Bennett and Lieberman who are adamantly opposed to a Palestinian state, all of them surrounding two heads of parties that represent Palestinian citizens of Israel, who make up about a fifth of the country’s population. The message is not subtle: vote for me, or you’ll get the Arabs.

Indeed, the closing weeks of the campaign have centred on the question of whether the anti-Netanyahu bloc of Jewish Israeli parties – currently forecast to do better than the Netanyahu bloc but to fall short of an overall majority in the Knesset – will do some kind of parliamentary deal with the mainly Arab parties, most of which have, historically, both refused to join Israeli governments and not been invited. Backed by that chunk of the media that is loudly and vociferously pro-Netanyahu, most notably the Fox News wannabe Channel 14, Netanyahu has succeeded in putting his opponents on the defensive.

A rare exception to that pattern came just this week when a Netanyahu uber-loyalist, Channel 14’s Yinon Magal, characterised Eisenkot as a Moroccan “monkey”. The racial slur was so crude that had it been used by the left to describe a politician of the right, it would have had Netanyahu denouncing Ashkenazi elitism from the rooftops (even though Netanyahu is, of course, a privileged scion of the Ashkenazi elite).

Tellingly, while the warm-up speakers in Modi’in mentioned the “monkey” remark, Eisenkot himself did not. To his admirers, that was the mark of a decent man reluctant to follow his opponents into the gutter. To the doubters, it was a sign of a politician still playing by Marquess of Queensbury rules – one who doesn’t quite appreciate what, or rather who, he is up against.

For an outside observer, the most puzzling question about this Israeli election is: how is this even close? How can the polls be showing the two blocs, pro- and anti-Netanyahu, neck and neck? Abroad, many will be baffled that Netanyahu can still be in contention given the devastation his government brought down upon Gaza, flattening much of the territory and killing more than 70,000 Palestinians, even if, as Israel says, one-third of them were Hamas combatants.

But even inside Israel, where the impact of the war on the people of Gaza is all too rarely discussed, it is no less of a riddle that Netanyahu is a serious candidate in these elections, let alone one who could emerge on top.

To start with the most elemental fact, the biggest disaster in the country’s history happened on his watch. The massacres inflicted on civilian Israel on 7 October 2023, at the Nova music festival and at a string of southern kibbutzim, are still fresh in the memory. Stickers depicting the faces of those killed on that day adorn bus stops and railway platforms from one end of the country to the other. As Oded Levi, who voted for Netanyahu in 2022 but was in the Modi’in crowd for Eisenkot, put it: “Whoever was prime minister [then] is responsible. He has to go. For this reason alone, we need a change.”

But it hardly ends there. Netanyahu promised a war that would destroy and eradicate Hamas. That didn’t happen. Instead, Israel destroyed its own international reputation, leaving the country isolated and fast becoming a pariah state. Netanyahu promised to destroy Iran’s nuclear threat and that too didn’t happen.

Add to that the “judicial coup” in the months before 7 October, where Netanyahu tried to weaken the restraint on his power represented by the supreme court, thereby splitting Israel in two, and the Qatargate scandal, in which his closest aides stand accused of taking money from Doha in return for boosting Qatar’s image. Along with his ongoing corruption trial, it all adds up to the mystery of why Netanyahu was not counted out long ago.

Any explanation begins with the loyalty of his base, built over three decades. Their support for him is unshakeable, unmoved even by reports that Netanyahu received credible warnings of a Hamas attack on 7 October and failed to act. They are kept on side by the PM’s enduring skill in crafting a narrative, in the case of 7 October, that everyone else is to blame except him, that he was kept in the dark by army and intelligence chiefs acting out of incompetence or something more sinister, a baseless claim advanced by his “poison machine” of media and online outriders. And he remains a consummate political operator, so gifted in the business of divide and rule that many can foresee him playing the coalition arithmetic on Wednesday morning far better than any of his rivals.

Still, that prospect has prompted a fierce reaction, one whose intensity can be felt thousands of miles from Israel. In the departure lounges of airports around the globe, you can find expat Israelis, many of them liberal and secular, heading home to vote on Tuesday. I saw it for myself as I travelled in a plane packed with those who felt it their duty to fly back and cast a vote to remove Netanyahu. That’s a group not picked up by pollsters and, who knows, in a contest that could turn on the fate of just one of the Knesset’s 120 seats, it may make a difference.

Some of that same determination was visible at the state ceremony in Jerusalem on Thursday marking the anniversary of the assassination in 1995 of the former prime minister Yitzhak Rabin, remembered still as a would-be peacemaker gunned down before a lasting accord with the Palestinians could be struck. It was not well attended – Netanyahu stayed away and sent a low-ranking minister – and it was tempting to view it as further evidence of how far to the right Israel has shifted in these past three decades, in this age of Bibi. Here were the luminaries of the old Israeli left, gathered in a burial ground.

And yet, Yair Golan, the leader of the Democrats, successor party of Rabin’s, was dismissive of such talk. A former general who served with Eisenkot, and a hero of 7 October who drove south to rescue people in his own car that fateful day, Golan told me: “I’m optimistic. I never went into battle thinking ‘all right, I’m going to be killed, I’m going to be wounded’. No, I’m going to win, and we are going to win.”

Golan even believes he and his fellow opposition leaders can agree on the beginnings of “some sort of a regional, strategic process in order to bring security for the long run”. He didn’t use the words “peace process”, but it’s clear what he meant.

The word “peace” became tainted for many Israelis, associated with moves such as the 2005 withdrawal from Gaza which Netanyahu and his allies have succeeded in casting as an early step on the road to 7 October. And yet it has not vanished. A video went viral earlier in the week showing scores of young Israelis at a Negev music festival dancing and singing to Shir LaShalom, the song for peace, the anthem of those 1990s peace efforts and the last song Rabin sang before he was shot leaving a peace rally 31 years ago.

Yes, the polls are deadlocked and, yes, Netanyahu is a political magician, but the sight and sound of those young people, like the queues for planes home, have given at least some Israelis the hope that change might be coming – that the age of Bibi might, at last, be drawing to a close.

As Trump’s time runs out, this could be his most dangerous legacy: a world divided into three

The Guardian Sat, 24 Oct 2026 05:00:24 GMT

We’ve heard much about the end of the west. At the proposed summit between Trump, Putin and Xi, those fears could crystallise

In the final two years of a US presidency, when Congress has been lost, approval ratings have sunk like a stone and their party has started to think about who’s coming next, the person occupying the Oval Office can feel their power draining away. Domestic legislation, particularly in an era where bipartisan cooperation is almost nonexistent, grinds to a halt. But as the days tick by until the end, and as presidents begin to think about their legacy, there is one part of the job where they still have power: the rest of the world.

In the final weeks of his presidency in 1992 George HW Bush sent 28,000 American troops to Somalia to help end a famine. For Bill Clinton, it was a quixotic attempt to bring peace to the Middle East by ending the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. Barack Obama restored diplomatic ties with Cuba, making a historic visit to Havana, as well as a final, successful push on the Iran nuclear deal.

In 10 days, Donald Trump will enter his own twilight zone. He is almost certain to lose control of the House and it’s not impossible he will face a Democratic Senate too. Any hopes of passing domestic policy – not that he’s bothered with that much during his first two years – will disappear. Instead, he will face a series of investigations that could lead, once again, to impeachment.

On the world stage, however, it will be a different story. And unlike Bush senior, Clinton and Obama, his ambitions won’t be peaceful. The first two years of his second term have been catastrophic; the final two could be even worse.

Once the midterms are over, the US is understood to be planning to restart its unwinnable war with Iran, already carrying out exercises with the Israeli military and withdrawing diplomats from the region. Trump’s sellout of Ukraine is well under way. In the past week he has argued that “Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine”, while his envoy Steve Witkoff met with Vladimir Putin in Moscow, praising him in a televised meeting as a “humanitarian…and I salute that, I commend you and I thank you again.”

On top of a reckless war in the Middle East and appeasement in Europe, the shadow of a new world order is emerging, which Trump will relentlessly pursue in his final years. Putin has proposed a summit between himself, Trump and China’s Xi Jinping, to be held in China next month.

Such an unprecedented meeting, were it to take place, would have potentially devastating consequences for the rest of us. The three leaders have ambitions to transform the way the world is governed, essentially dividing it into spheres of influence. One summit wouldn’t turn an idea into reality, but it would send us down a very dangerous path. In Europe, it would have an impact beyond Ukraine if the US refused to help protect nations threatened by Russia. In east Asia, the withdrawal of the American security blanket would cause enormous problems for Taiwan, South Korea and Japan, as well as Australia.

We’ve talked a lot about the end of the west over the past two years – this feels like a moment when many of those fears will crystalise.

The Trump administration’s ambition to divide the world into spheres and side with dictators over democrats has long been evident. Last year’s National Security Strategy was deeply critical of the US’s traditional allies in Europe and east Asia. But it was what it didn’t say that was most shocking. Both Russia and China avoided direct criticism. In six paragraphs describing the threat to Taiwan, China was not mentioned once. Elsewhere in the document, China was actually praised as “rich and powerful … us[ing] its wealth and power to its considerable advantage.” The section on Russia’s war in Ukraine failed to mention how it started and did not suggest that Putin should be defeated; instead it focused on how the US could help Europe and Russia mend their relationship. The 33-page document discussed the importance of the US controlling the western hemisphere, but made clear that so long as the US still had economic dominance, it cared little whether other parts of the world are protected. “The affairs of other countries,” it stated, “are our concern only if their activities directly threaten our interests.” For too long, it argued, America’s allies had “suck[ed] us into conflicts and controversies central to their interests but peripheral or irrelevant to our own”.

For Putin, this is a success almost three decades in the making. He has long viewed American support for democracy in eastern Europe and central Asia as “interference” in Russia’s backyard. Now he has a US president who agrees. Trump has also placed Putin on a far higher pedestal than Russia’s economy and its technological prowess deserves.

Xi, too, has welcomed the US’s rhetorical retreat from east Asia, particularly if it allows China greater maritime control in the East China Sea and South China Sea. World opinion on China has dramatically improved as that of the US has slid. As Chrystia Freeland, a former Canadian foreign minister, put it this week, “there has not been a president who has been more beneficial for China than Donald Trump”.

At stake is not merely territorial control. All three governments see the possibility of increasing economic ties. For the US and China, the bigger issues are future control of economic supply chains and technology platforms, while Russia’s fossil fuel resources are also a factor. All three are key players in the next space race, both in terms of commercial and military control. If these three nations begin to work together, at the expense of Europe and the rest of the world, it will fundamentally change the nature of geopolitics. A decade ago, talk of a multipolar world was based around the idea of the US, China and the European Union as the three most powerful blocs. Somehow, Brussels has been replaced by Moscow.

after newsletter promotion

Until now, the rest of the west has – on the whole – tried to muddle through. Nato still exists on paper, G7 and G20 summits may be chaotic but they still take place. Optimists in the Foreign Office point out that Trump turned up to the UN general assembly and his administration is still deeply involved in the UN’s day to day activities.

Mark Carney spoke of a “rupture” and warned the old post-cold war world was not coming back, but despite warm words from Emmanuel Macron, and renewed discussion about how Europe can protect itself without the US, there is still a sense that everyone is waiting for Trump’s time in office to end. A Great Powers summit makes this harder to ignore.

While US presidents seek foreign policy success in their final months, history suggests they rarely find it. Clinton’s Camp David talks collapsed after Ehud Barak and Yasser Arafat were unable to reach an agreement. Bush would argue that his initial intervention in Somalia eased a famine, but it ended in humiliation. A botched raid on a warlord led to the deaths of 18 US soldiers and several hundred Somalis. Obama’s diplomacy in Cuba and Iran succeeded, but were both promptly ripped up by Donald Trump.

Trump will get his photoshoot – and maybe that’s all he wants – but there is no guarantee that this unsavoury troika becomes a permanent geopolitical fixture. Trump’s foreign policy has divided his Maga movement and has shocked traditional conservatives. The Wall Street Journal editorial board described the proposed summit as “arguably the worst idea of the second Trump term”. A President Vance or Rubio might be less willing to throw in their lot with dictators; a President Ossoff or Ocasio-Cortez certainly won’t.

But just because Trump won’t win, doesn’t mean that the US won’t lose. He will be arriving in Shenzhen at the weakest moment in his presidency. An 80-year-old lame duck leader fated to limp towards the finish line unable to pass any legislation and threatened by two chaotic years of investigations into his alleged corruption. Opposite him will be two authoritarian leaders in their early 70s who believe the only thing preventing them from ruling their nations for another two decades is death. Indeed, given their “hot mic” discussions about longevity drugs last year, perhaps they both believe they can rule for even longer.

If it goes ahead, this summit will bring Putin back in from the cold and reiterate Xi’s position as a global leader who cannot be ignored. The image of the three leaders will come to define this era when the rules-based international order was torn apart and a new, uncertain period began to form.

Steve Bloomfield is the former international editor of the Observer

John Healey pledges to use budget to harness power of AI to bolster Britain’s security

The Guardian Sat, 24 Oct 2026 05:00:24 GMT

Chancellor says government to commit hundreds of millions to develop ‘distinctively British’ approach to AI

John Healey has pledged to use Wednesday’s budget to harness the power of artificial intelligence to bolster Britain’s security and prosperity against the risks in the accelerating global technology arms race.

As he prepares for his debut budget, the chancellor said that Andy Burnham’s government would commit hundreds of millions of pounds to develop a “distinctively British” approach to AI that would capitalise on the benefits of the frontier technology.

At a fork in the road as AI developments pose both existential threats and transformative economic potential, Healey said he would be making the biggest ever investment to guard against cyber risks and the disruptive potential of the technology.

As part of the measures in his tax and spending statement, he promised fresh investment for Britain’s AI Security Institute and other critical institutions, alongside allocating public money to support the use of the technology for good.

“AI will transform daily life: every firm, community, hospital, school and every aspect of our economy can benefit,” Healey said.

“I understand and share the concerns of working people, so I am setting out a distinctively British approach to AI – one that doesn’t leave workers behind and defends our national interest, while ensuring the benefits of AI-enabled growth are felt right across the country.”

Three months into Burnham’s premiership, Healey is poised to deliver a budget against an increasingly volatile backdrop as the war in the Middle East sends shock waves through the global economy, putting pressure on public finances and reigniting the cost of living crisis.

The chancellor has vowed to use his first budget to provide households and businesses with “breathing space” as the global surge in energy costs triggered by the war hits millions of families this winter. On Friday, the latest tensions in the Gulf sent the oil price to its highest level for six months, rising above $117 a barrel at one point.

However he will also use the opportunity afforded by the critical speech to the Commons to flesh out Burnham’s policy priorities for government after he replaced Keir Starmer this summer, and to spell out a vision for Britain amid the increasingly turbulent global economic outlook.

Aiming to harness the opportunities of AI to raise living standards, back UK businesses and support economic growth, the chancellor said he wanted to seize the opportunities of the technology as a central plank of Labour’s plan for growth.

It comes after official figures show AI investment has helped the UK outperform gloomy economic forecasts as the Iran war pushes up inflation and drags down business confidence, powering the country to the strongest growth performance in the G7 in the first half of this year.

However, there are growing fears over the security of the nation and critical industries as the technology opens up the danger of cyber-attacks, IT systems turning rogue and devastating job losses as companies invest in machines rather than humans.

It comes as websites around the globe went dark this week after a serious vulnerability was found in a computer language used to build much of the world wide web, in a development made possible by rapid AI advances. It also emerged this week that Barclays is cutting 5,000 jobs as part of cost-saving plans identified by bosses as the rollout of AI across the bank helps it make efficiency gains.

Healey said he wanted to use his budget to protect against risks while also nurturing homegrown businesses and talent, in order to cut Britain’s dependency on other countries that were also making strides in AI technology.

New investments would be made in AI chip design capability in Edinburgh, alongside a new AI Centre of Excellence in Manchester that it said would enable the UK to harness the technology’s benefits.

The government would also spend £10m a year to lead the UK’s work on understanding how AI will reshape jobs and industry, aiming to address concerns about potential job disruption.

As part of the plan the Treasury said it would back up to £300m in public-private investment in a new AI Biosecurity Lab, designed to serve as a world-leading institution bringing together scientific expertise to protect people from emerging biological threats.

It comes after the defence secretary, Wes Streeting, warned on Thursday that UK households should make preparations against the mounting risks from weather, cyber or other serious emergencies.

The advice to stock up on supplies to last 72 hours, in a campaign called Be Ready, comes as Silicon Valley bosses sound the alarm over the increasingly existential threats AI could pose, and amid growing official concern over the impact of the climate crisis, technological dependency and hostile state threats.

Dan Jarvis, the security minister, said: “I’m proud the UK has repeatedly been at the forefront of global efforts to use AI for the benefit of humankind.

“Today’s investment will help the UK seize the opportunities AI presents to strengthen our national security, while staying one step ahead of those who seek to use AI to do us harm.”

Andy Bloke appears vaguely normal on Gogglebox – but Kemi dodged a bullet

The Guardian Fri, 23 Oct 2026 23:16:33 GMT

PM and the Liverpool mayor prove to be naturals at watching TV, with a genuine connection and sense of fun

On nights like this a man can feel like he’s slipped through the looking-glass. I’m sitting on the sofa watching the TV, poised to make some gags about the prime minister and the mayor of Liverpool, who are themselves sitting on a sofa at No 10, poised to make some gags about what they are watching on TV.

Life doesn’t get more meta. The saving grace is that this episode of Gogglebox is a charity special for Stand Up to Cancer. Andy Burnham has requested that any journalist writing about the programme makes a donation to SU2C. I’m happy to oblige. Cancer is costing me a great deal more than money.

Meet Andy Bloke and his best mate, Steve Bloke. Two career politicians who still manage to look and sound vaguely normal. Not totally normal, mind. In real life, Steve Bloke would have said to Andy Bloke: “This is a total shithole you’re living in.” And Andy Bloke would have replied: “I know. It’s been a complete tip since Boris was here. You can’t get rid of the stains.”

You can’t deny that Andy Bloke and Steve Bloke are naturals at this. Not so bland that you want to turn off, a genuine connection with one another and a sense of fun that can’t be faked. Kemi Badenoch is reportedly annoyed she wasn’t invited on the programme.

The reality is that she’s dodged a bullet. Kemi just doesn’t have the woman of the people shtick. It’s something you’ve either got or you haven’t and she really doesn’t. If you let her on Gogglebox the only laugh you would get from her would be if she was livestreaming an execution from the US.

Mind you, it’s a slow burn. At first Andy and Steve look like they are feeling their way into the programme. But then so do the other celebs, Joe Lycett and his aunties, Stanley Tucci and his wife, Felicity, and Paul Whitehouse and Lenny Rush. The bantz feels a bit contrived and Andy Bloke – a Cambridge English grad – fails to recognise a photo of Margaret Atwood.

If Steve Bloke had been more on the ball, he’d have taken the piss mercilessly. But Andy and Steve are nothing if not a team. They’ve got each other’s backs and bond over filling in the blanks on members of the royal household in Only Connect.

“The king will be pleased with me at our next weekly meeting,” says Andy Bloke. He probably will be. I suspect Camilla will have made Charles watch this. The Man of the People meets the King of the People.

Halfway through, we get a reminder that this isn’t all about the laughs. There is the story of Callum who died at the age of 16 from brain cancer. Then the story of a woman whose mother died of pancreatic cancer when she was 11, was diagnosed with cervical cancer shortly after her child was born and whose husband died of bowel cancer a week after diagnosis. Sometimes shit really does happen to good people. All the celebs were fighting back tears. Andy was no exception.

“I’d like to see Match of the Day,” says Paul Whitehouse. “Why? To hear how crap Spurs are?” Lenny joked. Careful, Lenny, careful. We might be past the watershed but it’s still way too early for gags about Spurs.

But some football would have been nice. Andy Bloke and Steve Bloke would have been in their element. You could have made an entire programme of the pair of them pissing themselves laughing as Manchester United were beaten 4-1 by Como in the Champions League. It might even have earned a Bafta nomination.

For some reason, Andy Bloke and Steve Bloke were excluded from watching an X-rated natural history about some young birds that haven’t yet learned to fly and are so dim that they literally just stand there as tortoises eat them alive. Well, not all. One bird managed to hop on top of a tortoise shell. Though not before the tortoise had taken a chunk out of a wing. A happy ending of sorts. The celebs couldn’t quite believe they were being forced to watch such ultra-violence.

Normal service was resumed with a mercifully brief excerpt from Strictly Come Dancing. Brief because none of the real celebs had any idea who the celebrity contestants were. Andy Bloke admitted he still had PTSD from watching Ed Balls crashing around the dancefloor. Steve Bloke wisely helped himself to another beer. Maybe this was the way they used to do business when Andy Bloke was also a mayor.

We ended on an upbeat note. The Celebrity Traitors. Steve Bloke had no idea what was going on so Andy Bloke tried to fill him in as they cracked up over some crisps, pork scratchings and Skips. Me neither. I guess that was one were you had to be in the room.

“You should be quite good at this,” Andy Bloke said, encouragingly. “You can generally spot the wrong ’un in the room.” I guess that depends on how often you’ve been in the same room as Michael Gove.

Claudia Winkleman was announcing that the murder would be done in plain sight by boring a Faithful to death. Steve Bloke had the solution. Just make them watch the proceedings in the House of Commons. Boom boom.

Neither Steve nor Andy Bloke had much to say about Ross Kemp’s worrying levels of paranoia or Jerry Hall’s complete charisma bypass. How do you bore someone who is already boring? That could have been a question for Only Connect. Maybe we had come full circle. Or perhaps their gags about Rupert Murdoch got cut in the editing suite.

Five Great Reads: The fallout from French riots, supersized wealth and throwing rocks at the telly

The Guardian Fri, 23 Oct 2026 21:15:03 GMT

The Guardian’s weekend wrap of essential reads from the past seven days, selected by Jacqui Housden and Miles Herbert

Get this in your inbox every weekend. Sign up for Five Great Reads here

Hello and welcome to the weekend. The last seven days have been punctuated by political unrest in Europe with groups angry over the state of schools, the cost of living, and housing. Elsewhere, otherwise peaceful residents are throwing rocks at their tellies in their own personal revolt at omnipotent technology. You might want to hold off the coffee until after reading this one.

The protests gripping a string of European countries this month have largely been told through shocking pictures of violence – particularly on the streets of Paris. The riots in France have prompted questions over police tactics, as Emmanuel Macron’s government tries to get a handle on the civil unrest. Politicians are calling for ruthless sentencing, but lawyers blame the politicians for the poverty, and anger, behind their clients’ behaviour.

Fast-tracked fallout: Of the 2,500 people arrested during last weekend’s rioting and looting across the country, more than 900 are being fast-tracked through the courts using a procedure called comparution immédiate (immediate appearance). It sends them to trial straight or shortly after being taken into custody, or within three days if they are held in pretrial detention.

As Kim Willsher uncovers, most were young and unemployed, others in work with families. A 19-year-old student with no previous criminal record who was caught on his way home with several stolen black pullovers from a looted clothing store was fined and given a 14-month suspended prison term. “It was just a question of opportunity,” he said. “I thought: everyone else is doing it, why not me? I regret it.”

How long will it take to read: Two and a half minutes.

Further reading: What’s next for France after a weekend of riots? And pro-Trump Maga media is in a froth over the protests.

The midterm elections are fast approaching, and Donald Trump is “barnstorming the country” before Americans head to the polls on 3 November. With his approval rating collapsing, and polls showing Democrats could wrest back control of the Senate and the House of Representatives, some have called Trump’s midterm push a “desperation tour”. But can he rescue the Republicans, or is the increasingly authoritarian president making life harder for his Maga mates?

Could the democrats take Kansas? Washington DC bureau chief David Smith was in Park City, Kansas for a rally in support of Senator Roger Marshall, who is facing an unexpectedly strong challenge from Democrat Adam Hamilton. The state has been red since 1932, with no Democrat winning a Senate seat since “Amelia Earhart was the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic and the Nazis became the biggest party in the German Reichstag”. Smith was on the ground for what was Trump’s first campaign rally in the state for eight years, but Smith writes his presence could nationalise this local election, drawing attention to the consequences the Iran war has had on the heavily agricultural state.

Testing the old playbook: With the cost of living, foreign wars and government corruption at the forefront of voters’ minds, will Trump’s old tricks – “hurling insults, stirring bigotry and telling lies” – still work among a weary electorate? Notable quote: Largely dismissive of opinion polls, Darrell Claphan, a retired sales worker, echoed the sentiments of the Maga merch-wearing Trump crowd: “He’s doing fantastic. He’ll go down in history being the number one president at what he’s done for the country in my lifetime.”

How long will it take to read: Three minutes and some change.

Further reading: Is the blue wave real?

In the last decade, the rise of political violence has – tragically – been a worldwide phenomenon. And in Australia, federal politicians have had a growing sense that something was shifting in the country’s national life. This week’s alleged attack on MP Helen Haines, which made global headlines, saw that tide turn into reality.

From the global to the local: Those responsible for protecting politicians in Australia often take their cues from overseas, Guardian Australia’s political editor Tom McIlroy writes. When a gunman opened fire at the Canadian parliament in 2014, the government built a fence around Parliament House. Amid threats stemming from Covid-19 lockdowns, the Asio director general cautioned the warning light for political violence was “already flashing red”.

A turning point? “The alleged attack on Helen Haines shows something rapidly being lost in our politics,” Tom writes. “The shift in sentiment can no longer be dismissed as social media noise or harmless comment.”

How long will it take to read: Just over a minute.

Further reading: Politicians say more security would “let bad people win”; and Brendan Cox writes that the alleged attack on Helen Haines is a punch to the gut.

after newsletter promotion

Feature writer Sam Wollaston dropped in on the world of the uber-rich in Monaco at Europe’s biggest superyacht show. After committing a few fashion faux pas, and despite the boats on offer being out of his price range, Wollaston took a tour and got a feel for a few of the aquatic behemoths up for sale. You can’t escape their sheer size, Wollaston writes, but there is also “no escaping the truth”. The recreational boating industry produces about 16m tonnes of CO2 annually, and they are a “monstrous” symbol of global inequality.

‘Turds of the sea’: Superyachts are growing more and more popular among the world’s richest, and owners include Mark Zuckerberg, Roman Abramovich, and Sheikh Khalifa bin Zayed Al Nahyan of Abu Dhabi. A 2024 study looked at 23 superyachts owned by 18 billionaires, and it showed the average annual carbon footprint of each of these yachts to be 5,672 tonnes. It would take an average citizen more than 800 years to produce the same carbon footprint. The supersized boats’ anchors and chains also “act like the grim reaper’s scythe”, damaging the Posidonia seagrass which thrives throughout the Mediterranean.

Notable quote: “They just want something that’s big and flashy and comfortable, they don’t care about anything else.” – A yacht broker on what his clients are looking for

How long will it take to read: Just under six minutes.

Further reading: Can you enjoy a life on the ocean waves when it’s costing you £1,000 an hour?

It stands to reason that, as a growing number of people look for dumbphones over smartphones, in a bid to combat screen addictions and worries over privacy, their consumer habits might spill over to other tech too. The Guardian’s George Francis Lee spoke to people around the world who are fed up with their televisions.

‘The joke is on them’: We’re not talking luddites here. Among those now on the hunt for a “traditional” TV are a 71-year-old Illinois resident with a master’s degree in computer science, a Welsh woman who works in AI delivery and a public servant from Australia. Some are worried about privacy, others are frustrated at how quickly their devices slow down or need updating. “My friends all laugh at it when they come over,” Paul, who has a traditional telly admits, “but secretly I know the joke is on them. My little telly doesn’t spy on me, and has a DVD player built in.”

Notable quote: “It was enormously satisfying when I threw a rock through the screen.”

How long will it take to read: Three minutes.

Further reading: Can these dumbphone evangelists convince you to dump smartphones?

The Guardian view on Europe’s protests: the social contract has broken – and young people want solutions

The Guardian Fri, 23 Oct 2026 17:07:23 GMT

An electoral supercycle over the next year may redefine the continent’s future. But what’s happening on the streets is shaping it, too

France sneezed, and Europe has again caught the cold. The wave of unrest which began with teenagers at a high school soon drew in hundreds of thousands of people nationwide and then spread across the continent. Protests have filled the streets in Lisbon and Madrid, and have ignited into violence in Milan, Brussels and Tirana as well as in French cities.

French authorities say they are deploying 70,000 officers on Saturday and are allowing only marches organised by unions. They blame hard-left militants as well as opportunistic young perpetrators for last weekend’s destruction and looting, when a minority hijacked largely peaceful protests. But with fuel prices set to rise further over the winter, the demands and participants broadening, and President Macron utterly failing to meet the moment, there is no sign of an end to the wider discontent and no speedy resolution in sight.

Europe is experiencing distinct movements, with distinct causes, demands and actors, which should not be elided. In France, crumbling and overcrowded schools were the touchpaper, with Greek protesters echoing their complaints about educational underfunding this week. In Spain and Portugal, housing is the central issue. German students are angered by the possible reintroduction of compulsory military service. But those involved see the commonalities, with some Italian demonstrators chanting in French.

Underlying all these is the breakdown of the social contract. A generation expect, with reason, to be worse off than their parents. They are understandably angry at inadequate education and job precarity, are struggling to rent places of their own well into their 20s, and are paying for pensions which they don’t believe that they will ever receive themselves, while the climate crisis haunts their futures. They see that governments worried about debt and fearful of the bond markets either cannot or will not offer them solutions. It might be more remarkable if they were happy with their lot, or confident that casting a vote at their next opportunity would fix it.

Meanwhile, increasing inequality means that they watch others grow wealthy, sometimes profiting directly from their misfortune, with flats and houses treated as financial instruments rather than homes.

This unrest also echoes the wave of gen Z protests seen around the world last year – with some of those on the streets in France, Italy and Germany even borrowing emblems used earlier from Morocco to Madagascar. The affordability crisis, heavy-handed security forces and the sense that ordinary people are being left behind while governments have no convincing answers for them were at work in those cases too.

In Europe, far-right parties, egged on by the Trump administration, are seeking to capitalise on the unrest through lies that immigrants and open borders are to blame, and that a strong hand is needed to restore order. Within the next year, four of the biggest states – Spain, France, Poland and Italy – will hold elections, threatening a radical rightwards shift that could fundamentally change the EU. Yet these parties do not have real answers to the questions raised by protesters, and a financial crisis in France might yet highlight Marine Le Pen’s economic weak spot and National Rally’s internal divisions. The future course of the continent is being shaped, for better or worse, on the streets as well as at the ballot box.

The Guardian view on Caryl Churchill’s Triumph: a play for today

The Guardian Fri, 23 Oct 2026 17:06:30 GMT

At barely 20 minutes, this satire on strongman politics serves to jolt audiences out of their complacency

“Is this theatre for the TikTok generation?” one critic asked of the latest play by 88-year-old Caryl Churchill, lauded as Britain’s greatest living playwright. Triumph, her blistering satire on contemporary strongman politics, is barely 20 minutes long.

Cleverly spliced with Suetonius’s The Twelve Caesars, the play takes the form of a press conference given by a blond-wigged apparatchik, who smilingly extols the barbarities of an unnamed narcissistic emperor. If “Triumph” were a crossword answer, the clue might be “To greet a populist US leader in confusion – a win (7)”. Even given Churchill’s reputation for prescience, the play was uncannily timely. It premiered in London and New York on the same day that President Trump’s short-lived press officer Katie Zacharia was forced to resign. As the American comedian Robin Williams quipped of an earlier administration, “People say satire is dead. It’s not dead; it’s alive and living in the White House.”

Churchill is a playwright of ideas who, throughout her long career, has played with structure. Her 2012 play Love and Information depicted the fragmentation of modern life through 57 scenes and more than 100 characters. With just three actors, this new play is a triumph of form and content: as short and direct as a press conference, its purpose is to alert us to a global crisis. This is the theatrical equivalent of a political sketch.

A story arc in one act, it is not a highbrow version of the 60- to 90-second schlocky microdrama episodes for mobile phones, which have become so popular that Channel 4 is launching its own series. Short plays go back to Suetonius’s time. Chekhov, Beckett and Albee were all masters of the dramatic sprint. Churchill started out writing short radio plays, and in later years her work has become an increasing feat of compression.

But this brevity goes against a trend for theatrical maximalism. To persuade audiences back to theatres and cinemas after the pandemic, plays and films have been getting longer, perhaps to justify the price of a ticket. The Oscar-winning movie The Brutalist required a 15-minute interval in 2024. A two-part RSC dramatisation of Middlemarch has just opened at Stratford, where an epic Game of Thrones ended last month. However, a reducio spell has been cast on the six-hour, two-part Harry Potter and the Cursed Child juggernaut, which has reopened at half its original length.

A play in your lunch break or after a night out is not practical for many. And while mini dramas make use of empty theatre hours and fit around evening performances, only a playwright of Churchill’s stature could guarantee a sellout, weeklong run for a show briefer than an interval without audiences feeling short-changed. Triumph could be seen as a curtain raiser for a revival of her 1979 classic Cloud 9 at the National Theatre next month, and Three and a Bit, a new collection of “biting short plays” at the Almeida in January.

The Guardian’s Michael Billington called Churchill “theatre’s great disruptor”. With Triumph she is disrupting the conventions of theatregoing itself: a play isn’t always something to be enjoyed between an early supper, interval drinks and the last train home. She has turned the attention economy on its head. Like a Covid-era emergency press conference, Triumph interrupts its audience’s day to make them listen. It jolts us out of our complacency.

We are reclaiming real life after getting rid of Instagram

The Guardian Fri, 23 Oct 2026 15:41:58 GMT

Readers on taking back their lives – and brains – from social media algorithms

I couldn’t agree more with Georgina McNamara (The one change that worked: I deleted Instagram – and embraced the joys of a truly private life, 19 October).

Reading about the sheer relief of stepping away from Instagram resonates deeply with my own feelings over the last few years. There is an incredible quiet joy in reclaiming a truly private life, entirely free from the pressure to document, curate and perform our daily routines for an invisible audience.

This shift immediately brings to mind Jaron Lanier’s compelling points in his 2018 book Ten Arguments for Deleting Your Social Media Accounts Right Now. Lanier warned us that these platforms aren’t just neutral tools; they are behaviour-modification engines designed to hijack our attention and slowly erode our autonomy.

His argument that social media algorithms inherently reward outrage, tribalism and comparison to drive engagement feels truer today than ever. By participating, we unwittingly allow algorithms to alter our moods and warp our sense of reality, stripping away the simple contentment of just being.

In my own life, stepping back from that digital noise has been incredibly grounding. I’ve found that my most meaningful moments – whether I’m spending a few focused hours woodworking in my workshop, sitting down to figure out a new arrangement on the guitar, or just out walking the spaniels – are vastly richer when they exist solely in the present, without the impulse to photograph or share them.

Getting back to tangible, analogue realities has felt like taking a long, deep breath. Even organising a recent social evening at the local pub in Hipperholme reminded me how much more genuine our connections are when we are physically present, sharing a pint and a conversation rather than a screen.

A private life is not a smaller life; it is an unmediated one. As Lanier suggests, opting out isn’t just rejecting technology; it’s reclaiming our free will and our peace of mind. Guy Edmondson Hipperholme, West Yorkshire

Georgina McNamara’s article really resonated with me. I haven’t deleted Instagram, but I check it very infrequently now. While I didn’t post all that often, the compulsion to document experiences and turn moments into posts or stories, rather than being in the moment, was always there – and with it, the eventual anxiety about whether anyone had liked what I had posted.

I also realised that comparing my day-to-day life with others’ carefully curated highlights was making me unhappy: an endless stream of holiday photos made me keenly aware of how long it would be until I would next have a break, while other fitness instructors posting photos taken from strategic angles made me worry that I wasn’t as flexible as them in comparison, or that my technique was poor.

After reading some books and articles on cutting back on smartphone use, I took a number of steps to reduce my phone use, and used the One Sec app to trigger a breathing exercise whenever I opened Instagram.

It made me realise how often I checked Instagram as a reflex, and that I could be devoting this time to other activities that I found more fulfilling. The few occasions that I do check it these days, I find it a bit overwhelming.

I find that my mind is a lot quieter now and that I pay more attention to what is around me, appreciating what I see as a moment that doesn’t have to become a post or a story. And if I take a photograph of something, it’s because I like it, not because I’m concerned about whether someone else will. Laura Dobie Glasgow

I deleted my Instagram account after getting pregnant with my second child. At first, I muted it; when I returned, the algorithm had decided that, with all the information it had gathered on me, I must have taken a break due to baby loss. It bombarded me with images and messages about baby loss, until it realised this wasn’t the reason and started to fill my algorithm with “two under two” narratives. The juxtaposition was stark and insensitive. It felt awful.

I realised I didn’t want this platform having information about not just me but my family as well, and I hated that by feeding into it (with likes on obsessed-over images and funny captions), I was allowing it to dictate some of my parenting decisions through algorithms and advertised content. Since leaving it, my motherhood journey has been much happier, simpler and in my control. I completely agree that it’s the change that works! Stefanie Withey-Jones London

I enjoyed Georgina McNamara’s account of leaving Instagram, particularly her observations about the time spent checking reactions and seeking validation.

However, there is an important distinction to be made between sharing our lives and seeking approval for them. I use social media to share photographs with friends and family because I enjoy letting people I know see what I have been doing. For me, that is about connection, not validation.

There is another pleasure too that is rarely mentioned: unexpected reminders of photographs posted one, five or even 10 years ago. A holiday, a familiar face or an ordinary moment that I had forgotten suddenly reappears, bringing back the feelings associated with it.

It’s not just the memories themselves I treasure, but the unexpected joy of being reminded of them, often when they’re furthest from my mind.

The problem, perhaps, is not posting our lives online, but allowing other people’s reactions to determine how much we value those experiences. Nicky Atkinson Shoreham-by-Sea, West Sussex

I lasted only six weeks on Instagram. Unlike Georgina McNamara, I came to the party late, in my 60s. Almost immediately, I resented the way that posts were pushed into my feed. In no time at all I was spending hours watching posts of horse sanctuaries in the US and feeling depressed and resentful at whole sections of society. So I deleted my account – no small feat in itself, as the process is determined to keep you there.

Afterwards, I felt relief at getting back hours of my own brain time, but for months, I would think: “I could just pop on and look at x, y, z.” I’m glad that I’m off, and scared at how quickly I became addicted. Now when I look around I see that I am the only person on the bus or train who is not looking at a screen but at the outside world, and thinking for myself. Dr Hilary Redden Aberdeen

The one change that worked? I deleted all social media from my phone and instead installed the Guardian app with a subscription to news and well-curated content. No more time-wasting, bottomless doomscrolling for me. Do it, kids! Cecilia Scott Woking, Surrey

A tender sporting moment with Alex ‘Hurricane’ Higgins

The Guardian Fri, 23 Oct 2026 15:41:52 GMT

Paul Mitchell recalls snooker champion Alex Higgins tearfully celebrating his win with his young daughter

While I enjoyed your photo feature with its “groundbreaking images [that] have upended assumptions about how men behave, dress and project power” (Muscles, metrosexuals and male tears: the 39 pictures that changed the way we see men (for good and for bad), 17 October), I felt that a more fitting sporting example than Gazza’s tears would have been Alex “Hurricane” Higgins at the 1982 World Snooker Championship.

On winning the title, Higgins, a notoriously erratic and divisive figure, broke down in tears and pleaded for his wife and infant daughter to join him. It was not an act of image management, popularity-seeking or virtue- signalling. Rather, it was the spontaneous reaction of a man who simply wanted to share the greatest moment of his career with his young daughter.

The scene was made all the more poignant by what followed. With the benefit of hindsight, and in light of Higgins’s subsequent decline into sporting wilderness and personal hardship, that moment stands as a fleeting glimpse of unguarded joy and human vulnerability. In that respect, it remains one of sport’s most moving displays of emotion.

And if Alex Higgins, a man renowned for his toughness, volatility and refusal to conform, could openly weep in public and clutch his baby daughter at the pinnacle of his career, perhaps it serves as a reminder that showing emotion diminishes neither the man nor the achievement. Paul Mitchell Belfast

Remembering a time when Afghan women had a voice and agency

The Guardian Fri, 23 Oct 2026 15:41:47 GMT

John Griffiths says in the 1960s he witnessed women discussing politics with men in Afghanistan’s parliament

Your article, with its account of forced marriage, illustrates how Afghanistan’s 22 million women and girls need to be freed from Taliban-imposed misogyny (‘I am still a child, it cannot be good to be married’: how drought forces Afghan families to sell girls as brides, 15 October). It was not ever thus.

Under Russian suzerainty in 1965, four Afghan women were the first to be elected to the Wolesi Jirga, or lower house of parliament. In 1966, I watched two of them, bare‑headed and wearing western-style clothes, discussing a political topic with three of its male members and the future president Babrak Karmal.

I also saw several post‑puberty girls not wearing the burqa. This, and reforms such as secondary education for girls, was supplemented by highly visible aid. The two-mile Salang tunnel through the Hindu Kush mountains, linking north and south Afghanistan by road for the first time, is a good example. The problem is: how can we restore such freedom without the use of force, which seldom works. John Griffiths Author, Afghanistan: Land of Conflict and Beauty

Delving into the subtext of Winnie-the-Pooh

One of the best books about Winnie-the-Pooh (Editorial, 16 October) is The Pooh Perplex, a 1963 work by the American academic Frederick Crews. This is 12 essays written in the style of various schools of literary criticism, such as The Sacramental Meaning of Winnie the Pooh, where Eeyore is the Christ figure; À la Recherche du Pooh Perdu, which claims the book is permeated with Weltschmerz; and Another Book to Cross Off Your List, as it contains not one working-class character. I was surprised that your editorial mentioned Paddington, but not Mary Plain from the bear pits of Berne, who had a mentor in the form of the Owl Man (named for his horn-rimmed spectacles). Created by the Welsh writer Gwynedd Rae in the 1930s, she was the subject of more than a dozen tales. The stories were regulars on Children’s Hour and Jackanory. Paddington was a latecomer to my childhood reading. Dr Peter Glanvill Chard, Somerset
