Obama Issues Searing Attacks on Trump, Ramaswamy in Return to Campaign Trail

The New York Times October 24, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The 44th president appeared in Ohio on Saturday, kicking off a two-state swing with a rebuke of President Trump and Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican nominee for governor.

By Tim Balk and Emily Davies

Emily Davies reported from Cleveland.

Former President Barack Obama on Saturday attacked President Trump’s administration in searing and mocking terms, saying it was defined by “incompetence the likes of which we have not seen in modern times.”

Appearing in Cleveland at his first campaign rally of the midterm elections, Mr. Obama delivered his most forceful attack on Mr. Trump in recent memory. He also criticized a campaign ad from the Republican nominee for Ohio governor, Vivek Ramaswamy, saying it exemplified a coarsening of American politics.

Mr. Obama, who has been selective about publicly criticizing Mr. Trump, condemned his Republican successor’s stewardship of the country in terms that were personal and pointed. He said Mr. Trump’s second term had amounted to “two years of chaos and cruelty and corruption,” argued that top administration officials were not “not serious people” and said Mr. Trump had led the country into an economically painful war in Iran “that nobody asked for.”

“As a former president, I can tell you sometimes factors beyond a president’s control end up foiling the best-laid plans,” Mr. Obama said. But, he added: “That is not the case here. In this case, this administration’s actions are directly responsible for rising costs.”

Mr. Obama, describing Mr. Trump as “you know who” or “this guy in the White House,” said America had never had a president “excel so wildly at just straight-up grifting.” And he cast Mr. Trump as disconnected from Americans’ needs, engrossed instead by White House renovation projects.

“He should be on HGTV,” Mr. Obama said, ridiculing Mr. Trump’s focus on applying gold trimmings to the White House. “He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory. Just gold everywhere.”

The appearance by Mr. Obama, who is expected to also speak at a rally in Detroit later in the day, sets up a rare split-screen between him and Mr. Trump, who is scheduled to appear at a rally in Georgia in the evening and said at a recent rally that Mr. Obama had been a “rotten president.”

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Mr. Obama’s speech.

In Ohio, Mr. Obama was joining Dr. Amy Acton, the Democratic nominee for Ohio governor, and former Senator Sherrod Brown, the Democratic nominee for Senate in the state.

Dr. Acton’s race has consumed national politics in recent days, after her Republican opponent, Mr. Ramaswamy, aired an ad featuring Dr. Acton’s mother. Dr. Acton says she has not spoken to her mother since she was 12, after her stepfather was charged with raping her. The ad has split Republicans.

Mr. Obama assailed Mr. Ramaswamy over the ad, saying there appeared to be “no line” Mr. Ramaswamy would not cross.

“There’s a decency that we should expect out of our public officials,” the former president said. “And I don’t know what’s happened where the standards of behavior have gotten so low that somebody can run an ad like that.”

Dr. Acton also addressed the commercial, saying that Mr. Ramaswamy was targeting her family history to “save his struggling campaign.”

“It’s not going to work,” she said, “because compassion and decency still matter.”

Mr. Obama and Mr. Trump are presenting starkly different pitches in the final days before the midterms, with their parties locked in bitter battles for control of Congress and statehouses.

Mr. Trump, who is set to speak in Perry, Ga., on Saturday evening, has been pressing a message that Democrats are dangerous extremists. He has urged voters to pretend he is on the ballot, hoping to activate his party’s base. But polls show his approval rating has plummeted, and Republicans are on the defensive over high prices.

At a rally in Florida on Friday, Mr. Trump falsely accused Democrats of being communists and said a vote for Republicans would be a vote for “more money in your pockets, bigger paychecks for your families, lower taxes” and less crime.

The presidents have recently exchanged public criticisms — though Mr. Trump’s have typically been more frequent, forceful and direct.

Mr. Trump, who succeeded Mr. Obama in office in 2017, for years promoted a baseless, racist conspiracy theory that Mr. Obama was not born in the United States.

Mr. Obama has been selective about publicly criticizing Mr. Trump by name, though he has recently expressed disapproval of Mr. Trump’s approach to A. I., among other topics.

Mr. Obama has engaged heavily with midterm races, taping dozens of ads for candidates. But until Saturday, his time on the trail was limited to light campaigning in the spring with James Talarico, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Texas.

Mr. Obama made late endorsements over the weekend in Florida, backing David Jolly, the Democratic nominee for Florida governor, and Angie Nixon, the left-wing Democratic Senate nominee, who would be Florida’s first Black senator.

Mr. Obama was the last Democratic presidential candidate to carry Ohio, which was once seen as a quintessential swing state but has been drifting toward Republicans for years. Democrats have grown increasingly optimistic about their chances in the midterm elections in Ohio, though, as the state’s agriculture-heavy economy has buckled under the weight of the war in Iran and the president’s tariff policies.

He was set to travel next to Detroit to rally with Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the progressive Democratic nominee in Michigan’s pivotal Senate race. Dr. El-Sayed has been trying to shore up his support from Black voters. Republicans see his race against Mike Rogers, a Republican former congressman, as their best chance to flip a Senate seat.

In the evening, Mr. Trump will make his appearance in Georgia, a state Mr. Obama plans to visit later in the week. On Sunday, Mr. Trump is set to visit Michigan.

Mr. Trump has directly addressed Mr. Obama’s trip to Michigan in his own recent remarks and has reminded audiences that he won Michigan in 2016 and 2024.

Mr. Obama had challenged Mr. Trump over his policies in recent weeks, if in less scathing terms than he did on Saturday. Last month, he publicly criticized Mr. Trump over his approach to A. I. for the first time, warning that the technology could “deeply affect our health and our safety.”

“There’s no replacement for an effective, government regulatory structure,” Mr. Obama said at an event in upstate New York. “And the challenge we have is that, obviously, we have a president currently that has said that’s for losers.”

Patricia Mazzei contributed reporting.

Emily Davies is a political correspondent for The New York Times.

In Second Term, Trump’s Justice Dept. Submits to His Election Demands

The New York Times October 24, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

With moves in Alaska and California, the department has stepped up interventions in the midterm elections as the president’s instrument of unmediated executive power.

By Glenn ThrushKatie Rogers and Zolan Kanno-Youngs

Reporting from Washington

The Justice Department is sharply intensifying efforts to intervene in the midterm elections, goaded by a president unfettered by even the limited restraints of his first term.

The next several weeks represent a critical moment for federal law enforcement, a test of whether a department repurposed by President Trump as an instrument of unmediated executive power will be effectively mobilized as a guarantor of his political power.

In recent weeks, the department has taken several new steps, including an extraordinary effort to invalidate any potential Democratic victory in the Alaska Senate race, that reflect Mr. Trump’s growing agitation as his party faces the possibility of losing control of Congress precipitated by his sagging popularity.

On Thursday, the department asked a federal court to block certification of the election if the incumbent, Senator Dan S. Sullivan, were to lose narrowly, claiming that the presence of another candidate with a nearly identical full name tainted the election. The move, the first of its kind in generations, came in response to the president’s rants about the issue, officials said.

Hours after the papers were filed, Mr. Trump abandoned any pretext that department officials had acted without his say-so, telling reporters, “I’m the one that said do it.”

Mr. Trump has grown increasingly agitated about the dueling Sullivans, among other election-related grievances. He has demanded the department take legal action, even as some department officials raised concerns about the merits and constitutionality of the case, according to two people with knowledge of the situation, speaking on the condition of anonymity to avoid retribution.

The episode comes amid the department’s widening push to exclude large batches of mail-in votes on suspicion that some had been cast by noncitizens, despite evidence that such voting is exceedingly rare. At the same time, Attorney General Todd Blanche has abandoned departmental norms by promoting prosecutions and investigations of politicians, within 60 days of the election.

Late Friday, the department escalated the fight, sending letters to local election officials across California demanding that they help identify potential noncitizens on their voter rolls and set aside their ballots. The letters came with a threat. Those who failed to comply would “risk significant federal scrutiny.”

All of this has administration critics, and even some in the department, asking: Just how far are Justice Department leaders willing to go?

“The department is taking commands from the president and throwing spaghetti at the wall to file meritless lawsuits,” said Vanita Gupta, the No. 3 official at the department under President Joseph R. Biden Jr. “The ultimate goal is undermining faith in the election, intimidating voters and discrediting results the administration doesn’t like.”

It is by no means certain that any of these legal actions will ultimately succeed. But election officials from both parties have expressed concerns that it represents a dangerous effort to discredit functional election systems administered by the states.

Democrats on the Senate Intelligence Committee have grown increasingly worried that Mr. Trump may claim foreign interference in the election as a reason to seize voting machines, citing Mr. Trump’s dubious claims in a speech over the summer.

Over the past year, the department’s civil rights division, under an outspoken Trump ally, Harmeet Dhillon, has undertaken a series of actions intended to demonstrate they would aggressively pursue his agenda. This included an unsuccessful legal effort to obtain sensitive state voter data and dispatching 1,000 federal monitors to oversee elections, all the while sowing broader doubts about election integrity.

This has apparently not been enough for Mr. Trump, who has become increasingly impatient. He was especially fired up after a meeting in the Oval Office this month with election deniers, including Tina Peters, a former Colorado election official who was imprisoned for her role in a security breach of election systems before obtaining a pardon, two people with knowledge of the meeting said.

Lauren Bis, a White House spokeswoman, said in a statement that Mr. Trump “has done more than any other president to ensure our country has free and fair elections” and that “the Trump administration has been clear that anyone who illegally votes in our elections will be held accountable.”

Responsibility for executing this agenda has fallen to Mr. Blanche, who espoused a maximalist vision of executive power as Mr. Trump’s lead defense lawyer. He has charted a course of calibrated ambiguity when asked about the election, issuing words of reassurance even while plowing ahead with the new lawsuits.

Mr. Blanche has maintained that he will be guided by evidence, citing federal statutes that prohibit illegal voting by immigrants and others that require retention of records by state and local election officials.

He defended the department’s actions in a statement to The New York Times, saying the suit relied “solely on federal law” and was not intended to benefit any candidate or party.

“The Department of Justice does not seek to stop any ballot from being cast or to stop the certification of Alaska’s election,” he wrote. “This litigation seeks to ensure that after Alaskans cast their ballots, they are preserved in a manner so that only Alaska’s governing officials have the information necessary to make a determination as to whether Alaskan voters were confused or misled.”

Shortly before one of his deputies filed the Alaska suit, Mr. Blanche cast the department’s recent lawsuits as a good-government effort and dismissed the likelihood of a department effort to block certification of the results in any given state as a “doomsday scenario.”

Yet Mr. Blanche’s presence atop the department is itself significant. While he has pushed back on some White House directives, he is operating at the pleasure of a president who will not tolerate the institutional guardrails that existed in his first term, and personally steered the department’s legal campaign to punish his perceived enemies.

And he has made it clear that he believes Mr. Trump has the right to dictate department actions against the advice of officials, including himself, provided the president is not violating laws or the Constitution. In a recent interview, he claimed there was a “misperception that there’s this separation and independence between the Department of Justice and the White House,” and said he worked for Mr. Trump.

Many of Mr. Blanche’s predecessors pushed back harder. An antagonist of the first term, in Mr. Trump’s view, was former Attorney General William P. Barr, who refused to deploy the vast powers of federal law enforcement to pursue fabricated claims about a rigged election after the 2020 race.

Mr. Barr quit in December 2020 after publicly dismissing the baseless claims of election fraud that have animated the department in Mr. Trump’s second term.

“There’s a growing tendency to use the criminal justice system as sort of a default fix-all, and people don’t like something they want the Department of Justice to come in and investigate,” he said at the time, referring to the president and his allies.

The president has never forgiven him. At an event at the White House in late 2025, he stunned a gathering of federal prosecutors in a vulgarity-laced tirade against Mr. Barr, according to two attendees, speaking on the condition of anonymity to disclose details of a meeting intended to remain private.

Mr. Trump’s cardinal rule in staffing up his second-term Justice Department, according to current and former officials: no more Bill Barrs.

The White House has found two particularly cooperative partners in Mr. Blanche’s top two deputies, Trent McCotter and Stanley Woodward Jr. Mr. McCotter who has worked in the past with Stephen Miller, the president’s top domestic policy aide, the official pushing the department to crack down on alleged voting by unauthorized immigrants, those people said.

Both are in frequent contact with top West Wing officials, as many of their predecessors have been, often through the White House Counsel’s Office.

Mr. Woodward’s name was affixed to the lawsuit in Alaska federal court seeking to block certification of the coming Senate election in the state. At times, Mr. Woodward’s name on a legal filing indicates that subordinates were unwilling to do so themselves, former officials said.

Legal experts are dubious about the prospects of the Alaska suit succeeding. One described it as “one of the weakest election lawsuits I’ve ever seen.”

The only known effort by the Justice Department to preemptively block certification came nearly six decades ago, in a very different time and place. In 1968, the department sought to block an election by the Barbour County Democratic Executive Committee in Alabama because white members changed the rules to exclude Black candidates who had been denied their voting rights in the Jim Crow South.

Earlier this month, Mr. McCotter — who helped draft the $1.8 billion “anti-weaponization” fund proposal so toxic it imperiled Mr. Blanche’s nomination as attorney general — was the signatory on a suit seeking to block the counting of 20,000 mail-in ballots in California. It claimed, without providing detailed evidence, that many were not U. S. citizens.

One name conspicuously absent from both suits: Ms. Dhillon, whose staff would typically be responsible for overseeing election integrity cases. It was not clear why Ms. Dhillon was not listed on the lawsuit.

Ms. Dhillon, appearing in an interview on “60 Minutes” in the past week, downplayed the possibility that the department would interfere with the election.

“I can tell you that absent some shocking contingency that is unexpected, there should be no interruption in the usual course of counting and certifying the results in the states,” she said.

She went on to dismiss the proposal of deploying agents from Immigration and Customs Enforcement at polling places, even though Mr. Trump told a reporter this month that he had not yet made up his mind.

“Is the administration planning to send ICE agents out to the polling places?” asked the correspondent Lesley Stahl.

“There is no plan to do that,” Ms. Dhillon replied.

Her response was noted in the White House, which had enlisted Ms. Dhillon to appear on the show in the first place.

Mr. Trump watched the interview and was upset that Ms. Dhillon underplayed the threat posed by illegal voting and let other administration officials know about it, according to two people with knowledge of the situation.

Glenn Thrush covers the Department of Justice for The Times and has also written about gun violence, civil rights and conditions in the country’s jails and prisons.

Katie Rogers is a White House correspondent for The Times, reporting on President Trump.

Zolan Kanno-Youngs is a White House correspondent for The Times, covering President Trump and his administration.

In U. S. Gas Talks With Kremlin, Hidden Financing for Alaska Project Emerges

The New York Times October 24, 2026

Russia-Ukraine War

Advertisement

Supported by

Interviews and documents show a Russian energy giant secretly funded a U. S. firm. The deal has been discussed in talks to end the war in Ukraine.

By Anton Troianovski and Eric Lipton

Reporting from Washington

At first blush, the proposed venture looks like it would further the Trump administration’s goal of global “energy dominance.”

An American energy company intends to buy Russian technology and use it to access a massive supply of natural gas in Alaska, liquefy it and export it to allies abroad.

The Kremlin and the White House were interested in the idea. President Vladimir V. Putin discussed the plan last month with President Trump’s peace envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, people familiar with the negotiations said, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive diplomacy. It is one of a series of energy deals White House officials believe could help smooth relations with Moscow and eventually pave the way to end the war in Ukraine.

But it turns out that the company was not an all-American affair. The multibillion-dollar project has received secret funding from the same powerful Russian company that was to provide the technology, according to the energy executive who until last month led the U. S. firm and two others involved in company negotiations.

Joel Riddle, who was chief executive of the company, Polar LNG, until he resigned in September, said he had been misled about the sources of the start-up funding, which ostensibly came from a company in the United Arab Emirates.

Instead, Mr. Riddle said he learned, the true source of at least some of Polar LNG’s money was Novatek, a Russian energy giant under partial U. S. sanctions.

“It’s not only unlawful, but it’s not in the U. S. interest to have Russian technology controlling the commercialization of Arctic gas in the North Slope,” Mr. Riddle said in a brief interview.

These previously unreported tensions were also detailed in legal memos that Mr. Riddle attached to his resignation letter, which was reviewed by The New York Times. The memos, prepared by Baker Botts, an international law firm, said the Treasury Department’s sanctions enforcement unit had raised concerns that Polar LNG had ties to Novatek that might present “potential Russia-related sanctions concerns.”

Polar LNG on Friday issued a statement announcing a new acting chief executive, Tim Talkington, and described Mr. Riddle as a “disgruntled former employee.”

But in a statement to The Times, Novatek said on Friday that in fact, it was moving to acquire “minority shareholder” status in the Polar LNG project — a striking effort by the Russian energy giant to seek ownership of American gas production.

The project, if it happens, is a long way off. In addition to the sanctions issues that would have to be negotiated, the technology envisioned is highly complex and must overcome some of the most brutal weather conditions in the United States. It also is competing with another Alaska gas plan that already has the support of the Trump administration. But that the Polar LNG deal is being discussed at all shows how business deals of almost any stripe are on the table during the talks with the Kremlin.

The sequence of events illustrates the unorthodox, opaque mixture of deal-making and high-stakes diplomacy that has defined Mr. Trump’s attempts to end Europe’s bloodiest conflict since World War II.

What you should know about anonymous sources. The Times makes a careful decision any time it shields the identity of a source. The information the source supplies must be newsworthy, credible and give readers genuine insight.

There is no indication that Mr. Witkoff or Mr. Kushner were aware of Polar LNG or its ties to Novatek, even as the broad outlines of the deal came up in their talks with Mr. Putin beginning last year. A U. S. official, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss the closed-door talks, said that the deal had only been broadly mentioned and that no granular discussions had occurred.

The project, should it ever come to fruition, would doubly help Novatek, one of Russia’s biggest energy companies, first by using Novatek’s technology and second because the company would own an equity stake.

The Alaska gas discussions have taken place alongside talks to sell off part of another Russian energy giant, Lukoil, to the U. S. government and other investors, including some with business ties to Mr. Witkoff and Mr. Kushner, causing consternation among some Washington lawmakers and outraging some of Ukraine’s supporters. The pair have also discussed the possibility of U. S. involvement in future Russian gas exports to Europe. (The administration has said that Mr. Kushner and Mr. Witkoff were guided only by U. S. interests.)

Geoffrey R. Pyatt, who served as an assistant secretary of state for energy resources during the Biden administration, said the idea of bringing Novatek into the high north of Alaska is a terrible one. “It is terrible on environmental grounds, it is a terrible idea on economic and geopolitical grounds, and most importantly this feeds the belief that Putin can get an out-of-jail-free card.”

The efforts to bring Novatek equipment to Alaska have also included a businessman, Gentry Beach, with ties to the Trump family. A college friend of Donald Trump Jr., the president’s eldest son, Mr. Beach served as a finance vice chairman for Mr. Trump’s 2017 inauguration. Mr. Beach said in February that he had held negotiations with Novatek about bringing its natural gas technology to Alaska.

Mr. Beach could not be reached for comment. It was not clear if he remained involved in the project, or whether he was aware of Novatek’s potential ownership stake in Polar LNG.

A spokesman for Donald Trump Jr. said the two men were no longer close, adding that Mr. Trump was not involved in the Polar LNG project. Novatek’s statement said that Mr. Beach had no role in its discussions to take a stake in Polar LNG. The U. S. official said Mr. Beach was not involved in the administration’s discussions related to Novatek.

Mr. Riddle is one of at least three Polar LNG executives who recently resigned. As they departed, Trump officials were notified about their concerns related to the secret Russian financing. Mr. Riddle said the executives had urged administration officials to investigate the matter. The Energy Department, where the warning was sent, did not respond when asked about the matter.

“I felt like I did the right thing to notify authorities at the appropriate time,” Mr. Riddle said.

The Polar LNG plan called for the company to tap into the giant load of natural gas available in the northern reaches of Alaska, a byproduct of extensive oil extraction underway in the region.

Currently, there is no way to move most of the gas that is produced along with the oil, so energy companies inject it back into the earth.

Polar LNG’s proposal calls for it to buy a giant, 640,000-ton concrete-and-steel device from Novatek called a gravity-based structure that would be placed on the seabed just above the northern coast of Alaska, in an area known as Milne Point.

On top of that platform, equipment will be installed that would refrigerate gas supplied by an area oil producer, transforming it into a liquid that can then be loaded onto ships that travel through icy waters and deliver it to customers in Asia.

Novatek uses a similar approach to export natural gas from the Russian Arctic in a project called Arctic LNG 2. Mr. Putin said publicly last year that “we are discussing with our American partners” the possibility of using Novatek technology to produce liquefied natural gas in Alaska.

Korean-made ships with a special ice-breaking design that Polar LNG plans to use were initially built for Novatek, but delivery was stopped by the manufacturer after the United States imposed sanctions on the Arctic LNG 2 project.

From the start, Novatek was slated to supply the gas liquefaction station. But financing for the project was not supposed to come from Russia, according to executives involved in the effort.

Emphasizing the point, Polar LNG features images of the American flag and a bald eagle on its website, boasting that “Polar LNG helps ensure the United States leads,” adding that the project is “America’s Arctic Advantage.”

The company hired lobbyists in Washington and in Alaska to help push the project, according to federal and state records. In Washington alone, the company is spending $380,000 a quarter on lobbying, hiring a former Trump-era Interior Department acting assistant secretary, Adam Suess.

Novatek is already under U. S. sanctions that would require the Treasury Department to issue a license for its equipment to be used in Alaska. Recently passed sanctions legislation named after deceased Senator Lindsey Graham, Republican of South Carolina, makes things even harder: The bill specifically targets Novatek, as well as its Arctic LNG 2 project, because of the company’s ties to Mr. Putin.

However, Mr. Trump temporarily waived the law’s Russia sanctions last week, presenting the move as necessary to keep peace talks going.

During a meeting held at the Four Seasons Hotel in late August in Abu Dhabi between executives of Polar LNG and its parent company, Tech Wave Industrial Projects Management, top executives from Novatek were present. That was when Mr. Riddle began to appreciate that Novatek was directly involved in approving funding to keep the effort going, text messages reviewed by The Times indicate.

Tech Wave is an Abu Dhabi-based company that specializes in managing oil, gas and construction projects. Its chief operating officer is Bjorn Gundersen, who a decade ago was listed in oil industry trade publications as a senior executive at Novatek supervising LNG projects.

A second Tech Wave executive, Ahmed Farghaly, also worked for Novatek until recently. According to his LinkedIn profile, he left around the time the United States first imposed sanctions on one of Novatek’s LNG projects. Mr. Gundersen, Mr. Farghaly and Tech Wave did not respond to requests for comment.

Denis Solovyov, Novatek’s deputy chairman, as well as Leonid Mikhelson, the company’s chief executive, discussed their company providing as much as $15 million to Tech Wave to bankroll Polar LNG, the messages say. Asked about the messages and the Abu Dhabi meeting, Novatek said it could not comment on private correspondence, but that the company and Polar LNG had agreed to “provide each other with open communication.”

“All the necessary decisions were made at the meeting in Abu Dhabi,” Mr. Solovyov wrote in one message to Mr. Riddle sent in early September. “The first 5 million were supposed to arrive by today.”

It was several weeks after this exchange that Mr. Riddle resigned. Two other top Polar LNG executives, Dan Chandra, the company’s chief financial officer, and Jim Smith, a former Exxon Mobil executive who served as Polar LNG’s executive vice president, also have left in recent weeks.

Polar LNG, in a statement Friday, said that “Riddle was recently terminated from the company for cause,” adding: “The company is investigating claims concerning Riddle that may result in litigation.”

But Mr. Riddle resigned six days before the company issued him a letter saying it would terminate his employment immediately, in part because he had raised concerns that some of the company’s actions could be “subject to sanctions,” documents obtained by The Times show.

Questions about the potential ties to Novatek had by late this summer already reached Trump administration officials, according to a memo prepared by an outside law firm for Polar LNG, Baker Botts.

“Concerns regarding a perceived connection to Novatek will likely affect licensing or other regulatory approvals,” Baker Botts wrote in a memo to company executives that was shared with The Times.

In addition, the letter said that federal officials had already made clear in communications with the company that they were concerned that an investor in Polar LNG “has ties to Novatek and may be acting on Novatek’s behalf with respect to the project.”

Paul Luther, a Baker Botts lawyer who worked on the matter, declined on Friday to discuss it further.

Polar LNG would need a series of approvals from the federal government before the deal could move ahead, including a sign-off from the Treasury Department authorizing it to acquire the Novatek seabed platform, given that parts of the company are under sanctions. It would also require a permit from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to build a gas export facility.

Questions have already emerged about whether the Novatek device will function at the planned Milne Point location because of shallow waters there and the “potential disruption to traditional whaling and local opposition, particularly from the local native Alaskan population,” a lawyer for Polar LNG wrote in an internal company memo.

Certain Trump administration officials had already expressed skepticism about the Polar LNG plan, according to internal company documents seen by The Times and interviews with some of the people involved.

Part of the concern is that the Polar LNG project would be pitted against an even more ambitious plan to build a $50 billion, 800-mile natural gas pipeline to move natural gas from the northern slope to the southern coast of Alaska, where it could be more easily shipped out from existing ports there. That plan would also potentially supply Asian markets.

Both the Biden and Trump administrations enthusiastically embraced the gas pipeline project, which Japan and Korea may help finance to increase their reliable supply of natural gas.

“The pipeline makes far more sense,” said Matthew McManus, who until April 2025 served as a deputy director at the State Department’s Bureau of Energy Resources and is now at the National Center for Energy Analytics. “The Polar LNG project would face years of permitting and concerns about ties to Russia.”

Mr. Talkington, Polar LNG’s acting chief executive, said his company sought to seize “a generational opportunity to advance U. S. energy dominance, unlock profound benefits for the state of Alaska, and strengthen American Arctic navigation.”

The fact that discussions are even going on about using Russian equipment — and potentially a Russian-financed company — to move American natural gas to international markets is a further insult to Ukraine, and should not be a part of talks over a possible end to the war, said Ilya Zaslavskiy, a gas industry consultant who previously worked in Moscow and New York who now does research on Russian sanctions and energy issues out of Washington.

“Any approach by Novatek to transfer technology should be seen as a Kremlin attempt to co-opt U. S. policymakers in order to undermine U. S. foreign policy toward Ukraine and our allies,” Mr. Zaslavskiy said.

Rebecca F. Elliott contributed reporting.

Anton Troianovski writes about American foreign policy and national security for The Times from Washington. He was previously a foreign correspondent based in Moscow and Berlin.

Eric Lipton is a Times investigative reporter, who digs into a broad range of topics from Pentagon spending to toxic chemicals.

She Planned to Protest Trump. She Didn’t Plan on Getting Punched.

The New York Times October 24, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Blake Miley yelled “fascist” as President Trump spoke at a midterm campaign rally. The violence that followed “was not right,” she said.

By Jessica Contrera

The night before President Trump spoke in Youngstown, Ohio, this month, Blake Miley stayed up past 4 a. m., cutting out felt letters for a T-shirt that would say “RELEASE THE EPSTEIN FILES.”

The next evening, she went to the rally and stood up halfway through, revealing her shirt and yelling, “Fascist, fascist!” Almost immediately, Ms. Miley, 29, was tackled, held down and punched by male rally-goers as the president mocked her from the stage, calling her “scum,” “low-class,” and “a fat guy.”

As Mr. Trump barnstorms the country hoping to revive his base ahead of the midterm election, he is returning to an old habit: heckling protesters and encouraging violence against them. In Georgia last week, he expressed his love for a supporter who had responded to a protester by “slapping the guy around,” and promised to bring the slapper to Washington. In South Carolina on Wednesday, he praised an “incredible” punch that a rally-goer landed on another protester, saying, “He got whacked, man!”

Ten years after Mr. Trump shocked some voters by saying he would personally like to punch a protester in the face at one of his rallies, these skirmishes are now met by many with a shrug. Ms. Miley, who is identifying herself publicly for the first time, said she suspects that no one in power much cares that she got beaten up.

“I knew there was a really good possibility that this would happen,” she said. “But I don’t blame myself. It is not right what they did to me.”

Ms. Miley attended the rally alone, and had intentionally seated herself among people who seemed older, she said. She hoped it would keep her safe. But as soon as she started yelling, a man grabbed for her neck and then shoved her backward, video of the episode shows. When she stood back up, another man appeared to pull her to the ground, put her in a headlock, yank her hair and punch her in the face.

She remembers being hit twice, unable to get up until Mahoning County sheriff’s deputies intervened about 30 seconds into the brawl.

“What he doesn’t know is that his mother and father voted for me,” Mr. Trump continued about Ms. Miley, who is a woman. “Oh, he looks so terrible. And he’s going to get home and he’s going to get smacked.”

The deputies escorted Ms. Miley out of the arena. The men who attacked her were left alone. One raised his fists and high-fived those around him.

In the arena’s parking lot, Ms. Miley was shaking so severely that onlookers called her an ambulance. She said she spent a few hours at the hospital, was discharged, and drove in a daze to her mobile home north of Columbus. She threw her Epstein shirt in her closet and collapsed onto her bed.

Back in Youngstown, the Mahoning County Sheriff’s Department was getting flooded with angry calls from people who had seen video of the incident, demanding to know why no one had been arrested. The sheriff, Jerry Greene, said he had as many 800 phone messages, many of them containing raw abuse.

Video footage, Sheriff Greene said, clearly showed a woman being punched in the face. “I know what people saw, and if I saw that video, too, I’d be like, ‘My God, why didn’t the police do anything?’”

Sheriff Greene, who had changed parties to become a Republican in 2023, said that he is, in fact, doing something. He reviewed body camera footage, which he said shows that his deputies were pushing through the crowd to reach Ms. Miley and did not witness the punch.

He has identified three men who he said took part in the assault, including a New Jersey resident who said in a now-deleted Facebook post that he and two friends had “subdued her and threw her to the concrete.” Investigators believe the other two men, including the one who threw the punch, are local; none could be reached by The Times.

The sheriff said that all three would be interviewed in coming days. He is waiting for medical records from Ms. Miley’s trip to the emergency room, he added, to determine whether her injuries were severe enough to warrant felony charges instead of misdemeanors.

Three days after the rally, one of the sheriff’s investigators tracked down Ms. Miley through her mother, who, contrary to Mr. Trump’s presumption, does not vote.

She had not told her parents she was going to the Trump rally. Though she had been to a few local protests before, facing down the president and his most fervent supporters directly was out of character for Ms. Miley, who spends most of her days at home.

She frequently has seizures, she said, and after years of passing out while working at warehouses, nursing homes and retail stores, she has not held a job since April. Lately, she relies on financial help from her boyfriend, who works in an auto-parts store, and her mother, who is a nurse.

“Most days are quite monotonous for me,” she said. “I get up. I might wash dishes or do laundry. I work on my art.”

When she scrolls, her feeds seem to constantly be filled with news about Mr. Trump and how he is changing the country.

She is worried about the prospect of losing Medicaid, which is likely to happen next year unless she starts working, volunteering or going to school 80 hours per month under a new law that Mr. Trump championed. She is worried about the cost of gas and groceries for her grandparents, who are still working at ages 79 and 82. But Ms. Miley is particularly bothered about the millions of documents related to sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, she said, because of her own experiences with abuse in a past relationship.

She has watched every documentary she can find on Mr. Epstein, who before his arrest and subsequent suicide routinely communicated with politicians, celebrities and business executives — including Mr. Trump. Many of their names appear in the files of documents, some of which the Justice Department started releasing, with redactions, last year after months of resistance from the president.

Most days this year, as she waited for her boyfriend to come home for dinner, Ms. Miley felt as though she could do little about the actions of Mr. Trump. But this month, a video came across her TikTok feed of a protester interrupting a Trump rally in Vandalia, Ohio, and being escorted out.

It was something simple, something doable.

The president, she realized, would be back in her state just a few days later.

She said she did not coordinate with any formal protest group, and despite Mr. Trump’s allegation that she was paid, went on her own accord.

In the days after she came home with cuts on her face and bruises on her arms, she read dozens of posts about the incident. She noticed the commenters who called her brave, who seemed to far outweigh the ones that made fun of her. It bothered her that there were AI-generated images of the scene, but one showed her with her arms raised, her face defiant. “I’m with her,” the caption said.

A high-profile civil rights attorney, Subodh Chandra, is representing her for free. Mr. Chandra said he has been in touch with Sheriff Greene, and he feels “persuaded that they are trying to do their jobs.” If arrests are not made, he said, Ohio has a law allowing citizens to file charges for a judge to review.

Kitty Bennett contributed research.

Jessica Contrera is a national reporter for The Times, based in Ohio.

Republicans Are Crude, Craven, Cruel. It’s Not Working Anymore.

The New York Times October 24, 2026

Advertisement

Newsletter

By Jamelle Bouie

Opinion Columnist

In my column last week, I wrote about the Democratic Party’s dramatic change of fortune in the race to control the Senate. The expectation at the start of this election cycle was that Republicans would hold the chamber easily and, depending on the course of events, even expand their majority.

After all, just to maintain the status quo, Democrats had to defend incumbents in states that President Trump won handily. And to have any chance at a majority, they would need to defeat at least one incumbent — Susan Collins of Maine, for example — and overcome the Republican Party’s home-field advantage in at least two states.

A tall order if there ever was one.

But thanks to a set of Trump’s bad decisions — from his authoritarian occupations of American cities that enraged liberal voters to a war in Iran that has angered swing voters and independents with inflation and high prices — Democrats have turned what was supposed to be a bad Senate map into one where they stand a real chance of winning a decently sized majority in the chamber.

But while the fundamentals determine the overall shape of the electoral landscape, candidates and campaigns play a meaningful part in the final outcome. And it is in the realm of candidates and campaigns that I want to remark on two particular aspects of this campaign season.

The first is the wide gap in candidate quality between the Republicans and Democrats. In race after race, Democrats have managed to recruit and advance candidates who are well positioned to capitalize on changing political circumstances. Even if he were not facing off against Ken Paxton, an experienced but still strikingly weak candidate, James Talarico would still be an impressive recruit. He is a natural communicator — whose seminarian background and personal faith have been a great asset in winning over Texas voters — and he has proved to be both nimble and aggressive, able to hold Paxton’s feet to the fire despite facing an onslaught of cash from outside groups and actors, like Elon Musk.

You could say similar things of Adam Hamilton in Kansas, perhaps the surprise candidate of this cycle, who is running a competitive race against the Republican incumbent, Roger Marshall. Hamilton is a religious leader — the founder and senior pastor of the Church of the Resurrection, the largest United Methodist congregation in the United States — with broad appeal in a state that is, like Texas, known for its deep religious feeling. With his moderate politics, Hamilton has successfully presented himself as a bipartisan figure, with support from prominent Republicans in Kansas. It also helps that Marshall, a doctor, has struggled in the face of revelations that he took harsh and punitive action against his patients, dragging them to court for trivial amounts of money.

Other Democratic candidates, such as Josh Turek in Iowa, Sherrod Brown in Ohio and Troy Jackson in Maine, have also successfully capitalized on the Republican Party’s worsening electoral position. And even those Democrats who might be a little more progressive than their electorates — Peggy Flanagan in Minnesota and Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan — show a great deal of political talent and are well-positioned to win.

As for the Republicans, the opposite appears to be true. There are a few candidates in the field who may well outperform the fundamentals, like the Iowa Senate nominee Ashley Hinson. Michele Tafoya in Minnesota also seems to be keeping up with her opponent. But beyond them, Republicans are working with candidates who are just not up to snuff. In Georgia, Mike Collins has been marred by his associations with white nationalists and other extremists, and is headed for a crushing defeat in his race against the incumbent, Senator Jon Ossoff. Darline Graham in South Carolina is barely ahead of her Democratic opponent, and again, this is South Carolina. The aforementioned Ken Paxton is such a lackluster candidate that he may well deliver the Texas Republican Party its first statewide defeat for federal office since 1988.

Perhaps the most striking example of a candidate ill-equipped for a competitive race is Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican nominee for governor of Ohio. Ramaswamy ran unsuccessfully for the 2024 Republican presidential nomination, then returned home to Ohio to try to lead the party there. Perhaps the fact that Republicans were not anticipating a competitive year is how Ramaswamy managed to win the nomination. Either way, he is currently poised to lose to the Democratic nominee, Amy Acton.

In apparent desperation, the Ramaswamy campaign commissioned an advertisement featuring Amy Acton’s mother. The two have not seen or spoken to each other since 1978. As a child, Acton testified against her stepfather, who was charged with sexually abusing her. Acton’s mother took her husband’s side, and the two fled the state. In the advertisement, Acton’s mother calls her daughter a liar, someone who “lies about her past.” The evidence says otherwise. To give one example, documents released by Mahoning County officials in Ohio corroborate Acton’s claim that she lived in a tent as a child.

The Ramaswamy camp, which includes fellow Ohioan JD Vance, thinks the ad is effective. But it’s been condemned by people on both sides, including the state’s Republican governor, as crude, craven and cruel. There is a chance, as well, that it blows back on Ramaswamy, undermining his campaign in the critical final stretch of the election. It is the kind of move that a more seasoned and competent candidate might have avoided. As it is, Ramaswamy’s gambit may well drag down the entire statewide ticket.

We’re still 10 days away from Election Day, so I’m not going to make any grand pronouncements about the outcome. But I will say that if Republicans do lose the Senate, and if they lose it badly, it will be a testament to one of the most striking political dynamics of the Trump era.

It is very possible that Trump was the only Republican who could have stitched together his particular electoral coalition. It is undoubtedly the case that Trump has some special sauce that makes him a formidable general election candidate. But this has not extended to the rest of the Republican Party. No other Republican is able to mimic Trump’s particular style of politics. And while Trump’s endorsement is a powerful force in Republican primaries, the president does not actually have a great track record of picking candidates who go on to win general elections.

Trump is in absolute command of the Republican Party, but outside of his own victories, he has steered it, more often than not, into troubled electoral waters.

My column this week was on the Trump administration’s attempt to denaturalize and expel Representative Ilhan Omar of Minnesota.

It should be said that the drive to denaturalize Omar is, by itself, a startling attack on the liberty of all Americans. It’s a move that harks back to the worst of the nation’s past — those moments when the government sought to shape, define and ultimately choose who would be “the people” of the United States.

I joined my colleagues Michelle Cottle and David French for an episode of The Opinions. I’ll also talked a little about Representative Omar for a video. And I talked a little bit about my process and approach to writing with political scientist Hanna Sistek, media historian Sage Goodwin and communication scholar Julius Freeman at the Center for American Political History, Media and Technology at Purdue University.

Sue Halpern on the totalitarian aspirations of the Silicon Valley elite for The New York Review of Books.

Anne Applebaum on the United States’ imperial adventure in Venezuela for The Atlantic.

Kim Phillips-Fein on Elon Musk for Dissent magazine.

Jessica Winter on Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s vision for New York public schools for The New Yorker.

Laura Marsh on “You Can See Everything” for The New Republic.

I saw this sign in Chicago the last time I was there and liked it quite a bit.

A delicious way to use up the odds and ends of herbs, greens and cheeses you might have in your fridge. Also very kid-friendly if, like me, you have to think about those things. Recipe comes from NYT Cooking.

Ingredients

Salt and black pepper

4 cups chopped spinach, Swiss chard or other mild greens (tough stems removed)

4 cups chopped arugula, watercress or other peppery greens

1 cup chopped fresh dill or parsley leaves and tender stems, or a combination

6 scallions, trimmed and thinly sliced, whites and dark green parts separated

1 pound tubular or curvy pasta, like rigatoni or fusilli

2 tablespoons unsalted butter

4 garlic cloves, peeled and thinly sliced

8 ounces cream cheese (1 cup), cut into ½-inch cubes

4 ounces mozzarella, grated (1 cup)

4 ounces crumbled feta (1 cup)

Directions

Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil. Heat the oven to 450 degrees.

In a 3-quart/9-by-13-inch baking dish, toss the chopped spinach, arugula, herbs and scallion greens with 2 teaspoons salt and a few grinds of black pepper. Squeeze the mixture with your hands to wilt, then set aside.

Cook the pasta in the boiling water until 2 minutes shy of al dente; reserve 1 cup pasta water, then drain pasta and set aside. Return the pot to the stove.

Melt the butter in the pot over medium heat. Add the scallion whites, garlic and a pinch of salt, and cook until softened, 4 to 5 minutes. Add the cream cheese and pasta water and stir until smooth. Stir in the wilted greens, half the mozzarella and half the feta until combined. Stir in the pasta until combined. Taste and adjust seasonings as needed.

Transfer the pasta to the baking dish, then top with remaining mozzarella and feta. Bake until the sauce has thickened and turned bubbly, and the top has browned in spots, 10 to 15 minutes. If you like a crisper top, broil for a few minutes.

Jamelle Bouie became a New York Times Opinion columnist in 2019. Before that he was the chief political correspondent for Slate magazine. He is based in Charlottesville, Va.

Netanyahu Has Reinvented Himself. Will Voters Think It’s Enough?

The New York Times October 24, 2026

Israel’s Election

The Oct. 7 attacks marred Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s image as Mr. Security. Ahead of elections, he’s trying to sell Israelis on the new, hawkish version of himself.

The Oct. 7 attacks marred Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s image as Mr. Security. Ahead of elections, he’s trying to sell Israelis on the new, hawkish version of himself.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel speaking to supporters at a mall in Holon, Israel, this month. Credit... Avishag Shaar-Yashuv for The New York Times

Supported by

By Isabel Kershner

The reporter has covered 10 Israeli elections and followed Prime Minister Netanyahu on many campaign trails.

Benjamin Netanyahu looks thinner and paler these days. Gone is the swagger of previous political campaigns. But he remains tireless, traipsing among shopping centers and television studios, trying to persuade a weary and polarized country to return him to office for up to another four years in Israeli elections on Tuesday.

At 77, he is already Israel’s longest-serving prime minister. If he is to extend that tenure, he has to sell the deeply divided electorate on the new, more hawkish version of himself — and of Israel.

Mr. Netanyahu’s career will forever be defined by the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel, the deadliest day for Jews since the Holocaust. He long had a reputation for being risk averse and avoiding military confrontations, even as he cultivated an image as Israel’s Mr. Security. But that image, as well as Israel’s confidence in its own defense, was badly damaged that day.

So Mr. Netanyahu, known by friends and foes as Bibi, reinvented himself. Instead of sticking to Israel’s previous security doctrine centered on short wars of defense, he has waged Israel’s longest war on multiple fronts — against Hamas in Gaza, Hezbollah militants in Lebanon, the Houthi militia in Yemen and, together with the United States, Iran.

He has doubled down on Israel’s occupation of the West Bank, allowing Jewish settlements to proliferate and settler violence against Palestinians to escalate, further aggravating Israel’s international isolation.

“He understood that if he wanted to survive, not only politically but as a historic figure, he had to change,” said Mazal Mualem, an Israeli political commentator and Netanyahu biographer. “He killed off the old Bibi and delivered a new one into the world,” she added.

After the Oct. 7 attacks, Mr. Netanyahu promised total victory over Hamas and other enemies. While Israel’s military campaign has left those adversaries battered, the wars have been inconclusive. Now, he says there is more to be done, and that he is the one to do it. “We must complete the elimination of the Iranian regime,” he said on Tuesday.

It is unclear whether he will get the chance. Days before what many Israelis view as the most fateful election in the country’s history, Mr. Netanyahu and his Likud party are in a tight race against an opposition led by Gadi Eisenkot, a centrist and former military chief. Opinion polls show the opposition slightly ahead but lacking enough seats to guarantee a governing coalition.

Mr. Netanyahu may have lost some of his luster, but he is a master politician who has maintained a loyal base of supporters and cultivated strong political alliances, meaning that he cannot be counted out.

As prime minister for most of the past 17 years, in addition to a three-year term in the 1990s, Mr. Netanyahu has evolved along with the Israel he has largely shaped.

He returned to power in late 2022 after a brief hiatus. Shunned by other mainstream parties because he faces corruption charges, Mr. Netanyahu formed a governing coalition with the participation of far-right extremists who had been considered beyond the pale by most Israeli politicians.

At the time, he told Israel’s Parliament that the country was in its “golden age” after “the quietest and safest security decade in our history.” Even as he repeated a pledge to block Iran from developing a nuclear weapon, he trumpeted his aim to “widen the circle of peace” with the goal of ending the Arab-Israeli conflict.

Instead, on the morning of Oct. 7, 2023, thousands of gunmen surged across the border from Gaza, overrunning Israeli communities, army bases and a music festival, killing about 1,200 people, according to the Israeli authorities, and taking 251 hostages.

Mr. Netanyahu has not taken personal responsibility for government failures that preceded the attacks, including his policy aimed at fostering quiet in Hamas-run Gaza rather than confronting the militant group, or the military and intelligence lapses that left Israel vulnerable. He has blocked an independent state inquiry into what went wrong.

Mr. Netanyahu says that his security chiefs chose not to wake him on Oct. 7.

But Mr. Netanyahu and Israeli security leaders repeatedly downplayed signs that Gaza militants were gearing up for an assault, including reports of heightened Hamas activity from female military spotters and the acquisition of a Hamas battle plan.

Israel’s war against Hamas killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, according to Gaza health officials, prompting accusations of war crimes against Mr. Netanyahu from rights groups and foreign governments.

Critics and former Israeli officials also say he prolonged the war in Gaza, which Israel launched in response to the Oct. 7 attacks, and delayed deals for the release of hostages — to keep his far-right coalition partners on board and remain in power. The prime minister’s office did not respond to a request for comment.

The wars have also overstretched the military and taken a toll on many Israelis, who have performed repeated tours as reserve soldiers. At the same time, Mr. Netanyahu has extended the exemption of ultra-Orthodox Jewish men from mandatory military service, bending to the demands of his ultra-Orthodox coalition partners who say religious study is a higher priority.

Israel’s conduct in the Gaza war has also left the country increasingly isolated and facing international boycotts and embargoes. Although Mr. Netanyahu, who spent part of his childhood in Pennsylvania, prides himself on speaking “American,” support for Israel in the United States is at an unprecedented low, said Daniel B. Shapiro, a former U. S. ambassador to Israel.

“There’s no way you could reverse that without a change in leadership, in the face of Israel,” he added.

Mr. Netanyahu’s vision of an Israeli Sparta — an insular, self-sufficient, militaristic society — which he offered at an economic conference in 2025, has been deeply unsettling for many Israelis, who have traditionally enjoyed economic and other ties overseas.

In the past, Mr. Netanyahu was loath to preside over an open-ended war. “I am not eager for unnecessary wars,” he said in 2018 amid tensions along the Gaza border, adding that he was working to ease the economic crisis in the enclave to prevent an escalation in violence.

For a quarter-century, mostly under Mr. Netanyahu, Israel lived largely within its border fences after withdrawing from southern Lebanon in 2000 and from Gaza in 2005.

Now, saying it is acting to protect Israeli border communities, Israel is again occupying swaths of territory in Lebanon and Gaza, and expanded the area it occupies in Syria. Military policies of containment have been set aside. On Sunday, Mr. Netanyahu published his updated national security doctrine, putting a priority on pre-empting threats.

After Israel killed Hezbollah’s longtime leader in Lebanon, in 2024, Mr. Netanyahu summed up his philosophy by invoking a Talmudic teaching on pre-emptive action. “If someone rises up to kill you,” he said, “kill him first.”

On the campaign trail, Mr. Netanyahu continues to sound an alert about what he deems threats external and internal, stoking fear of Israel’s Arab citizens and questioning the legitimacy of the political parties that represent them.

On a recent weeknight, security officers ushered Mr. Netanyahu into a grimy food court at a shopping mall in Holon, a Tel Aviv suburb. About 200 people were waiting for him.

“Bibi, King of Israel!” the crowd chanted, repeating a common refrain.

Struggling to be heard over an inadequate sound system, Mr. Netanyahu delivered a stump speech of barely 90 seconds.

“Do you want Mansour Abbas?” he asked, referring to the leader of an Arab political party that could play kingmaker in a close election.

“No!” the crowd cried.

“Well go out and vote Likud!” he exhorted, before being whisked away.

“I love him,” said Shimon Karni, 48, who was in the crowd. “I’m proud of what he’s done for Israel and the Jewish people,” he said. “May he be our prime minister till he’s 120.”

Mr. Netanyahu’s supporters call him a unique leader.

“The prime minister is a proud Israeli patriot who believes with every fiber of his being that he is the only leader capable of dealing with the challenges facing Israel,” said Ofer Golan, a former adviser to Mr. Netanyahu. “And I believe he is right.”

Since the last election, Mr. Netanyahu and his allies have also begun to target what they call enemies in the deep state, including Israel’s attorney general and top judges.

This transformation of Mr. Netanyahu began long before the Oct. 7 attacks, analysts say, dating it to 2019, when he was indicted on charges of bribery, fraud and breach of trust in three separate but related corruption cases. On trial since 2020, he has denied any wrongdoing and accused the deep state of trying to oust him through a judicial putsch after failing at the ballot box.

Mr. Netanyahu once pointed to Israel’s democratic institutions as a beacon in the Middle East. After he was indicted, “he perceived the legal apparatus as a direct foe,” said Yohanan Plesner, the president of the Israel Democracy Institute, a nonpartisan research group.

In January 2023, Mr. Netanyahu’s justice minister, Yariv Levin, announced a plan for a sweeping judicial overhaul. Mr. Netanyahu said it was necessary to rein in what he called an overactive judiciary, restore the balance between the branches of government and give more power to elected officials.

Opponents of the plan said the proposed measures would remove checks on government power and lead to a dictatorship of the majority. Mass protests erupted across the country. Some Israelis feared a civil war. Israel’s security chiefs said they warned repeatedly that the protests and social schism weakened Israel in the eyes of its enemies and would lead to war.

Mr. Netanyahu’s critics say he became engrossed in his personal troubles and surrounded himself with a shrinking coterie of loyalists.

“He was of course a man of many capabilities, but more important, he had a detailed strategic vision,” said Ehud Yaari, an Israel-based fellow of the Washington Institute for Near East Policy. His aims included developing relations with African nations and expanding agreements with Arab Gulf states.

“But instead of focusing on the big goals, he began his personal war,” Mr. Yaari said. “It was a different Netanyahu, with different priorities. His attention drifted elsewhere.”

For years, Mr. Netanyahu pursued formal relations with moderate Arab Gulf states to bypass Palestinians or pressure them into greater territorial compromise. After the Abraham Accords of 2020 normalized Israel’s relations with Morocco, Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates, the big prize was to be Saudi Arabia.

But Mr. Netanyahu’s far-right partners prevented him from proposing an eventual pathway to Palestinian statehood as the Saudi government demanded. In the past, he had paid lip service, at least, to the idea of a demilitarized Palestinian state.

“To preserve his coalition, he gave up on that too,” said Gayil Talshir, a political scientist at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.

Instead, he has proceeded in lock step with members of his government seeking to eventually annex the West Bank. His policies there, together with his failure to tackle mounting violence by Israeli settlers against Palestinians, contributed to the recent imposition of sanctions by several countries once among Israel’s staunchest allies.

“We all wonder where his head is at, where his personal value system is,” said Shalom Lipner, another former aide to several Israeli leaders, including Mr. Netanyahu. He added, “We’ve seen him shift to be able to stay in the chair.”

Isabel Kershner, a senior correspondent for The Times in Jerusalem, has been reporting on Israeli and Palestinian affairs since 1990.

Why Democrats Could Find It Hard to Win the Senate Despite Their Strong Polls

The New York Times October 24, 2026

Democrats are increasingly optimistic about the midterms. But they are being outspent by Republicans. And they are trying to compete in states that favored President Trump by large margins.

Democrats are increasingly optimistic about the midterms. But they are being outspent by Republicans. And they are trying to compete in states that favored President Trump by large margins.

Credit... Julia Demaree Nikhinson/Associated Press

Supported by

By Lisa Lerer

Democrats have a hefty advantage in national polls. President Trump is playing defense, campaigning through deep-red corners of the country that he won by overwhelming margins just two years ago. And assumptions that Democrats will win control of Congress have become conventional wisdom in many quarters, from longtime political observers to social media to the oddsmakers in prediction markets.

But as Democratic dreams of midterm victories grow bigger, some strategists quietly worry that expanding expectations are crowding out signs of a more challenging political reality.

Control of the Senate hinges on victories in red states that favored Mr. Trump by significant margins in 2024, including some that Democrats have not won in decades. Republicans are outspending them by eye-popping amounts in key races. And after its performance in 2024, the Democratic Party as a brand still remains unpopular among voters.

All of that has left some in both parties wondering: Could the much-discussed blue wave end up looking more like a splash?

“The election can be summed up in the following sentence: Can huge amounts of Republican money defeat huge Democratic advantages in issues, candidates and political climate,” said Senator Chuck Schumer, the minority leader from New York.

Strategists in both parties believe it is increasingly unlikely that Republicans will be able to hold on to their House majority. But among Democratic donors, activists and voters, hopes of winning control of both chambers have grown so high that some fear any other result could feel like falling short.

“I am concerned that we have an overheating of expectations,” said Molly Murphy, a pollster who worked on the 2024 campaigns of former President Joseph R. Biden Jr. and former Vice President Kamala Harris. “People often assume in a wave you win everything, and what happens in a modern wave is you win far more than normal.”

The kind of broad wins that once defined wave elections are largely a thing of the past, Ms. Murphy said, destroyed by gerrymandering that has left relatively few House seats truly competitive.

In 2018, the most recent midterm election considered a landslide election, Democrats won 41 House seats and control of the chamber. But Republicans gained two Senate seats and expanded their majority.

This year, there’s near-universal agreement among politicians, strategists and activists that Republicans face steeper political headwinds than Democrats. Mr. Trump’s approval rating hit a new low this week, views of the economy are dismal and Democrats lead by 11 points on the generic ballot — a measure often used to gauge a party’s strength.

The sharp deterioration of the national political environment for Republicans has transformed the electoral map, forcing their candidates on the defensive in surprising places. This week, Senate Majority PAC, the main super PAC for Senate Democrats, began airing $1.2 million in television ads in Mississippi — a state that hasn’t elected a Democratic U. S. senator since 1982.

That’s a striking reversal of expectations from two years ago, when Democrats began plotting a midterm strategy and winning control of the Senate seemed nearly impossible. Then, Republicans — and some Democrats — scoffed when Mr. Schumer publicly discussed recruiting a Democratic candidate for Senate in Mississippi.

The question is whether the Democrats’ momentum is strong enough to lift their candidates in deep red states to victory. To win control of the Senate, Democrats must flip four Republican-held seats, and keep all of their own.

Of the 10 Senate battleground contests, four feature Republican incumbents: Senators Dan Sullivan of Alaska, Jon Husted of Ohio, Susan Collins of Maine and Roger Marshall of Kansas. And five are happening in states that Mr. Trump won by 11 points or more in 2024.

“Structurally, the Senate is built to be Republican, and the question is whether this wave can breach that levee,” said Liam Donovan, a Republican strategist. “It is incredibly hard.”

Polling, early-voting turnout and the results of recent special elections suggest that Democrats are far more enthusiastic than Republicans this election cycle.

But those measures, particularly early-vote returns, can be misleading. Turnout can flip on Election Day, particularly if Republicans successfully leverage their campaign war chest and Mr. Trump’s tour through Republican strongholds to drive their supporters to the polls.

“Trump is probably going to do some good in these red-leaning states when he comes in,” said David Kochel, a veteran Republican political strategist from Iowa, where Mr. Trump held a campaign rally on Thursday. “There’s still a lot more Republicans in Iowa and Kansas than there are Democrats.”

In Sioux City, Iowa, on Thursday night, Mr. Trump offered plenty of MAGA red meat, attacking Representative Ilhan Omar of Minnesota, and urging Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican candidate for governor in Ohio, not to take down an ad featuring the estranged mother of his opponent that has drawn bipartisan backlash. And, Mr. Trump told the crowd, he had the “right” to run for a third term.

“I’m asking you to pretend I’m running,” he said, repeating a frequent refrain. “Pretend I’m on the ballot.”

This year, as in several recent election cycles, Democrats harbor considerable anxiety about the accuracy of polling. Some strategists worry that pollsters are oversampling Democrats, particularly in red states, who may be more likely to respond to questions about the election.

A historical assessment of congressional polls conducted by The Economist this week found that the more partisan a state, the more the polls have underestimated the strength of the dominant party.

If that trend held true this year, it would temper Democratic expectations in states like Alaska, Texas, Ohio, Iowa and Kansas.

And even if the polls favoring Democrats turn out to be accurate, many individual Senate races are quite close, in some cases within the margin of error.

“There will be two explanations if the wave is just a ripple,” said Howard Wolfson, a veteran Democratic strategist. “One is there is a massive polling error. The second is that the Democrats didn’t have enough money to put enough races into play and make the races that were in play sufficiently competitive.”

Republicans currently have an advantage of about $650 million in general-election advertising, according to a review of past and future ad reservations across federal and state races by AdImpact, a media-tracking firm.

Their edge is most pronounced in the Senate: In the seven races that the Cook Political Report rated as tossups, Republicans are outspending Democrats on advertising by more than $320 million, according to a separate tally by AdImpact.

The lack of Democratic funds limits the party’s ability to mount aggressive campaigns in the kind of districts that would fuel a wave, said Mr. Wolfson, a political adviser for Michael R. Bloomberg, the former mayor of New York City, who spent about $80 million bolstering Democrats this fall.

So far, the polls haven’t shown significant shifts since more money started pumping into races.

But the spending is being felt not only in the barrage of campaign ads, said Jason Roe, a Republican strategist based in Michigan, but also in efforts to push Republican voters to the polls. Republicans have embraced a version of the strategy that helped them capture the White House in 2024, focusing on driving loyal Republican voters who typically skip midterm elections to the polls.

And just as in 2024, they have gotten plenty of outside help, including from Elon Musk, who has quietly funneled more than $276 million into building a huge turnout operation to help Republicans.

The impact of that work might not be clear until Election Day.

“I have never seen more money spent on the ground in my life — it is obscene,” Mr. Roe said. “If you are a Republican voter, you are going to get harassed to no end to turn out.”

He added: “The question is: How many of those people are so unhappy with Trump or Republicans that they don’t vote for us when they get there?”

Some Democrats also worry that their party’s still-battered brand could hurt their support in November. Even as Democratic candidates gain support, polling shows lingering disapproval of their party overall.

Just 28 percent of voters said they are satisfied with the Democratic Party, in the recent New York Times/Siena poll, eight points lower than satisfaction with the Republican Party and the share of voters who approve of Mr. Trump’s job performance.

Republicans have tried to capitalize on that skepticism by casting Democratic candidates as far-left radicals who want to turn the country into “a socialist hellscape.”

Matt Bennett, a vice president at Third Way, a centrist think tank that presses for a more moderate Democratic approach, worries that some of the party’s more progressive candidates, including Senate nominees Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and Troy Jackson in Maine, are underperforming Democrats competing in traditional red states.

Is there a scenario in which Democrats win in red states but squeak by in blue ones? Mr. Bennett doesn’t rule it out. Midterms, he said, can produce strange results.

“Every single one of the Senate races is on a knife’s edge,” Mr. Bennett said. “The results could be super weird.”

Lisa Lerer is a national political reporter for The Times, based in New York. She has covered American politics for nearly two decades.

Israel Cracks Down in West Bank City After Deadly Attack

The New York Times October 24, 2026

Israel’s Election

Advertisement

Supported by

Hundreds of Palestinian families fled their homes as the Israeli military raided Hebron. The operation came a day after Palestinian gunmen killed two soldiers.

By Aaron Boxerman and Fatima AbdulKarim

Aaron Boxerman reported from Tel Aviv, and Fatima AbdulKarim from Ramallah, the West Bank.

The Israeli military began a sweeping crackdown in the West Bank city of Hebron overnight on Saturday, evicting hundreds of families and demolishing buildings a day after Palestinian gunmen killed two Israeli soldiers in the occupied territory.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had vowed to retaliate for the deadly shooting, which took place just days before a pivotal national election and against a backdrop of intensifying violence in the Israeli-occupied West Bank. Mr. Netanyahu is neck and neck in opinion polls with a bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief of staff and his leading challenger in the first major vote in Israel since the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attacks ignited the war in Gaza.

On Saturday, Israeli forces were searching homes, making arrests and using loudspeakers to tell residents in Hebron’s Deir Baha neighborhood to leave, said Yousef Jabari, the city’s mayor. At least 2,000 Palestinians live in the area, many of whom have already fled, he said.

“This is not only collective punishment, it’s election propaganda,” said Mr. Jabari. “Netanyahu wants images of displacement, destroyed buildings and repression to appeal to voters.”

Khaled Fahd Qawasmi, the deputy mayor, said more than 200 Palestinian families were believed to have been displaced since the operation began overnight.

The Israeli military said the raid would last for several days in response to the attack on Friday, in which two Palestinians opened fire on Israeli troops near a checkpoint outside of Hebron. The gunmen were killed in a subsequent shootout, the military said.

Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir, Israel’s military chief of staff, said in a statement that the soldiers had prevented “an even more serious attack.” The military said a large cache of ammunition was found in a vehicle used by the attackers.

The two shooters have not been officially identified, and it was unclear whether they acted alone or on behalf of a militant group. Hamas, the Palestinian armed group based in Gaza, praised the attack but stopped short of claiming responsibility for it.

Israeli forces quickly moved to encircle Hebron, the largest Palestinian city in the West Bank, sealing off the city’s main entrances and exits. Israel Katz, the defense minister, vowed to replicate an operation in the cities of Tulkarm and Jenin, where Israeli officials have occupied entire neighborhoods and displaced tens of thousands of people.

Mr. Netanyahu and Mr. Katz said a similar campaign would be carried out in the two gunmen’s Hebron neighborhood. They did not specify the neighborhood, but Mr. Jabari said it was probably Deir Baha.

“We will evacuate the residents, we will go house to house, we will also confiscate the weapons there, and all terrorist infrastructures will be dealt with and destroyed,” Mr. Netanyahu said.

The Israeli military said Palestinian civilians would be allowed to leave through designated checkpoints but did not say whether they would be permitted to return. An Israeli military spokesman did not respond to a request for comment.

Violence in the West Bank has been escalating lately. In recent weeks, extremist Jewish settlers have initiated dozens of attacks against Palestinians during the annual olive harvest, a cultural touchstone for many Palestinians. Masked Israelis have assaulted Palestinians gathering olives, beating them with clubs and hurling stones.

The heightened strife comes just days before an Israeli election that Israelis and Palestinians, who cannot vote in it, view as existential. Mr. Netanyahu, who has led the most hard-line, right-wing government in Israeli history, is fighting for his political life.

Some Israeli analysts have said the vote may be influencing the prime minister’s decision to start a major military operation in the West Bank. Both Mr. Netanyahu and his opponents have sought to burnish their security credentials to woo Israeli voters rattled by three years of war.

Israeli forces also began razing buildings near the scene of the attack in the Farsh al-Hawa neighborhood on the western outskirts of Hebron. The Israeli military said it was “demolishing illegal structures that could pose a security threat.”

One of the houses belonged to Riyad Mreish, a Palestinian who spent more than two decades working in Saudi Arabia. Mr. Mreish said he had poured the savings he had accumulated during his time abroad into the home.

“I haven’t slept a moment,” Mr. Mreish said. “I cannot comprehend what happened.”

Israel regularly demolishes Palestinian homes in West Bank areas under its direct control, arguing that they were built illegally. Palestinians say Israel almost never issues Palestinians any permits for legal construction, forcing them to build without them.

Heedo Abu Laban and Adam Rasgon contributed reporting.

Aaron Boxerman is a Times reporter covering Israel and Gaza. He is based in Jerusalem.
