The Eyes of Elizabeth Holmes

The New York Times October 24, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Maureen Dowd

By Maureen Dowd

Opinion Columnist, reporting from Washington

You’d think we’d be weary of flimflam artists, tech vampires and alternative realities by now. But no.

It’s like Gertrude’s lust for Claudius in “Hamlet”: “As if increase of appetite had grown / By what it fed on.”

In a time of deceit — political, algorithmic and every other way — a meditation on deceit has taken the culture by storm.

Meditation is not the right word, actually. It’s more like a film noir thriller, with a manipulative femme fatale, a destructive romance, a man who’s meant to play the fall guy, and an atmospheric cottage by the sea.

The three-hour documentary about Theranos fraudster Elizabeth Holmes, “You Can See Everything,” is paradoxically titled, because you can’t see much of anything. (Except her naked narcissistic fiancé preening in the shower.) Holmes is busy obscuring the truth and building an illusory world where her dangerous fraud about comprehensive medical testing with a pinprick of blood was just an innocent hiccup.

“I know I didn’t commit any crime,” she assures the filmmaker Nathan Fielder, training her big, blue Furby eyes on him. She doesn’t think she has ever lied in her life, she says. It was all just a misunderstanding. Never mind the threatening lawyers like David Boies she sicced on anyone who questioned her phantom technology.

Holmes abandoned her Steve Jobs black turtleneck in favor of J. Crew-looking soccer mom sweaters. But she remains the perfect avatar for our age: She promised tech that would help humanity and then unleashed a deception that could have hurt humanity.

Holmes and her partner, who had two children before her 11-year sentence for fraud began in Texas in 2023, wanted a sympathetic documentary charting her last weeks with her family before she got locked up. They stumbled upon Fielder, who directed the movie along with Lance Oppenheim, and ended up starring in it.

Fielder originally did not intend to appear onscreen, but Holmes irresistibly drew him into her web, and the resulting game of cat-and-mouse between the two magicians is astonishing.

The deadpan Fielder is a Canadian-born satirist who worked with Sacha Baron Cohen on the 2018 mockumentary “Who Is America?” and on his own shows, “Nathan for You” on Comedy Central and “The Rehearsal” on HBO, where he has built elaborate ruses. He is a master at spinning his own absurd reality, and so is Holmes.

The sparring of these two raises the question: ls there any point searching for the truth or is it better to settle into our own fractured, subjective realities?

At 30, Holmes became the first self-made female billionaire, after she dropped out of Stanford at 20 and started Theranos. But she’s no role model for women. When she got in trouble she embraced victimhood, turning from a confident Silicon Valley founder who dominated every room into a damsel in distress. In court, she blamed her lover/partner, Sunny Balwani, who got an almost 13-year sentence for helping Holmes defraud investors of more than $700 million. She said he abused her psychologically and sexually and controlled everything, from her clothes to her diet. The jury was unconvinced.

Holmes tries to turn Fielder into a film noir sap, someone who will believe her lies about her lies, be drawn to her emotionally and come to her rescue. And the documentary projects, then calls into question, a scenario where her current lover/partner, Billy Evans, is manipulating her, asking for a cut of the documentary’s profits supposedly behind her back, taking over her X account and putting up foul-mouthed posts pretending to be her, releasing a hologram of Holmes that he nonchalantly acknowledges might be used by some men online for porn.

The woman famous for her guile — suckering George Shultz, Jim Mattis, Henry Kissinger, Sam Nunn, Larry Ellison, Rupert Murdoch and other brainy older men — plays guileless, acting as if she can’t even scramble eggs without her controlling fiancé’s help, or understand the simplistic joke in the classic Abbott and Costello “Who’s on first?” comedy routine. Fielder jokes that if Holmes had “just said that Theranos was a comedy bit, maybe you could get off scot-free.” The couple talk about building “monuments of love” to each other, but it’s more like monuments of manipulation.

Tyler Shultz, George Shultz’s grandson, who was an intern and researcher at Theranos and then left and blew the whistle on Holmes, said on “CBS Mornings” that Holmes took in Fielder enough to allow doubt to creep in about Holmes’s guilt.

“She knows that she was lying,” Shultz said, “because she created this whole web of lies that you would not have needed to create if you actually believed the lies.”

Shultz said the harm to real patients was horrible and Fielder never laid out the dimensions of her crimes.

“We told people that they had H. I. V. when they did not,” he said. “We told people that they had cancer when they did not. We told expecting mothers that they had lost their unborn child when they had not.”

Amanda Seyfried, who won an Emmy for playing Holmes in Hulu’s “The Dropout,” also wonders if Fielder is too “protective of her.” The actress reprises her role in some scenes in the documentary and visits Holmes’s family after she goes to prison, getting chided by Evans for her Hulu portrayal.

Evans is a handsome, buff man, the scion of a wealthy hotel family who is now determined to work with Liz, as she is known now, to straighten out the problems with her blood-testing method. But as the film goes on, there’s a Dorian Gray effect, where his face grows scarier, twisted into a mask of rage and subterfuge. Is Evans, not Fielder, the sap? As in film noir, the boyfriend carries a rod and is vowing vengeance.

Whether or not you think Fielder isn’t tough enough on Holmes, it is impossible to look away from her. Her unblinking gaze is like the disembodied blue eyes in the haunting billboard in “The Great Gatsby,” and both represent the same thing: moral decay.

The Times is committed to publishing a diversity of letters to the editor. We’d like to hear what you think about this or any of our articles. Here are some tips. And here’s our email: letters@nytimes. com.

Maureen Dowd is an Opinion columnist for The Times. She won the 1999 Pulitzer Prize for distinguished commentary. She is the author, most recently, of “Notorious.” @MaureenDowd • Facebook

What This Democrat’s Surge in Texas Says About the Midterms

The New York Times October 24, 2026

The Interview

The Interview

Credit... Devin Oktar Yalkin for The New York Times

Supported by

By Lulu Garcia-Navarro

Democrats have Texas-size dreams this election of flipping a state that has eluded them since the 1990s. While the Democratic candidate for Senate, James Talarico, has gotten most of the attention and money in that fight, another Democrat, Gina Hinojosa, has looked surprisingly competitive against the most powerful politician in the state: Gov. Greg Abbott, the Republican running for an unprecedented fourth term.

Hinojosa is a Texas state legislator who represents parts of liberal Austin. Her political rise began on her local school board, where she was inspired to run for the State Legislature because of cuts to public school funding under Abbott. That became one of her signature issues, which she has carried over into her run for governor.

When she began her campaign, she was seen as the longest of long shots: a Latina with little statewide name recognition and not a lot of financial support. Today, the most recent New York Times/Siena University poll shows her narrowly ahead of Abbott, and national Democrats are finally taking notice, directing money toward the race in these last few crucial weeks. I asked Hinojosa whether that will be enough to overcome an extremely well-funded Abbott, who declined our interview request. We also talked about why she is focusing on affordability, education and data centers rather than what she calls “culture-war issues” and how she is trying to pull in disaffected rural MAGA voters. Can she win? And what will it say about Texas if she does?

Subscribe: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Amazon | iHeart

I was told by a Texas reporter that in some ways you ran for governor — a position last held by your party in 1995 by another woman, Ann Richards — as a sacrificial lamb. It was the longest of long shots, you had no real chance, but basically some Democrat had to do it and so it might as well be you. Did you see it that way too? No. I wouldn’t have given up a year of my life away from my family to be on the road all across the state to be a sacrificial lamb. I am running to win. It is not an easy endeavor to do this, and it took everything out of me from this last year.

Texas keeps breaking Democratic hearts. What are you doing differently than, say, Beto O’Rourke, who was the last Democrat to run against Abbott? He had a lot of name recognition, a lot of momentum behind him nationally, and yet he still lost by 11 points. I don’t know that I can compare my candidacy to Beto’s. It’s a different time. In 2026, the data centers have been a physical manifestation of a governor doing the bidding of the moneyed interests and leaving the people of Texas to fend for themselves. And so in that way, rural Texas has felt betrayed by Greg Abbott because many of these data centers have descended upon rural Texas where there are no rules really.

I was in the Panhandle, Amarillo, talking to residents where they are fighting the world’s largest data center. It is called Project Matador. Its investors are Rick Perry, our former governor, and his son. They negotiated a deal to get all of their water in this drought-prone area for the data center from the city water supply. When residents asked what happens if we run out of water, the response they told me they got from municipal water was, Well, we will have to turn off the residents’ first. That’s the environment we’re living in in Texas. And so people understand that we are fighting a fight where it’s all of us in the same boat versus like 15 billionaire tech dudes.

When you go to these rural areas, are you trying to get disaffected MAGA voters to turn your way? What is the overall plan on who to persuade, because obviously your time and your resources are finite, so you have to pick and choose who you’re trying to get to listen to your message. It’s everybody. I have not picked and chosen. I have been all over the state with all communities. To be clear, it is not a moderating message. It is reaching out to Democrats, Republicans, independents, with a populist message. And yes, I need Trump supporters to support this race. Trump won Texas, Trump won the Latino vote in Texas. Absolutely, they are invited to be part of this coalition.

What’s been the thing that’s most surprised you when you’re out among communities that you wouldn’t naturally see as supporting you? I mean, you represented Austin, which is one of the most liberal places in the state. I was in Red Oak, Texas, where they have big-acreage lots and a school down the street. They invited me in because they have seven data centers moving into their community, including one that’s 900 acres large right next door to the home that I was invited into. And I was sitting in a living room with MAGA. They knew Greg Abbott had sold them out, but they weren’t sure about me. They had questions. So I sat down and I said: OK, let’s go. Ask me. And they wanted to ask me culture-war questions, right? They wanted to ask me about constitutional carry. I said, “What you call constitutional carry, I call permitless carry, and I voted against it because I believe we should have background checks to have a gun.” They asked me about Shariah law. And I said, “I don’t really know what Shariah law is, but what I worry about is that regular Muslim Texans are going to be discriminated against because people think they are practicing this thing that probably most of them don’t even know what it is.”

And so we engaged, which I think is a rare thing for people of different political parties. It’s rare for elected Democratic leaders to sit down with MAGA and say, “Let’s talk,” and to agree to disagree where we disagree, to find common ground where we do, but then ultimately to recognize, while we have been fighting these culture wars for 10 years in this country — culture wars that are not winnable because they depend on your personal experiences, your lived experience — the only winners have been the tech giants that are amassing our money and our power and all of our data and, if you believe recent reports, are about to blow up the world if we don’t come together fast to save ourselves.

How persuasive do you think you’ve been? I think people are tired of fighting culture-war fights. I think there is an opportunity, if we choose to take it, to forge a new way forward that is almost post-partisan in recognition of disappointment, again, in both parties. Because both parties, frankly, are corrupted by corporate influence. I mean, I see it in the Democratic Party, too. I have seen so many Democrats grandstand on culture-war issues, only to vote with corporate interests, and none of us are better for it.

I want to learn a little bit more about you and your background. Your father was a Democratic Party chair in the state for 13 years and was a judge. Your mom was born in Mexico. What was your family like growing up? My parents started off as legal aid lawyers. They represented farmworkers, and I was born to high school sweethearts. They were very young when they had me, so in some ways I grew up with them. I grew up in Brownsville, on the border with Matamoros, Mexico, and back then we used to cross back and forth all the time. We’d go for breakfast on the weekends to Mexico. We would go shopping for things in Mexico. We were a binational community.

Because you know the area really well, I am curious what you think has been happening down in the Rio Grande Valley. In 2016, it was a 60-point-plus Democratic area, and then, in 2024, Trump won it. What do you think Republicans figured out to catch fire there? There were a couple of things happening. One, Latinos along the border were angry about border security. Remember, this was at a time when we had the caravans crossing. We had people sleeping under bridges. It felt chaotic. It did not inspire confidence. Border communities were angry about that, and those are mostly Latino communities. I also think that Latinos vote their pocketbooks, and Trump was promising to deliver a kind of economic prosperity that was appealing.

But fast forward to today, and yes, we all want border security, but these ICE raids are making us less secure, not more secure. People are really angry about the racial profiling that’s happened. We’ve even had American boys, on their way to enlist in the Marines, pulled from their car by ICE and beaten. We had a man who was killed in Houston a few months ago on his way to work, a case of mistaken identity where they shot first, asked questions later. I could go on. That is the reality we are dealing with in Texas, and Latinos are angry and scared.

As you know, many people see Democrats as weak on the border. Abbott has used his authority to send the National Guard down to the border, among other things. What approaches of Trump or Abbott do you agree with? Because we have seen the border become a much more secure place. Illegal crossings have plummeted under the Trump administration. I think we cannot treat people who have been in our communities for 20 years, hard-working, law-abiding members of our community, like we are treating somebody who needs to be vetted coming across the border. Those are two different kinds of people who need to be treated differently. We should have a path to legalization for people who are here. We should also have order at the border and security at the border.

But what specifically would you do differently than Governor Abbott? Would you repeal S. B. 4, which is the Abbott law that makes unauthorized entry into Texas a [state] criminal offense? Well, I wouldn’t have the power to repeal that as governor.

But would you propose it? Do you think it should be repealed? I don’t support it, and I voted against it, and I stand by my record. But I’m not going to pretend like I’ll have the power to convince the Legislature to do that. Even if I win, we still have Republican control of everything in this state. My agenda will be one that 99 percent of us agree on, which is to secure the American dream, to save Texas public schools, put money in your pocket — a populist agenda, rather than fight fights that I know I can’t win.

That’s interesting. So what you’re telling me is that you might not agree with S. B. 4, which also authorizes the state to remove those here illegally — typically a federal function — but you’re not going to try to change it because you feel like you can’t do it. So then what’s in it for Democrats who want to see substantial changes to the law in Texas, if you won’t be able to deliver on key issues for them? This is not a blue state. This is Texas, where we have Greg Abbott putting the Texas National Guard in detention centers so that these private prison companies can maximize their profits. We have kids being locked up with their parents because Greg Abbott allows for the licensing of these detention centers for little kids to be locked up. We have a governor who turns the other way when Texans are being mowed down on our streets. There is a lot besides the repeal of S. B. 4, and having a governor who has the courage to stand up for Texans will be night and day in this state.

I’m just trying to understand, if you become governor, how you would address some of the things that you see are wrong. What would you do in terms of ICE? I will use everything from the bully pulpit to the courts to defend the rights of Texans.

Do you think ICE needs to be reformed? Reimagined? Disbanded? I think what is happening needs to stop. ICE should not be doing this. They should not be here. What they are doing is causing more danger to the people of Texas than it is protection. People fear them. People are angry at them. It is chaotic. These guys are not trained. They should not be here.

Staying with the border, one of the people you’ve spoken out about is Elon Musk. SpaceX is based in the valley. It even has a town called Starbase there. It employs thousands of people. Musk has pledged $20 million to a local school district down there. You’ve been very critical of him and the way he has operated his businesses in Texas. Tell me why. I’m actually more critical of the way Abbott lets him abuse our resources. I blame him less than I blame our weak leader, who doesn’t defend Texans. The record is that Elon Musk has given Greg Abbott half a million dollars to his campaign, and he has received $1.6 billion in property-tax breaks for his company, Terafab. He’s received tens of millions of dollars in cash from the state of Texas for Starbase. He has received the governor’s intervention in contracting for broadband so that he could receive a $100 million broadband contract. This is the reality we are living in.

Elon Musk has also been an enormous contributor to the Republican Party — tens of millions of dollars being poured into the race in Texas in particular, but all over the country. How do you see his role in the politics of your state? He has an outsize influence, to say the least. You should not be able to spend that much money. It’s gross that he has that kind of influence over our political system.

There must be some tension there because he is a big employer in the state. He moved a lot of his businesses to Texas. You want people to have good-paying jobs. So how do you imagine that you would manage that relationship with someone who clearly supports a different agenda? I launched this campaign with this saying my grandmother used to tell me growing up: No te dejes. There’s not a direct translation for this saying, but it basically means: Know your worth, and fight to defend it. Elon Musk is lucky he is here. Yes, there are good jobs that he is providing, but also he’s getting tremendous taxpayer dollars that is not justified.

Do you think he should get out of the state? He doesn’t need to get out of the state. He just needs to abide by the rules like everybody else does. We all pay our taxes. Why shouldn’t Elon Musk pay his taxes in Texas, too?

You’ve described the way that many Texans feel disempowered and the way that the economy has functioned, in your view, against ordinary Texans. But I do think Republicans would argue that their policies have made Texas one of the most business-friendly states in the entire country. It has the second-largest economy after California. Isn’t that good stewardship of the state? There’s no question that corporations love Greg Abbott and Texas, but the reality is we have the most people without health insurance of any state, despite the fact that Texans worked more hours than the national average. We have the most children without health insurance of any state. We have the most people disconnected from their electricity because they cannot afford to pay their bills. We have the most bankruptcies of any state in America, and it is small businesses that are struggling to keep their doors open. We have over 150 school districts operating at four days a week because they can’t afford to operate at five days a week. Despite the fact that we pay 85 percent more in property taxes under Greg Abbott. That is his record. We have nothing to show for it. So yes, there’s a lot of money that flows through Texas. There is a lot of money that is made in Texas by the people of Texas, but the people are not sharing in that economic wealth.

OK, we’re going to pivot a little bit to something that you’ve talked about, which is seeing yourself as a populist and not a liberal or a progressive. Your voting record in the State House is, by all accounts, pretty liberal. You were, in 2019, ranked the most liberal member of the Texas House, and it was a title that you openly embraced. So I’m curious how you define “populist” and “progressive,” and tell me why you’ve landed on “populist” as a label for yourself. I think “populist” meets the moment of our time. The one fight in this country is about economic power, and populism is about economic power. We see that things are so stacked against working people in this country. Listen, it’s just a label, but if I were to pick a label to describe my politics, it is economic populism. It happens to be a type of politics that is rooted in our Texas history. It was L. B. J.’s grandfather, who was part of the Farmers’ Alliance, that organized farmers against big railroads that were taking advantage of them. Now we have working Texans who are up against big tech. And so I chose this title to define my politics because I think this has to be the politics of the moment to meet the challenges of the moment.

Is part of it also that the progressive or liberal label could be perceived as pretty toxic by certain members of the state that you’re trying to get to vote for you? No, it is not that. But I think those labels have been associated with culture wars, and I just don’t think that the culture wars are the fight of 2026.

Being a progressive could also be about the way you use taxation to redistribute wealth. It could mean the way you want the health care system to work in terms of supporting Obamacare or Medicare for all. It’s not just a label that has to do with culture wars. I think it means more than that. It may mean more than that to you, but to a lot of people, it means the culture-war fights, because those are the fights we’ve been fighting for the last 10 years.

So that comes back to my thing that it’s toxic. No, it’s not that. It comes back to that it doesn’t meet the political moment. It is not what 2026 is about. Look, we are facing an almost existential crisis in this country because tech giants are having their way with us. There is one fight, and we are so caught up in fighting each other in a divided nation, fighting each other over the ways we disagree about social issues and culture wars that we’re all about to lose. And so I’m not going to perpetuate that anymore.

You clearly understand that some of these issues motivate people. You released a very personal ad early in your campaign talking about the issue of abortion. In Texas, abortion is almost completely banned from conception with no exception for rape or incest. In your ad, you discuss something very personal. Can you tell me the story and why you wanted to talk about it? So in my first pregnancy, shortly after I was married, I was diagnosed with a fetus that had trisomy 18, which was described to me by doctors as not compatible with life. I had to make a decision about whether or not to terminate that pregnancy. I had a week’s time to decide that. I consulted with my priest and the nun at my church. I prayed with my husband. We both took that time to figure out what to do. My family was so supportive. I had a small Christian community that held my hand along the way, and I ultimately decided not to terminate that pregnancy and carry it forward to term. She didn’t make it. She died at nine months of pregnancy at birth. And it made me who I am. I probably would not be here had it not been for that experience. It showed me my strength and really put things in perspective for me.

That’s such a very personal and painful story. What were you hoping people would understand about you from that? I think Texans want to know who are you, why are you doing this, what motivates you. It was a formative experience in my life. And I think the thing that I wanted to communicate is that this is first and foremost a human experience. We have politicized pregnancy in this country, but there are so many women, so many families, who have had their hearts broken by pregnancies gone bad. I wanted to try to connect with people on a human level with what my human hardship was and how it made me stronger.

Do you see abortion as a culture-war issue, or do you see it as something that transcends that — as an issue of health care or an issue of human rights? I think it is an issue of human rights. I think it’s a health care issue. There are women who are dying in Texas because they can’t terminate a pregnancy when they are in crisis because doctors are facing 99 years in prison. We just had our governor delay the release of the maternal mortality report in this state until after the election, but we’ve heard so many stories of women dying, and we know it’s going to be bad. So absolutely, it is all of those things.

What would you like to do if you’re governor on that issue, understanding that the Legislature is what it is? I do think that we can come together in a bipartisan way to save women’s lives. That is the commitment I’ve made on the campaign trail.

Obviously, as a woman, you are hoping to appeal to women, including, as you’ve mentioned, MAGA women. I just looked at the latest Marist poll, and you are ahead with women, but not by much. Are you doing well enough with women? Are you worried about that? Well, the only reason we’re winning six major polls out of the last five weeks is because of our strong support from women. So I feel good about our support from women. But look, we take no demographic for granted.

A different demographic: Prominent Latinos wrote a letter to Democratic leadership imploring them to give you financial support. They wrote, “We are asking you to invest in a competitive race with the largest Latino electorate in the country following an election cycle where Republicans made alarming inroads with Latinos.” Do you think the national Democrats ignore Latino candidates like you? I don’t really follow other races, but I would like them to invest in this race. We have an opportunity of a generation to win here. We’ve been dealt a phenomenal hand in Texas, and it would be very helpful to have more national support. There’s no doubt there are big national stakes in this race. We know that Republicans in Austin want to redistrict again in Texas, redraw maps, and they have decided to do so next year if they win. We know there’s no Democratic control of Congress when that happens.

We need a governor in Texas who will veto rigged maps, and I will be that governor. So those are the stakes. And again, this is an opportunity of a generation to win. In 2026, yes, Latinos are key to that winning number. Beto got 64 percent of the Latino vote in 2018. When I get that, I win because there are more of us in the voting population in Texas in 2026. This is not the time to be playing small ball.

Do you think the head of the Democratic Governors Association, Gov. Andy Beshear, was disrespecting your candidacy? Because he was reluctant to invest. I have a good relationship with him. They did send $1 million. I’m grateful for that.

One million dollars is not a lot in Texas. It’s such a big state. It’s helpful. Ninety-five percent of our contributions come from small-dollar donations. I’m proud of what we’ve been able to raise.

You just mentioned that Texas Republicans are planning to redraw the maps, which could be very, very problematic for Democrats in Congress. Did you make the case to the national party about that? Yes, I did make that case, and I have made that case from the very beginning. Absolutely, those are the stakes, and we’ve been talking to anybody who will listen. That’s why I think you’re hearing Democrats across the country really want to make sure we have the investment we need to win, because the stakes are so high and because the opportunity to win is even higher. For the first time, we have a ticket running in Texas. We’ve had Beto in the past, we’ve had Colin Allred in the past, but it was just them. Now we have me, we have James [Talarico], we have Democrats running up and down the ballot. For the first time, we have Democrats running in every Texas House seat, Texas Senate seat, congressional seat. We have an opportunity of a generation to win in Texas.

Well, let’s say you do win. It will be a political earthquake. What do you think it will signify? The thing that I am most excited about when I win is the feeling Texans will feel to know their power again. To know that we can go up against big money, probably the biggest in the country, and entrenched politics — Greg Abbott is probably the most entrenched incumbent there is in America — and that we could win. And I just know there’s going to be this feeling of almost liberation when we feel our power again. That’s the thing I’m most looking forward to.

Gina Hinojosa has run a plucky and smart campaign in Texas. When she decided to run against the powerful Republican Governor Greg Abbott, she had little name recognition and support from national Democratic leadership. Now, just over a week away from the election, she is close in the polls and has a shot at winning. I wanted to understand what she wants to do if she gains power, what Latinos are thinking about her race and why she thinks Democrats outside of the state were late to get on board. Do you think Texas is ready to go blue?

This interview has been edited and condensed. Listen to and follow “The Interview” on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, YouTube, iHeartRadio or Amazon Music. Follow us on Instagram and TikTok.

The New York Times October 24, 2026

Chemical plants and other industrial facilities had been required to curb their toxic emissions. A New York Times investigation shows how they got out of it.

By Maxine Joselow and Eric Lipton

Maxine Joselow reported from Clairton, Pa., and Richmond, Va. Eric Lipton reported from Port Neches, Texas.

They are among the biggest sources of cancer-causing pollution in the United States: chemical manufacturers, steel-making plants, facilities that sterilize medical devices.

In 2024, they were required to take steps to reduce their toxic emissions. That all changed when President Trump returned to office and gave them a pass.

It was the biggest presidential intervention in the Clean Air Act since the bedrock environmental law was enacted more than 50 years ago.

Mr. Trump has gone further than any president in dismantling regulations designed to protect the environment, resulting in dirtier air and water. Even so, his aid to specific polluters stands out. To understand these efforts, The New York Times reviewed more than 10,000 pages of government documents and conducted more than 70 interviews.

Here are five takeaways from our investigation.

Mr. Trump exempted 202 facilities in 39 states and Puerto Rico from new regulations that the Environmental Protection Agency had adopted during the Biden administration.

The new rules came about because the Clean Air Act requires the E. P. A. to periodically study the latest pollution controls and impose them if they are affordable and effective.

The rules required medical sterilizers, chemical plants and steel facilities to monitor for emissions of cancer-causing gases along their property lines by 2027. If they detected certain levels of the gases escaping into communities, they had to fix the leaks. And they had to post the findings publicly, so that neighbors could see what was in the air.

When it comes to chemical manufacturers, the government estimated companies would have to spend about $440 million to install equipment to comply with the new rules and about $163 million each year after that.

That would amount to less than 1 percent of the chemical industry’s annual sales.

The chemical industry criticized the rules as expensive, unnecessary and unworkable. Its lawyers filed petitions with Congress, the E. P. A. and federal courts to overturn or at least delay the regulations. It also challenged the scientific findings underpinning the policies.

Yet the industry lost again and again as agency officials and the courts concluded its claims lacked merit.

As soon as Mr. Trump returned to office, though, the industry players saw an opportunity to change their fortunes. Less than two weeks after the inauguration, trade groups asked the E. P. A. administrator, Lee Zeldin, to push Mr. Trump to exempt them from the rules. A trade association for the medical device industry, which uses ethylene oxide, donated to Mr. Trump’s inauguration fund and to his campaign affiliate, MAGA Inc.

They kept their pressure up until they got what they wanted.

On July 14, 2025, the chief executives of Dow, BASF, Eastman Chemical and Huntsman Corporation sent a letter directly to Mr. Trump, and shared it with the E. P. A.

“We write to bring to your attention the urgent need for action on requests submitted earlier this year for presidential exemptions under the Clean Air Act to provide relief from unnecessary and ineffective obligations imposed by E. P. A.,” they wrote.

Three days later, on July 17, Mr. Trump began answering their pleas.

Never before had a president let specific polluters off the hook with the stroke of his pen.

An obscure provision of the Clean Air Act allows the president to issue exemptions from rules if a manufacturing disruption would undermine national security and the technology needed to comply is not widely available. President Richard M. Nixon signed the law in 1970, but the provision had never been invoked.

Yet Mr. Trump approved the requests for waivers even though the technology was readily accessible and the industry’s national security arguments had little detail to substantiate them, according to documents reviewed by The Times.

The E. P. A. set up a special email inbox for requests for exemptions. Companies flooded the agency with submissions.

The waivers were good for two years, with the possibility of an extension. The reprieve for the companies gave Mr. Trump time to stock the E. P. A. with former industry insiders who worked from within to gut the rules altogether.

For example, Mr. Trump nominated a former top lobbyist for the Advanced Medical Technology Association, or AdvaMed, a powerful trade association, to lead the agency’s air regulation office. The former lobbyist, Aaron Szabo, had been helping the industry fight the regulations under the Biden administration. Now he oversaw the effort to rewrite them. Documents reviewed by The Times indicate that Mr. Szabo helped handle the waiver requests and then pushed employees to pull back on enforcement.

The president’s decisions were a huge victory for an industry that backed his re-election campaign and continued to donate to his pet causes once he took office again.

AdvaMed boasted earlier this year in a letter to members that its lobbying efforts, which included political contributions to Mr. Trump’s causes, had paid off in the form of curbs on air toxics rules that saved companies millions of dollars in upgrades per plant.

“Membership has its privileges,” the group wrote.

That is how many Americans live within three miles of at least one facility that received a permission slip to pollute from Mr. Trump.

Before the E. P. A. finalized the new rules in 2024, it held meetings to warn people who lived near facilities that sterilize medical devices about the elevated cancer risks.

These facilities use ethylene oxide, a colorless, sweet-smelling, toxic gas. The agency’s research had found that long-term exposure to ethylene oxide increased the risk of leukemia, multiple myeloma and other types of cancer, particularly for people living close to where the gas is produced or used.

“You see these pretty buildings and you think they’re OK,” said Wayne Powell, who lives a five-minute drive from a sterilizer outside of Richmond, Va., that resembles an ordinary warehouse. “But you don’t know that they’re harboring things that are hazardous to our health.”

How Trump Gave the Worst Polluters a Free Pass

The New York Times October 24, 2026

Middle schoolers on their way to class in the shadow of a flare from the Indorama Ventures chemical facility in Port Neches, Texas. Video by Meridith Kohut.

Supported by

The president temporarily waived clean-air rules for industrial facilities that spew cancer-causing gases. Then his appointees worked to gut the regulations altogether.

By Eric Lipton and Maxine Joselow

Graphics by Mira Rojanasakul

Eric Lipton reported from Port Neches, Texas. Maxine Joselow reported from Clairton, Pa., and Richmond, Va.

Within sight of a southeast Texas middle school stands a chemical plant that President Trump excused from new federal rules intended to curb its cancer-causing pollution.

About a 30-minute drive from Pittsburgh, a steel-making facility has spewed carcinogenic chemicals near homes for years. Mr. Trump gave it a similar waiver from recent clean-air rules.

And on the outskirts of Richmond, Va., the owners of an industrial warehouse emailed the Trump administration asking for their own waiver. Their wish was granted. Nine months later, the facility accidentally released a large plume of carcinogenic gas into the community.

In total, since taking office again, Mr. Trump exempted 202 facilities in 39 states and Puerto Rico from clean-air regulations that were going into effect. Some were among the country’s worst industrial polluters, including chemical manufacturers, copper smelters and coal-burning power plants. About 3.3 million people live within three miles of at least one affected facility.

71 coal plants, 71 chemical plants, 40 sterilizers, 19 steel-related facilities and 1 copper smelter exempted from clean-air regulations.

Note: The number of people near each facility was determined using the 2024 population in each census block-group within a three-mile radius of each plant. Block-groups that were partly within the radius were population-weighted with 2020 census block population counts. Source: Data from the Environmental Defense Fund and Environmental Integrity Project. The New York Times

The exemptions represent the biggest presidential intervention in enforcement of the Clean Air Act in the half-century since President Richard M. Nixon signed the bedrock environmental law. And that is only one of the ways the Trump administration is dismantling a variety of federal environmental protections.

Before Mr. Trump’s return, the chemical industry was losing its fight to block or at least delay tougher E. P. A. requirements to reduce toxic emissions. It had pleaded with agency officials, filed lawsuits and appealed to Congress. But officials and the courts had largely rejected the industry’s claims of undue expense and regulatory overreach.

Now, Mr. Trump is prioritizing the economic interests of corporations and easing costs for polluting industries, and their immense clout is striking.

The president’s exemptions were good for two years, with the possibility of an extension. The reprieve for the companies gave Mr. Trump time to stock the Environmental Protection Agency with appointees who had lobbied for the industries they now regulate. Those officials then quickly went to work from the inside to gut the rules altogether.

Mr. Trump has taken an expansive view of executive power in his second term. On the environmental front, he has unilaterally shredded regulations, withheld science funding appropriated by Congress and ordered coal plants that planned to shutter to continue running.

Even so, his evisceration of the new Clean Air Act rules stands out.

Many of the details of how the Trump administration aided the chemical industry are being reported here for the first time. In one upside-down moment, industry executives provided the agenda for a meeting with E. P. A. staff and then effectively presided over it.

Mr. Trump also nominated Aaron Szabo, a former lobbyist for the Advanced Medical Technology Association, or AdvaMed, a powerful trade group, to lead the E. P. A.’s air regulation office. Once there, Mr. Szabo helped handle the waiver requests and then pushed employees to pull back on enforcement, documents show.

To understand how Mr. Trump gave a free pass to some of the worst polluters, The New York Times reviewed more than 10,000 pages of government documents and spoke to more than 70 people familiar with the efforts, including former E. P. A. officials and industry executives.

“These companies, with their campaign contributions and the revolving door of former lobbyists and executives that now work in the regulatory agencies — that is where the petrochemical industry gets its power,” said Brent Coon, a Beaumont, Texas, lawyer who has spent decades squaring off in court against petrochemical firms over environmental and health risks.

The Clean Air Act requires the E. P. A. — created in 1970 to protect public health and the environment — to periodically review the latest pollution controls and impose them broadly if they are affordable and effective. The most recent review began under the Biden administration, which in 2024 finalized new, tougher requirements.

In granting the waivers to those rules, Mr. Trump cited an obscure clause in the act that allows exemptions if complying with new rules would threaten national security and if the necessary technology is not widely available.

Yet the president approved the waivers even though the equipment was readily accessible and the industry’s national security claims had little detail to substantiate them, documents show.

The Biden administration pushed through the new pollution requirements after evidence emerged about the health threats posed by ethylene oxide, a colorless gas used to make products like plastic soda bottles and to sterilize medical devices like pacemakers.

E. P. A. researchers had concluded that ethylene oxide was 30 to 60 times as carcinogenic as previously thought, particularly for people who live near plants where the gas is made or used. The agency held meetings to warn community members about the elevated risks.

Outside Richmond, home to one of the country’s largest commercial sterilizers of medical devices, some residents left one of these briefings wondering whether recent cancer diagnoses among neighbors were tied to the plant, though it is virtually impossible to prove pollution caused a specific cancer case.

“You see these pretty buildings, and you think they’re OK,” said Wayne Powell, who lives a five-minute drive from the plant, which resembles an ordinary warehouse. “But you don’t know that they’re harboring things that are hazardous to our health.”

As recently as April, the plant, owned by Sterilization Services of Virginia, had a mishap. A faulty valve caused 580 pounds of ethylene oxide to leak from large drums and waft in a toxic plume over nearby homes, state records show. The plant’s state permit allows it to discharge no more than 400 pounds of ethylene oxide in an entire year.

Representatives for Sterilization Services of Virginia did not respond to calls seeking comment.

The new rules required not only sterilizers but also chemical plants and steel facilities to monitor for emissions of cancer-causing gases along their property lines by 2027. If certain amounts of the gases got out, the operators had to fix the leaks. Some facilities also had to build special containment systems — akin to giant breadboxes — to reduce gas releases.

On April 9 of this year, 580 pounds of ethylene oxide leaked from the Sterilization Services of Virginia plant outside Richmond, Va. This modeled simulation shows the spread.

Though the facilities would still have to follow pollution limits already in place, the industries fought the E. P. A.’s new mandates, calling them expensive, unnecessary and unworkable. They also challenged the Biden administration’s scientific findings.

“It is critical that regulation of our industry is based on sound science and that those regulations reflect a reasonable assessment of the risks and benefits involved,” Brendan Bradley, a spokesman for the American Chemistry Council, an industry trade group, said in a statement.

The Trump administration did not ask companies to present an exhaustive case for why they deserved a waiver from these new requirements. It was as easy as sending an email to the E. P. A. and invoking the obscure exemption language in the act, a provision that no president had ever used.

Taylor Rogers, a White House spokeswoman, said in a statement the waivers were necessary to protect American manufacturing.

“Exemptions were issued due to crushing Biden-era regulations that required large swaths of our industrial base to adopt technologies that don’t exist outside the imagination of Biden’s E. P. A. bureaucrats,” she said.

Mr. Trump’s decisions rewarded industries that backed his re-election campaign and continued to donate to his pet causes once he won.

AdvaMed boasted earlier this year in a letter to members that its lobbying efforts, which included political contributions to Mr. Trump’s causes, had paid off, saving the industry millions of dollars in upgrades.

“Membership has its privileges,” the group wrote.

The chemical plant in Port Neches, Texas, just south of the meandering Neches River, is a vital cog in American manufacturing. It is among the country’s biggest producers of ethylene oxide.

The plant’s owner, Indorama Ventures, is a major employer in the region and supports local schools, including Groves Middle School. It provides a football training complex through which its chemical pipelines run. It also sponsors the annual Fish-O-Rama Fishing Tournament to raise money for local science and math programs.

The plant also has a long history of releasing toxic pollutants into the community, state records show.

On more than 500 occasions since 2003, it has experienced malfunctions or other failures that resulted in releases of air pollution or toxic chemicals, frequently in violation of its permit, Texas records show.

From his front yard, dotted with baseballs and children's bikes, Cody Coburn can see the flares that burn off excess toxic gases from the plant across the street. Some nights they rattle his windows, suggesting a possible malfunction at the plant.

The incidents leave Mr. Coburn and his wife wondering if they are taking a risk living there with their young sons. “We’ve talked about moving away,” he said.

The violations continued after Indorama, based in Bangkok, purchased the facility from the Texas-based Huntsman Corporation in 2020.

A particularly alarming incident occurred in early 2022. A control valve failed, sending 57,000 pounds of pollutants into the air, including ethylene oxide, records show. The discharges continued for nearly a week.

That 2022 incident, and others like it, put Indorama on the radar of E. P. A. officials who were rewriting the rules for chemical plants.

These kinds of facilities had long used models to estimate their emissions. The problem was, no one could say if the estimates were accurate.

The E. P. A. decided to find out. The agency emailed the managers of the Indorama plant and 10 other facilities, ordering them to install temporary devices at the edges of their properties to measure toxins in the air.

Career E. P. A. employees were stunned by the results, said Brenda Shine, then the agency engineer who supervised the data collection.

Based on data provided by the plant, agency staff had estimated the tests for benzene, a gas linked to cancer, would find about 0.02 micrograms per cubic meter of air — a relatively small amount. But the actual air sampling revealed benzene levels nearly 50 times as high. It also found three times as much ethylene oxide in the air as estimated.

Similar conditions were found at other plants, but Indorama’s tests showed the worst results.

The public health implications were enormous.

An additional one in every 500 people who lived near the plant for most of their lives was likely to develop cancer from exposure to ethylene oxide, a March 2024 EPA report concluded. That risk is 20 times the 1-in-10,000 level that the E. P. A. typically considers to be the highest acceptable cancer risk when it evaluates carcinogens.

That cancer threat from the Indorama plant could be cut by 95 percent, the E. P. A. found, if better pollution controls were installed.

“There was a sense of urgency,” said Joseph Goffman, who supervised Ms. Shine’s work as the head of the agency’s air office during the Biden administration. “It really alarmed local communities.”

Indorama executives argued that the E. P. A. had gathered samples while the plant was undergoing maintenance, so the results did not reflect normal operations, records show. But when agency inspectors returned in 2024, they still found ethylene oxide leaking in multiple locations and drifting across the facility’s fence line.

A spokeswoman for Indorama declined to address detailed questions from The Times about the plant and cancer risks because they involve continuing regulatory discussions.

“Indorama Ventures recognizes the importance of protecting the health and well-being of our employees, neighbors and surrounding communities,” Patricia Sakamiti, a company spokeswoman, said in a statement.

The test results were a critical factor in the E. P. A.’s approving the new air toxics rules.

Those rules required Indorama and other facilities to limit leaks from valves and upgrade flares so that they could burn off more toxic gases before they were released. The companies also had to install monitors around a plant’s fence line. The results would be publicly posted, letting neighbors see what they were breathing.

The E. P. A. estimated that similar improvements would cost about $440 million to install and $163 million a year to maintain for all affected facilities. That would constitute less than 1 percent of the industry’s national sales.

For that price, millions of people who live near these plants would be at a lower cancer risk, the agency concluded.

Indorama said the E. P. A. had acted “beyond its statutory authority” when it required the fence line tests and that the demands were based on a “flawed risk assessment.” Executives from plants that use ethylene oxide to sterilize medical devices, including the one outside Richmond, joined the protests.

So did companies like U. S. Steel, which operates a facility in Clairton, Pa., near Pittsburgh. The plant bakes coal at up to 2,000 degrees Fahrenheit, turning it into coke, an ingredient in steel making.

U. S. Steel, in a statement at the time, said it was committed to working with the E. P. A. in supporting regulations that were “well grounded in law” and science. “Unfortunately, the 2024 coke rules do not meet these criteria,” it said.

Eleven days into the second Trump administration, Lee Zeldin, the newly sworn-in E. P. A. administrator, received a request from the American Chemistry Council and American Fuel and Petrochemical Manufacturers, the two biggest trade groups for the chemical industry.

They wanted Mr. Zeldin, a former Republican lawmaker, to push the president to give them relief from the Biden-era rules.

The trade associations, in their petition, laid the groundwork for the Trump administration to intervene for national security reasons, arguing that the new requirements could cause them to curb or cease production. “National security includes economic security and protection of domestic production of chemicals vital to public health,” the petition said.

The chemical and medical device industries were also busy writing a flurry of checks to Mr. Trump’s causes.

AdvaMed sent $125,000 to his inauguration fund and $1 million to MAGA Inc., one of Mr. Trump’s campaign affiliates. The latter donation was made on the same day in April 2025 that AdvaMed’s chief executive, Scott Whitaker, attended a candlelight dinner with Mr. Trump at his Mar-a-Lago resort.

“Yes, I met with President Trump and was grateful for the opportunity to introduce our lifesaving industry to him,” Mr. Whitaker said in a statement, adding that ethylene oxide did not come up.

One of the E. P. A. officials who was copied on the request for regulatory relief was Mr. Szabo, a senior adviser who was awaiting confirmation to lead the agency’s powerful Office of Air and Radiation, which oversees regulations intended to curb toxic pollution.

In Mr. Trump’s first administration, Mr. Szabo had served as a White House lawyer, helping review new regulations. But before that term ended, he moved to the lobbying world, representing oil and gas companies, chemical manufacturers and coal-burning electric utilities.

His clients included AdvaMed, and Mr. Szabo secured private meetings with the E. P. A. and the White House through 2024 to help the medical device industry fight the Biden-era changes, records show. Before Mr. Trump’s re-election, Mr. Szabo also helped draft the E. P. A. chapter in Project 2025, the conservative blueprint for a second Trump term.

From his new perch within the E. P. A., Mr. Szabo began participating in gatherings at the agency’s headquarters with former clients and working on the industry’s wish list, according to emails reviewed by The Times.

Brigit Hirsch, an E. P. A. spokeswoman, said in a statement that an ethics agreement Mr. Szabo signed last year permitted him to work on “general” matters that affected various industry players but not “particular” matters that narrowly affected his former clients until one year passed.

E. P. A. officials held at least 40 meetings with chemical industry executives in 2025, agency entrance logs show.

Mr. Szabo coordinated these efforts with two deputies who had joined the E. P. A. after stints in industry: Abigale Tardif, a former lobbyist for the oil refiner Marathon Petroleum and American Fuel and Petrochemical Manufacturers, and Alexander Dominguez, a former American Petroleum Institute lobbyist.

Mr. Szabo also reached out to Emily Underwood, a senior White House lawyer, suggesting that the president could invoke the Clean Air Act exemptions, documents show.

“Thanks Aaron! Can we just see the copy for POTUS’ proposed mention of/remarks on this?” Ms. Underwood responded.

Ms. Underwood, when reached by phone, told The Times that the agency took the lead on these efforts: “The best person to talk to on that would be Aaron Szabo at the E. P. A.”

Mr. Szabo declined to comment. Ms. Tardif did not respond to requests for comment.

The same day that he corresponded with Ms. Underwood, Mr. Szabo appeared before the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee for his confirmation hearing. It was Ash Wednesday, and Mr. Szabo, a Catholic, bore a cross of ashes on his forehead.

Mr. Szabo told senators that he had a personal stake in clean-air rules because he had cystic fibrosis, a lung disease exacerbated by air pollution.

“Growing up, I could feel the impact of poor air quality in my lungs,” he said.

A week later, the E. P. A. created a special inbox to receive requests for waivers from the rules. Companies soon flooded the agency with submissions.

To understand the newfound power of the chemical industry inside the E. P. A., consider a meeting in May 2025 at the agency’s satellite offices in North Carolina.

Nearly a dozen senior chemical industry executives flew in and gathered in a large conference room. Another 30 industry members joined on a video call. The participants represented some of the industry’s biggest players, including Dow, BASF and Huntsman.

The agenda was set by the chemical industry rather than its regulators.

“To provide some structure to our discussions, we prepared the attached agenda,” Leslie Bellas, a vice president for regulatory affairs at American Fuel and Petrochemical Manufacturers, wrote to the E. P. A. team.

The de facto moderator was Brendan Mascarenhas, a lobbyist for the American Chemistry Council, according to meeting minutes and participants.

Industry officials were not shy about their demands then and at follow-up gatherings with E. P. A. officials, the minutes show.

First, they wanted the E. P. A. to rescind its scientific finding that ethylene oxide was much more likely to cause cancer than previously thought. The determination had formed a legal basis for many regulations, and with it gone, the rules would fall like dominoes.

Companies also wanted to roll back requirements for fence line monitors. And in the event of a leak, they wanted to keep plants running longer before shutting down for repairs.

That same month, the chief executives of Dow, Chemours, OxyChem and the American Chemistry Council gathered with Mr. Zeldin at his office in Washington.

Chris Jahn, the head of the chemistry council, wrote on social media afterward that they discussed transforming the E. P. A. so that it focused on “pro-growth policies,” while also “protecting human health and the environment.”

By July 2025, when Mr. Trump had still not granted the waivers, executives grew anxious.

The deadline for the first of the new pollution controls was only a year away, and it would take nearly that long to install the necessary equipment. So the chief executives of Dow, BASF, Eastman Chemical and Huntsman wrote a letter directly to Mr. Trump and shared it with the E. P. A.

“We write to bring to your attention the urgent need for action on requests submitted earlier this year for Presidential Exemptions under the Clean Air Act to provide relief from unnecessary and ineffective obligations imposed by E. P. A.,” they wrote.

Three days later, on July 17, Mr. Trump began answering their pleas.

A series on the Trump administration’s historic weakening of environmental protections, and the resulting increase in air and water pollution.

He issued his first exemptions for 50 chemical plants and 40 sterilizers. His order said that “the current compliance timeline would undermine our national security,” and that the sterilizer rule relied on “technologies that do not exist in a commercially viable form,” even though the breadbox-like enclosures were already in use in some states.

The E. P. A. pointed to Mr. Trump when asked about the exemptions. “This decision was made by the White House, as it is a presidential authority,” Mr. Szabo wrote to one Texas Republican lawmaker.

Then, two of the former lobbyists within the E. P. A. turned to weakening the underlying rules.

One was Ms. Tardif, who had represented the oil refiner Marathon Petroleum in meetings at the E. P. A. as recently as December 2024. In a June 2025 email, an official at American Fuel and Petrochemical Manufacturers thanked her for “productive discussions” about “reconsideration” of the chemical plant rules and copied an official at Marathon.

The other was Mr. Szabo, who asked his staff this spring to strike the same provisions from the sterilizer rule that he had once represented AdvaMed in opposing, including the requirement to install the enclosures.

He delivered an even bigger victory to his former clients by summer.

In a memo dated Aug. 13, E. P. A. staff members warned Mr. Szabo that removing the fence line monitoring requirement for all affected chemical plants would be “difficult to justify” in court. They also noted that the Clean Air Act required the E. P. A. to address “air toxics that pose the greatest potential health threat,” including those tied to cancer.

Despite those warnings, Mr. Szabo issued the order to kill the mandate that same day.

It would be one of Mr. Szabo’s final acts at the agency. This month he resigned and took another job at a law firm that has represented industry groups in their challenges to some of the same Clean Air Act rules.

In Clairton, smokestacks at U. S. Steel’s facility release clouds of steam and chemicals. Thanks to the Trump administration, the plant no longer has to curb some of its toxic emissions, at least for now.

Melanie Meade’s house, in her family for generations, sits on a ridge overlooking the plant. In her backyard, it often smells like rotten eggs or burning rubber, and time outdoors makes her feel lightheaded.

Ms. Meade said she knew she faced an elevated risk of cancer, which killed her older sister and several of her neighbors. But she cannot afford to buy a comparable house elsewhere. So she stays.

A spokesman for U. S. Steel, Andrew Fulton, said in an email that Clairton Coke Works had never been fined for exceeding benzene emissions standards. The company plans to invest up to $2.5 billion in its plants in southwestern Pennsylvania, but none of it will be spent on new pollution controls in Clairton, Mr. Fulton said.

“It would be premature for U. S. Steel or any other regulated company to invest in controls while the rule is under reconsideration,” he said.

In Groves, Texas, which sits adjacent to the Indorama plant, some residents were surprised to learn that Mr. Trump had waived requirements designed to protect their health. Their reactions were mixed.

Chris Borne, the mayor of Groves, appreciates Indorama.

“I have full faith in our facilities where I live,” said Mr. Borne, an electrician who has handled jobs in many of the area’s chemical plants. “Sometimes the rule makers, they go too far.”

Others were angry about the administration’s moves.

“Making things great again — I thought that meant making all things great, including our health,” said Lance Bridges, who voted for Mr. Trump in 2016.

As Mr. Bridges spoke, his 22-year-old daughter pushed a toy scooter carrying his granddaughter in front of their house.

A few weeks later, the Indorama plant had another accidental discharge. Gases started seeping into the community at 6 a. m. on Sept. 11, shortly before students began streaming into school.

State records show that the leak continued for eight hours.

How a Small Student Protest Spread Across France

The New York Times October 24, 2026

Unrest in France

Advertisement

Supported by

A movement that began with a few high schools has broadened to encompass labor unions and other activists.

By Leo Sands

The nationwide unrest in France began with a handful of student demonstrations at high schools in suburban Paris last month.

Now, in cities across the country, antigovernment marchers are protesting expensive living conditions, high fuel prices and conditions in schools. Using the unrest as a smoke screen for vandalism, rioters and looters have also joined in.

With the protests in their second month, the police have arrested thousands, and politicians are divided over how to respond.

Here is a breakdown of what has happened.

Soon after returning from the summer break, students at a high school in the working class Parisian suburb of Créteil staged a protest, according to videos posted to social media on Sept. 18. The high schoolers objected to inadequate resources and high workloads.

Within days, students elsewhere around Paris initiated similar demonstrations. At schools in the capital’s poorest suburbs, students blocked entrances to protest crumbling infrastructure, overcrowded classrooms and what they say are flaws in the admissions system for higher education.

By Sept. 29, the unrest had spread to around 400 schools around the country, according to rally organizers.

The union of high school students said the blockades were a protest against a “lack of teachers and staff, dilapidated schools, overcrowded schedules and classrooms.”

Students barricaded the entrances to some schools with obstacles including e-bikes, while others threw projectiles and set fire to trash cans.

The French education minister, Édouard Geffray, said that some of the students’ demands were “legitimate” but condemned the confrontational nature of their protests. He said that students had chased teachers and targeted school principals with firework-launching tubes.

By the end of September, nearly 80 people had been injured, and the authorities had detained more than 440, including many minors.

Within days, the number of schools engulfed in the protests had doubled. According to the Interior Ministry, by Oct. 2, they had spread to more than 1,000 schools across France, including 220 that were blockaded. University students also began taking part.

Around this time, the authorities said that the protests were mutating from legitimate expressions of educational grievances into something more dangerous, accusing people of shooting mortar-style fireworks, burning public buildings and looting.

By Oct. 2, nearly 400 police officers and over 230 school employees and students had been injured. The number of arrests climbed to 3,000.

The actions widened in October to encompass labor unions, parents and other activists, as different grievances converged into a mass protest.

On Oct. 6, around 256,000 people marched through Paris and 40 other French cities, according to the Interior Ministry. A union of high school students said protesters had occupied some 1,800 high schools.

The protests were mostly peaceful, but a fire was ignited in Lyon, and police officers used tear gas, including in Paris. The total number of arrested rose to 6,000, the authorities said. A major union of French judges and prosecutors and a human rights group accused the police of using disproportionate force, including against children as young as 14.

Two days later, on Oct. 8, smaller demonstrations were staged throughout the country, rallying around 71,500 people. The following week, the Interior Ministry said that 160,000 people joined marches on Oct. 13 across France.

More than half a million people joined 110 antigovernment marches throughout France on Oct. 17, according to an official estimate. A major union, the C. G. T., put the number even higher, at 800,000. Using either count, it was the largest day of protest since the demonstrations began in September.

Many of the marchers were peaceful, but some were not. Around the country, rioters vandalized around 1,500 shops, the authorities said. In Paris, where over 100,000 people marched peacefully, a few hundred rioters faced off against officers. According to the police, the rioters burned cars and smashed storefronts.

In the large town of Limoges, in central France, rioters set fire to the 19th-century City Hall. In a moment captured on video, the building’s spire collapsed in flames.

President Emmanuel Macron appealed for calm after the rioting, some of the most destructive unrest in decades.

In an evening broadcast on Oct. 18, Mr. Macron said that he would seek to lower gas prices. But he also warned, “Those who looted will have to pay back, and those who sought to bring down the Republic will be held accountable.” According to a government tally, rioters had ransacked at least 3,000 businesses over that weekend.

The government ordered curfews beginning on Monday for neighborhoods in several cities, including Paris, Lille and Nice. Other cities, such as Marseille, restricted large gatherings.

Laurent Nuñez, the interior minister, said that the police had been inadequately prepared, and he announced on national radio that he had offered his resignation to Mr. Macron, who had refused it. Mr. Nuñez said that police ranks would be reinforced for this weekend.

Leo Sands is a correspondent for the Breaking News Hub of The New York Times based in London.

How the Most Ruthless Ad of the Midterms Divided Republicans

The New York Times October 24, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The fallout from Vivek Ramaswamy’s brutal spot targeting his Democratic rival in the Ohio governor’s race showed that even in the Trump era, a political attack can be seen as going too far.

By Reid J. Epstein and Campbell Robertson

The most explosive advertisement of the midterm elections has split Republicans and again posed the question of what is fair game for campaign attacks in American politics.

In the days since the leak of the ad from Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican nominee for governor of Ohio, many fellow G. O. P. politicians have denounced, disavowed or distanced themselves from the spot. Yet President Trump and Vice President JD Vance have defended the ad, a remarkably ruthless one even by the standards of modern political campaigns.

The ad features the estranged mother of Mr. Ramaswamy’s Democratic opponent, Amy Acton, calling her daughter a liar and urging Ohioans not to vote for her. Ms. Acton has said that she has not spoken to her mother since she was 12 years old, when she was removed from her mother’s custody after her stepfather was arrested and charged with raping her.

The outrage over the ad’s dark backstory has left Mr. Ramaswamy, a billionaire entrepreneur who exemplifies the anything-goes, attack-at-all-costs ethos of Trump-era politics, at the center of a self-created political firestorm.

The Republican disagreements over the ad show that major figures in the party can still become divided over the rules and red lines of political warfare in the Trump era. And they set the stage for high drama on Election Day in Ohio, a state that has trended solidly Republican in recent years but now has outsize importance in the midterms. The overarching political question is: Will a potential backlash to Mr. Ramaswamy hurt other Ohio Republicans in competitive races, especially Senator Jon Husted, who is trying to fend off a well-known Democratic rival in a vital race for Senate control?

There is now a degree of unpredictability in the state. Campaigns in both parties do not know how voters will react.

Mr. Ramaswamy, who along with his aides declined to be interviewed for this article, said at a campaign stop on Friday that he had no regrets. The ad, he suggested, was his attempt to change the rules of engagement for Republicans in Ohio — just as Mr. Trump has done in Washington.

“What we need is a governor at the top just like President Trump is for our country — a governor for this state who stands strong, who says we will not play on your terms,” he told a crowd in Strongsville, a Cleveland suburb. “We will stand for what we know is right and true, and we will not apologize for it.”

There had been rumblings for weeks in Ohio political circles that Mr. Ramaswamy’s top aides were in touch with Dr. Acton’s estranged mother.

Dr. Acton’s troubled childhood was no secret, and had been the subject of reporting during her high-profile stretch as the pandemic-era health director for Gov. Mike DeWine, a Republican.

Mr. Ramaswamy had been trailing Dr. Acton in many public and private polls. Like other Republicans, he was confronting voter frustration with high gas prices, tariffs and Mr. Trump’s leadership.

Producing the ad was a politically hazardous move for Mr. Ramaswamy, a 41-year-old start-up founder who has shown a high tolerance for risk since he emerged on the scene during his 2024 campaign for president. During that race, he presented himself as a full Trump acolyte and made plenty of enemies with his brash style before placing fourth in the Iowa caucuses, dropping out and endorsing Mr. Trump.

The Ramaswamy campaign was still testing the ad to gauge its effectiveness when the spot burst into public view late Monday.

D. J. Byrnes, a left-leaning local journalist known as the Rooster, published the ad online, calling it “loathsome.”

The spot, which took little time to spread widely online, showed Dr. Acton’s 82-year-old mother, Donna Arthur, using harsh language to denounce her estranged daughter.

“Don’t let her become your governor,” Ms. Arthur said.

The backlash was immediate and intense.

As the controversy swirled, Mr. Ramaswamy reached out privately to other Ohio Republicans to gauge their reaction, according to three people briefed on the exchanges. He felt the coverage by the news media was unfair and wanted a chance to explain his thinking, even if it did not lead to public support for running the ad.

Governor DeWine called the ad “deeply, deeply troubling” and “just plain wrong,” and he urged Mr. Ramaswamy — whom he has endorsed — to take it down. Mr. Husted, who faces his own tight election against former Senator Sherrod Brown on Nov. 3, said he would not have run the ad. Republicans in close races in other states, like Representative Ashley Hinson of Iowa, who is running for Senate, said it should come off the air.

Not only has Mr. Ramaswamy so far declined to back away from the ad, but his campaign also bought more than $4 million in Ohio airtime to show it to viewers.

Supporters of Mr. Ramaswamy echoed his contention that he has been treated unfairly by the news media and argued that there had been no public anger when Dr. Acton’s campaign had attacked him.

“Democrats and the media are trying to change the subject from ‘she’s a liar’ to ‘she was abused as a child,’” Beth Lear, an Ohio state representative from just north of Columbus, wrote in an opinion essay published Friday in The Columbus Dispatch. “It’s a masterful attempt to manipulate voters’ emotions by making Amy a victim.”

The ad served as an attempt to shift the focus of the campaign in its final days from frustrations about Mr. Trump’s economy to a referendum on Dr. Acton’s honesty. But in so doing, it placed Mr. Ramaswamy’s own morals and ethics in the spotlight, and reminded voters that Dr. Acton survived a seriously troubled childhood.

Mr. Ramaswamy has, in a sense, run a political psychology experiment on his home state. Will voters in Ohio be outraged that he has tried to secure a political advantage through a woman estranged from her daughter over allegations of rape, or will they better recall the accusation that Dr. Acton is lying?

“We ran an ad about lying,” Mr. Ramaswamy told the crowd in Strongsville. “Amy Acton is lying. She has been lying this entire campaign about me.”

But at a pumpkin festival on Friday night in Circleville, Ohio, Mr. Ramaswamy’s running mate, State Senator Rob McColley, said the campaign did not believe Dr. Acton was lying about her childhood abuse.

“Oh no, that is horrible,” Mr. McColley said. “We are accusing her of lying in her adult career.”

Dr. Acton’s campaign has almost run out of words to express its disgust over the ad. A spokeswoman, Addie Bullock, has called it “despicable,” “disturbing” and “disqualifying.”

“Ramaswamy will do anything, including embrace child sex predators, to get what he wants,” Ms. Bullock said.

Court documents from Mahoning County, Ohio, back up the descriptions by Dr. Acton and her brother of the events of her childhood. In 1978, when Dr. Acton was 12, her stepfather, Cledith Arthur, was arrested and charged with raping her.

He pleaded not guilty and was indicted by a grand jury, after which Ms. Arthur lost custody of Dr. Acton and her brother. A month later, court records show, Mr. Arthur fled the area, and a warrant was issued for his arrest. The Arthurs appear to have lived the ensuing decades in Pennsylvania, and according to Dr. Acton’s brother, they stayed together until Mr. Arthur died in 2004.

In the campaign ad, Ms. Arthur accuses her daughter of lying about her past but does not address the rape allegations.

It is not clear where Ms. Arthur lives now, and she did not respond to messages this week.

She had been living in her car with some cats in the Calvary Church parking lot, just outside Boalsburg, Pa., according to the Rev. Stacy Sublett, the church’s pastor. Mr. Sublett said that he had tried to find Ms. Arthur permanent housing in the area but that she declined the assistance.

He said he was not aware of friends or family who came to see her.

Jessica Contrera contributed reporting from Akron, Ohio, David DeKok from Boalsburg, Pa., and Kevin Williams from Circleville, Ohio. Kitty Bennett contributed research.

Reid J. Epstein is a Times reporter covering campaigns and elections from Washington.

Campbell Robertson reports for The Times on Delaware, the District of Columbia, Kentucky, Maryland, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Virginia and West Virginia.
